21350-roister-doister-written-probably-a:
Nicholas Udall, master of Eton and then Westminster School, wrote Ralph Roister Doister before 1553. Edward Arber edited this reprint in 1869 from the unique copy at Eton College. The play is counted the earliest surviving English comedy. Its hero is a boastful fool who believes himself irresistible to women.

Matthew Merrygreek, the witty parasite, eggs Roister on to court Dame Custance, who is betrothed to Gawyn Goodluck. A love letter read with the pauses in the wrong places turns praise into insult, the play's most famous joke. Udall built his schoolboy comedy on Roman models, and English drama's comic line starts here.
ady-candle-in-the-dark-1655:
Thomas Ady's Candle in the Dark, published in 1655, is a direct attack on the witch-hunters of his day. Ady was a physician in Kent who had watched trials rest on dreams, spite, and forced confessions. His title promises a small light against a great darkness of error.

He argues that witchcraft prosecutions rest on false testimony and melancholy, the sickness of mind his age mistook for sorcery. Scripture, rightly read, gives no warrant, he says, for hanging old women on such evidence. Ady's lonely protest helped prepare the later English turn against the witch trials.
agrippa-fourth-book-occult-philosophy-16:
Robert Turner puts a pack of rite texts in English in the Fourth Book of Occult Philosophy set, out in London in 1655. The lead text bears Agrippa's name, though sages doubt he writ it. It teaches how to call and bind souls by name, hour, and rite. With it stand Agrippa's Geomancy, the craft of fate by earth marks, and two more famed texts of the art.

Peter de Abano's craft and the Arbatel, a book of bright souls, fill the set. Turner gave English mages their chief store of rite. The book is a grimoire shelf in one.
alan-of-lille-de-fide-catholica-1855:
Alan of Lille was the universal doctor of the twelfth-century schools. He wrote De Fide Catholica contra Haereticos, On the Catholic Faith Against the Heretics, in four books around 1200. The text here is drawn from the Migne Patrologia Latina, volume 210, in its 1855 reprint, and it is in Latin. Alan aimed his book at the Cathars, the Waldensians, the Jews, and the Muslims in turn.

He tries a bold method: to argue from reason and from texts his foes accept, since they scorn his own authorities. The work is the first systematic anti-heretical summa of the schools. Alan's wide reading fills it with authorities marshaled like troops. It shows the classroom arming itself for the age of the Inquisition.
alexander-letter-aristotle-india-1555:
The Letter of Alexander to Aristotle purports to be Alexander the Great's own report on the marvels of India. This text follows the edition of 1555. No one now credits Alexander with it, but the Middle Ages believed every word, and copied it for a thousand years.

The letter describes dog-headed men, headless folk, and giant ants that dig gold. Rivers of fire and trees that speak crowd the march eastward. Such tales seeded the whole medieval monster-race tradition. Mapmakers placed these peoples at the world's edge for centuries. Antiquity's tallest travel tales live here, the cornerstone of a long, strange geography of wonder.
arbatel-of-magick-turner-1655:
Robert Turner's 1655 English translation made the Arbatel of Magick open to English readers for the first time. The Arbatel, whose Latin title means On the Magic of the Ancients, is a Renaissance handbook of spiritual wisdom. Its author is unknown, and its tone is prayerful rather than dark.

The book teaches the Olympic spirits, planetary powers said to govern the ages of the world in long turns. Its short aphorisms join magic to humility, charity, and trust in God, warning the reader against greed and pride. Protestant readers prized the Arbatel as godly magic, and it shaped English occult practice for centuries.
arxiv-2511-20255:
Ahmed, Benito, and Pérez-González unlock particles trapped by interference using rhythmic driving. Their 2025 paper applies Floquet engineering to a flat-band lattice. In the diamond chain, all energy bands are flat. Destructive interference cages particles in tiny regions. That Aharonov-Bohm caging forbids any escape.

Periodic driving at high frequency rewrites the rules. Two tunable quasi-flat bands appear under the drive. One perfectly flat band stays pinned at zero energy. New tunneling paths emerge from drive-induced symmetries. The chain effectively becomes a dimerized lattice. Charge oscillates between opposite boundaries coherently. Those boundary modes carry minimal bulk leakage. Two-particle entanglement can be generated on demand. Experiments could access it with current platforms. The dispersive character cannot be undone by flux alone. Driving is intrinsically responsible for the escape. Flat-band devices become reconfigurable quantum hardware. Spectral fine structure links directly to moving entanglement.
arxiv-2511-20455:
Ashton, Brandstetter, and Mishra chart what a foundation model for fluid flow would cost. Their 2025 paper looks ahead at AI in computational fluid dynamics. Engineers simulate fluids for cars, airplanes, and even blood flow. Today that work is expert-driven and compute-hungry. AI surrogate models promise a new paradigm for the field.

The authors break industrial simulations into core components. They propose the first scaling law built for CFD inputs. It covers both generating training data and training the model. Two regimes emerge from the law's estimates. Sometimes data generation dominates the total compute bill. Other times model training is the expensive part. High-fidelity transient data offers the best route to a foundation model. Concrete public estimates of cost and time are provided. GPU-native solvers must generate datasets far more cheaply. Solvers and learning frameworks should be designed together.
arxiv-2511-20855:
Mohammad R. Tavakol and Wenshan Cai design in 2025 materials that bend light the wrong way, but only in one direction. Negative refraction flips a beam to the same side of the surface normal, a trick hyperbolic materials perform well. The catch is reciprocity: ordinary optics treats forward and backward beams alike. Tavakol and Cai break that symmetry by modulating the material's properties in time at the slab's faces, forming photonic time crystals.

Two devices prove the idea. An optical version stacks AZO and ZnO layers between time-modulated dielectric sheets, and a microwave version uses a wire medium between modulated resistive surfaces. Simulations with a custom solver show isolation above 46 dB for the optical device and 11 dB for the microwave one. Forward beams refract negatively while backward beams are blocked, a route to one-way lenses and shields.
arxiv-2511-21355:
Gaurang Agrawal and Matt Wilson ask whether one of quantum theory's core rules can be proved instead of postulated, in 2025. The generalised Born rule says measurement probabilities come from composing states and effects, and compositional theories of physics usually assume it outright. The authors start from the most naive reading of textbook quantum theory, processes, states, and effects equipped with a probability function obeying only basic compatibility requirements.

Agrawal and Wilson show that any theory with that modest structure is equivalent to one where the generalised Born rule holds exactly, so the rule is forced rather than freely chosen. They then add noise to the theory, modeling realistic imperfection. Noise tightens the link between the theory's internal scalars and true probabilities. It upgrades that link from a bare monoid homomorphism to a semiring isomorphism, a complete match of addition and multiplication on both sides.
arxiv-2511-21455:
Marcus Michelen and Oren Yakir give a cleaner proof of a universality law for random polynomial roots in 2025. A Kac polynomial has random coefficients, independent draws with mean zero and fixed variance. Its roots are known to crowd evenly around the unit circle as the degree grows. Local universality says the roots' correlation pattern is always the same limiting one, even zoomed to the microscopic scale of one-over-n spacing near a fixed point of the circle.

Earlier proofs reached this through the polynomial's logarithmic potential, a heavy detour. Michelen and Yakir instead compare the rescaled polynomial directly with its limiting Gaussian analytic function and push the correlations across with a soft argument. Their proof is self-contained, using only basic complex analysis plus an anti-concentration bound due to Esseen. That bound says a random sum rarely lands too close to any single value.
arxiv-2511-21555:
Diana Singh and her coauthors watch silver memristors light up as they switch on, in 2025. Memristors are resistors whose resistance remembers past current, and silver-based versions can emit light when defects form inside their switching layer. The team studied planar devices where a silver filament grows across a gap, combining electrical stimulation with two optical probes: electroluminescence and photoluminescence imaging.

Singh and her coauthors found that the activation phase fills the gap with fluctuating light signals before any switching occurs. Those fluctuations trace silver clusters being generated, diffusing, and clumping together as they assemble the conductive filament. Strikingly, the optical activity begins before any measurable current flows, exposing ionic and structural dynamics invisible to electronics alone. Once switching starts, the emission settles into the device's working state. The findings show how to control light emission in such devices for future neuromorphic circuits.
arxiv-2511-21955:
Meyer and colleagues build a wireless link for comparing portable optical clocks through open air. Sharing optical-clock precision is hard: microwave links are too coarse, and optical links need precise pointing and clear weather. Their answer is to convert the clock's optical signal into a 90 gigahertz millimeter-wave carrier, which is far easier to beam across free space in all weather and with relaxed pointing.

Their system synthesizes the millimeter waves with a residual timing instability of 2 parts in ten to the fifteenth at one second, improving into the ten-to-the-minus-seventeen range with averaging in their measurements. They then demonstrated a phase-stabilized free-space comparison link over 110 metres, a first of its kind, with one-second instability in the ten-to-the-minus-fourteen region in the reported tests. The main limitation is thermal drift in out-of-loop fibers; kilometer-scale links are next.
arxiv-2511-22055:
Hao, Liang, Lin, and a large team of dental and AI researchers present OralGPT-Omni, the first multimodal large language model specialized for dentistry. General medical vision-language models perform inconsistently and unreliably on dental images and sometimes hallucinate findings, partly because dentistry lacks large expert-annotated datasets. To teach genuine diagnostic reasoning, the team built TRACE-CoT, a chain-of-thought dataset that mirrors how dental radiologists work through cases step by step before concluding.

Training proceeds in a four-stage paradigm combining that reasoning supervision with broad dental image data. Alongside the model, the authors also release MMOral-Uni, a unified benchmark of 2,809 open-ended question-answer pairs across five imaging modalities and five clinical tasks. OralGPT-Omni scores 51.84 overall on MMOral-Uni and 45.31 on the panoramic-radiograph benchmark, dramatically ahead of GPT-5, and the code, benchmark, and models are promised fully public.
arxiv-2512-00655:
Future wireless systems pair huge antenna arrays with high frequencies, creating near-field conditions where wavefronts are curved. Panagiotis Gavriilidis and George Alexandropoulos study sensing-aided near-field beam tracking in 2025. Traditional far-field beamforming models become inadequate when spherical wavefront curvature matters.

The chapter asks how far far-field approximations remain effective for path gain prediction and beam design. Sensing information can help track beams that must follow users through the near field. Getting near-field models right is foundational for the high-capacity links promised by next-generation networks. Near-field effects grow as arrays enlarge, so the questions will only sharpen with time. Beam tracking keeps the link aligned as users move through that near field.
arxiv-2512-00855:
Miikka Kuutila and a large team of software researchers introduce a survey instrument in a 2025 paper. Recent software engineering research stresses sociotechnical questions, how tools and people shape each other. That shift calls for psychometric scales, questionnaires with tested reliability, built for this field.

The team defines technical and sociotechnical infrastructure for software work. They then develop and validate the Software Infrastructure Attitude Scale, which measures how professionals feel about that infrastructure. A validated scale gives future studies a shared yardstick. Researchers can compare teams and firms, and track how attitudes link to outcomes. Teams can also use it to see how people feel about the tools they use each day.
arxiv-2512-01355:
Kisun Lee sets the first cost bounds for a certified path-tracking method. Homotopy tracking follows a solution path from an easy case to a hard one. The Krawczyk test can certify each step as safe. Past work lacked firm bounds on how much work that takes.

Lee gives clear step-size bounds that ensure the test passes. He also bounds the step count by the weighted length of the path. Those bounds cut the cost of interval math in each step. Fewer steps mean faster certified solves for systems that arise in robotics and design.
arxiv-2512-01555:
Johannes Kellendonk and Lorenzo Scaglione study shape traits in one-dimensional non-repeating models. Such models lack a repeating lattice. Their inner degrees of freedom feed protected shape numbers. Links between those numbers are called bulk-edge correspondence.

To handle finite local complexity, they add a step called augmentation. That step extends the models in a controlled way. With it, they trace how inner traits feed each number. The work helps design non-repeating materials with protected edge states for light and chip tools. Augmentation adds room without changing local rules. That trick may serve other non-repeating settings where the numbers resist direct attack.
arxiv-2512-01855:
Zhuang reports beam tests of pre-production timing detectors for the ATLAS upgrade. The High Granularity Timing Detector will join ATLAS for the high-luminosity LHC. It must tame pile-up in the forward region. It also gauges luminosity bunch by bunch. Low Gain Avalanche Detectors form its base.

Beam tests check pre-production sensors before mass build. Timing precision and radiation tolerance are key scores. Passing sensors earn a place in the final detector. The upgrade will let ATLAS sort collisions far denser than today's runs. Forward placement is the hard part, since pile-up is worst where tracks crowd, which is exactly where this detector must perform.
arxiv-2512-02355:
Loops in a space, and when two loops count as the same, form its fundamental group, a basic fingerprint of shape. Fanxin Wu studies in 2025 those loop groups for fixed path-connected Polish spaces from the viewpoint of descriptive set theory, which grades how complex mathematical objects are.

Wu shows that many analytic equivalence relations arise from such loop structures, and that many provably do not. He also studies the free group built over an equivalence relation, a construction linking logic and algebra. The results map a border between topology and set theory that few papers cross deliberately.
arxiv-2512-02555:
Zheng Fang and seven co-authors work on search relevance for online stores, where wording often misleads. Classic term matching, such as BM25, misses meaning when shoppers and sellers use different words. Neural models read meaning better, but they need hard training examples that are scarce within each product domain.

Their system, ADORE, is an autonomous relevance engine built for e-commerce search. It aims to find or build the domain specific hard cases that neural models lack. Sharper relevance means shoppers see products that match intent, and sellers reach buyers who truly want their goods. Each hard case the engine finds makes the next round of search a bit less blind than the last.
arxiv-2512-02655:
Mao-Jun Yan, Chun-Sheng An, and Cheng-Rong Deng revisit a puzzling bump in the meson spectrum, the a1(1420) signal. Mesons are short lived particles whose patterns test the strong force. Some signals may not be plain quark states, but molecules bound from other mesons.

The team assesses axial vector states formed by pseudoscalar and vector meson interactions in coupled channels. Leading order chiral theory drives the interactions, and unitarized amplitudes reveal poles that mark states. Sorting real states from interaction effects sharpens the map of the low lying meson family. Each pole found or ruled out trims the list of forms the strong force can build at low heat.
arxiv-2512-02755:
Charles Creffield and three co-authors shake a lattice model to conjure one of physics' most wanted toy universes. The Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model links superconductivity, black holes, and quantum chaos, yet it resists laboratory realization. Its hallmark is random, all to all interaction between particles.

Kinetic driving, a chosen form of shaking, removes single particle processes in a Hubbard type model. What remains behaves like quasi random all to all coupling. A working recipe would let cold atom or solid state labs test ideas about chaos and gravity on a bench top. A bench top twin of a black hole model sounds wild, but the math match is what labs can check by hand.
arxiv-2512-02855:
Nathanaël Berestycki, Vladislav Guskov, and Fredrik Viklund measure how unlikely shapes arise in a random growth model. The Hastings-Levitov model grows a cluster as tiny particles attach one by one. In the small particle scaling limit, smooth random curves describe the growth.

The authors prove a large deviation principle for this limit. The rate function is the relative entropy of the driving measure in the Loewner-Kufarev equation. Entropy formulas for rare shapes help physicists and mathematicians price improbable patterns in diffusion driven growth, from bacteria colonies to electrodeposition. Rare shapes rule the tails of growth, and tails are where floods, crusts, and clots do their worst harm in the real world.
arxiv-2512-03255:
Sudden changes in a time series can mark key turning points. Federica Spoto, Alessia Caponera, and Pierpaolo Brutti study change point detection in this 2025 work. Their data are functional, meaning each point is a curve, and the process lives on a sphere.

Finding changes fast matters in climate science, economics, and medicine. Changes may be abrupt or gradual and arise from many causes. A method built for spherical functional data fits fields like weather and geophysics. It helps analysts spot shifts in global patterns as they emerge. Sphere-valued data arise in climate and geophysics, where change points mark regime shifts.
arxiv-2512-03555:
Shape optimization can need thousands of costly simulations. Lucie Kubíčková, Ondřej Gebouský, Jan Haidl, and Martin Isoz speed it up in this 2025 work. A global search over component shapes is infeasible when each test is expensive.

Their method pairs multi-objective evolutionary algorithms with deep neural networks. The network's architecture is set on the fly during the search. Learned surrogates replace most simulations, making global search viable. Faster design cycles help engineers in aerospace, automotive, and energy fields. On-the-fly architecture search avoids fixing the surrogate before the problem's shape is known, letting the network grow with the design space.
arxiv-2512-03655:
Yong-Shou Chen proposes treating viruses and hosts as two chaotic systems locked in a measurable duel, in this 2025 solo paper. His V-Reactor Dynamics framework defines a reactivity parameter from replication, immune neutralization, and drug interaction cross sections. The aim is prediction before outbreaks, not after.

That single parameter sorts within-host courses into growth, plateau, and clearance phases. A scaling law ties it to the transmission dynamics governing whole populations. Retrospectively, Chen reports, the model separates SARS-CoV-2's spread from SARS-CoV's lethality and anticipated Omicron waves. Measuring cross sections in vitro could, in his account, price lockdown trade-offs and flag threats preemptively.
arxiv-2512-03855:
The universe's expansion is speeding up, and modified gravity theories try to explain that acceleration without a cosmological constant. Rajdeep Mazumdar, Kalyan Malakar, and Kalyan Bhuyan rebuild one such theory, f(Q) gravity, in a 2025 preprint. Their reconstruction is driven by fractional holographic dark energy, using the Hubble horizon as the theory's infrared cutoff.

The rebuilt model contains a geometric dark energy component and returns to general relativity in the right limit. The authors pin down its free parameters with recent DESI baryon acoustic oscillation data, earlier compilations, and cosmic chronometer measurements, using Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling. The model's expansion history fits observations closely and beats the standard model on several statistical scores. Diagnostics show a smooth shift from deceleration to acceleration, in the quintessence regime. Energy conditions mostly hold, and perturbation analysis confirms dynamical stability.
arxiv-2512-04155:
Most exactly solvable quantum models are closed systems, sealed off from their environment. Zihao Qi and Yuan Xue solve an open one in a 2025 preprint: a dissipative version of the Yao-Lee spin-orbital model, where loss acts on the spin sector. Their trick rewrites the relaxation dynamics as fermions hopping through a doubled space governed by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian.

Strong and weak symmetries of the model protect an exponentially large family of non-equilibrium steady states, making the system a workable dissipative spin liquid. Looking at transient behaviour, the authors find the single-particle spectrum of the dynamics contains an exceptional ring in momentum space, a loop of spectral singularities. As dissipation strengthens, a parity-time symmetry breaks, governing the crossover from oscillatory relaxation to plain decay. The model gives researchers a rare solvable laboratory.
arxiv-2512-04555:
Pritam Kadasi, Abhishek Upperwal, and Mayank Singh present ADAPT, a method that learns how to split a training budget across tasks when tuning language models. Instruction tuning mixes many task kinds, from math to reading passages. Hand-set mix ratios waste tokens on tasks that help little. Their 2025 arXiv paper treats the mix itself as something to learn, under a hard token budget.

ADAPT keeps a live spread of shares across tasks. Meta-gradients nudge the shares toward a smooth worst-case score on held-out checks. Tasks that help get more tokens; the spread cannot collapse onto one task. The team ran three small open models on twenty task types from Natural Instructions. Budgets ran at small slices of the full token pool. ADAPT beat fixed mixes, both even and size-based, on out-of-domain tests. Frugal tuning matters for labs that cannot afford full runs.
arxiv-2512-04755:
Stian Lybech, Daniele Gorla, and Luca Aceto develop a way to prove smart contracts safe even where their code escapes static type checks. Blockchain contracts often use fallback functions, which catch calls that match nothing else and resist ordinary typing. Once deployed, contract code cannot change, so users need assurance before trusting it. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses proof-carrying code: the contract's creator ships a formal proof of type safety, stated through the semantics of types, and users merely check the certificate.

The test bed is TinySol, a distilled form of the Solidity language. The authors give types a meaning through a typed operational semantics. As the concrete payoff, they enforce information flow control and non-interference with security types, so secrets cannot leak through the fallback path. Checked proofs could make untypable but vital contract features safe to use.
arxiv-2512-05055:
Radu Precup and Andrei Stan extend the Nehari manifold method beyond the setting where it was born. The method is a staple of critical point theory, used to find solutions of equations that come from an energy. Many equations of interest, though, have no energy behind them, which puts them outside the method's reach. The authors rebuild the approach for that nonvariational world, where equations are handled as fixed point problems.

Their construction defines a radial energy that plays the role the usual energy plays in the classical case. Solutions found this way are pinned down inside ring-shaped regions between cones, and that localization is what lets the method deliver several distinct solutions rather than one. Two representative applications show the abstract results at work, giving analysts a Nehari-style route into problems that variational methods cannot touch.
arxiv-2512-05155:
Hollis Williams connects two ways of describing how fields twist over surfaces. One is surface holonomy, central to higher gauge theory and string theory's Wess-Zumino terms. The other is nonabelian multiplicative integration, accumulating noncommuting quantities along a surface. In the abelian setting he reads the Stokes law as a statement about curvature obstructing higher holonomy, and follows what that interpretation implies.

From it he derives a global, three-dimensional version of the Stokes relation. He shows it reproduces the familiar Wess-Zumino phase formula. In that formula, the phase difference between two surfaces sharing a boundary is fixed by the integral of a three-form curvature over any volume spanning them. The results give multiplicative integration a geometric meaning in terms of surface holonomy and tie it to the theory of bundle gerbes. Williams closes with extensions to nonabelian gauge theories and links to Wilson surface operators and symmetries.
arxiv-2512-05255:
Linda Bolay and eight co-authors present an algorithm that tracks a satellite battery's charge and health while it flies. Lithium-ion batteries power satellites. Knowing their state of charge and state of health accurately is essential for safe, reliable operation. Yet both quantities drift on very different timescales and cannot be measured directly. The team's method estimates them together, in a nested design.

A physics-based battery model, extended with a degradation model for the capacity lost as a surface film grows, supplies the predictions. Two extended Kalman filters then do the estimating: one follows the fast-moving charge, the other the slow creep of health, with one filter nested inside the other to respect the two timescales. Tested on synthetic data and on in-flight records from the Japanese satellite REIMEI, the algorithm estimates both states adequately and reveals how trustworthy the chosen model is.
arxiv-2512-05555:
Alexey Paznikov and four co-authors remove most of the cost of hunting data races without removing any of the safety. Dynamic race detectors like ThreadSanitizer flag concurrency bugs by instrumenting every memory access, and the resulting slowdown keeps them out of production. Most of those checks guard accesses that are safe, or duplicate a check an earlier one already settled. The authors attack both wastes with compiler-integrated static analysis inside the LLVM-based detector.

Safe accesses lose their instrumentation entirely, with a proof the optimized detector misses no race the original would catch. Redundant classes of checks collapse to one representative each, and a dynamic trick skips instrumentation altogether when only one thread is running. On real applications — caches, databases, a full browser — runtime instrumentation calls fall by as much as nine tenths and programs speed up. The optimizations are on their way upstream into ThreadSanitizer itself.
arxiv-2512-05655:
Filip Tomić, Stefan Tutić, and Milica Žigić construct a new wavelet, a small wave used to split signals by scale. Analysts care how smooth such a wave is, and how fast it and its frequency picture fade away. Smoothness is often measured against Gevrey classes, a graded family of very regular functions. The team's 2025 paper builds a smooth wavelet that lies in a wider, extended Gevrey class, beyond all the classical ones.

Their construction starts from the Lemarié-Meyer wavelet and stretches the support of its low pass filter. The wider support lets them control how the filter decays at a key point. From that control come global decay bounds for the wavelet and its transform. The rates are written with the help of the Lambert W function. The example shows the extended classes are not empty theory. They house concrete, well behaved wavelets that classical classes cannot describe.
arxiv-2512-05755:
Vu Le, Hoa Duong, and Tuan Nguyen ask which Lie algebras behave like injective or projective modules. In module theory, such objects are marked by extensions splitting apart. Lie algebras form a non-abelian category, so extensions can split in two senses, called trivial and semi-trivial. The team works with finite dimensional Lie algebras over a field of characteristic zero.

Their first result reverses a classical theorem of Jacobson: an algebra splits every extension by it, in the trivial sense, exactly when it is complete. The dual hope fails: for every nontrivial algebra, some extension refuses to split trivially, so no projective analogue exists. Restricting to central extensions rescues a dual idea, called cocompleteness, which holds exactly when a certain cohomology group vanishes. Semisimple algebras come out both complete and cocomplete. The team gives algorithms and tables of the small algebras of each kind, up to dimension four.
arxiv-2512-05855:
Bernardo Español and five co-authors give the wanderings of heavy particles in turbulent swirling flows a thermodynamic reading. Particles carried by turbulence do not simply follow the fluid. The team studies their velocity changes across scales, using simulation and laboratory data. Those changes turn out to be consistent with a Markov process through the inertial range: the next step depends on the present state, not the whole history.

A Markov process can be compressed into a Fokker-Planck equation, and the team extracts its drift and diffusion directly from data. The coefficients vary with scale, exposing how inertia filters the turbulence and how bursts of intensity come and go. They also compute entropy produced along each path. Its fluctuations obey the integral fluctuation theorem, and under stated conditions the detailed one too. The work bridges stochastic thermodynamics and particle laden flows.
arxiv-2512-06155:
Caleb Gross reframes the security researcher's oldest problem, where to look first, as a search engine problem. The best researchers are often the best prioritizers. SiftRank ranks targets with a language model. Batches of about ten are ranked listwise, until scores stabilize. Shuffled batches smooth the model's inconsistency.

It needs no first stage retrieval, starting on thousands directly. It found a vulnerability fixing function among two thousand candidates in under two minutes, for under a dollar. No embeddings, no fine tuning, just an API. A cheap ranker could reorder what gets audited.
arxiv-2512-06255:
Shijie Wang and five co authors improve how computers find near matching images, such as two bird species that differ only in beak shape. Most training for this task uses bare class names as labels, which throws away the rich detail packed into those names. As a result, models learn the classes they have seen but cope poorly with new ones.

Their method, LaFG, asks a large language model to spell out the traits hidden in each class name. A second model then checks those traits against images, trims what is missing, and borrows useful traits from close classes to build a shared trait list. From that list the team builds a word portrait for each class, and trains the search model to match it. The aim is search that can tell fine apart classes apart, even ones it never saw in training.
arxiv-2512-06355:
Aurelien Manchon and five co authors work out how fast the orbital motion of electrons in a certain crystal state fades away. In the t2g states of many oxides, an electron's orbit can point in ways that carry useful order, much like spin. Dirt knocks the electron about, the crystal field twists the orbit, and the two effects fight.

Using a method that avoids small step approximations, the authors compute the fade rates for both the simple dipole form of the orbit and its four poled cousin. With weak dirt, each knock chips the orbital order, so the fade time tracks the time between knocks. With strong dirt, the crystal field is averaged out, and the link flips. The two forms of orbital order also drive each other through the crystal field, which makes the response to a fresh injection of orbit rich and tangled.
arxiv-2512-06455:
Matthew Blomquist, Stephane Gaudreault, and Maxime Theillard present Characteristic Bending, a method for moving quantities along with an incompressible fluid, one whose volume never changes. Standard schemes trace each point backward in time to find where its value came from. Errors from the time steps, from sampling, or from a velocity field that is only nearly volume preserving can quietly break that volume rule and warp the result.

Their insight is to treat the backward trace as a reference map between the current shape of the fluid and its start. A projection step then bends that map back to the nearest truly volume preserving one, wiping out the spurious squeezing while keeping mass and fine features. Tests in two and three dimensions, including flows with several phases run by the classic fluid equations, show gains in robustness and accuracy. The method can drop into existing schemes as a direct swap.
arxiv-2512-06655:
Jehyeok Yeon, Federico Cinus, Yifan Wu, and Luca Luceri make AI safety steering smarter by respecting how safety behavior is wired. Sparse autoencoders pull apart a language model's internal activations into features that can be nudged at run time to refuse harmful requests. The standard training treats those features as independent, yet refusal seems to ride on spread out structure across many neurons, not single switches.

Their method smooths the learned directions over a graph of neurons that fire together, so related features share strength. A two gate controller then applies the resulting directions while the model runs. On three safety benchmarks the method raised refusal of harmful requests while keeping refusals of harmless ones low. Swapping it into an existing pipeline on a mid sized open model lifted safety scores by wide margins, and it held up across several model families and under jailbreak attacks.
arxiv-2512-06755:
Rizwan Jahangir and Daisuke Ishii ask whether concrete geometric cycles account for all the abstract classes inside a special cohomology theory for toric varieties. Toric varieties are spaces built from fans, simple fans of cones, which makes their geometry unusually computable. Their intersection cohomology, a refined theory for singular spaces, is known in this case to be especially clean, so its rational classes and its Hodge classes coincide.

The authors state a compatibility between cycle classes built combinatorially, from the fan, and those built geometrically. Their central question is whether the torus invariant combinatorial classes span the whole even degree theory. Assuming that compatibility, they verify the spanning claim for varieties up to dimension three, with the smooth like simplicial case settled outright. A worked non simplicial example in dimension three, computed from classic formulas for toric counts, shows the framework in action.
arxiv-2512-07055:
Nur Fadhillah Binti Rahimi and co-authors time the inner life of a burst of light from atoms packed close together. When excited emitters sit near each other, they can radiate in chorus, a phenomenon called superradiance first framed by Dicke in the nineteen fifties. The team studies the opening moments of that chorus, asking in what order its features arrive: shared coherence, the emission peak itself, and quantum entanglement between the emitters.

Their analysis finds a strict temporal hierarchy. Relative coherence builds first, before the correlated emission reaches its peak. Entanglement then dips to its minimum, and spin-spin correlation reaches its own low point last. The ordering suggests enhanced coherence is the forerunner that makes the joint flash possible. When spin correlations fade to nothing, entanglement and correlated emission become linked in time.
arxiv-2512-07355:
Alexandre Rocchi, Thomas Fel, and Gianni Franchi reconcile two schools of thought about what a concept is inside a neural network. One school builds models around human-labeled concepts, insisting the machine reason through named ideas. The other trains sparse autoencoders and lets concepts emerge on their own, then struggles to say whether the discoveries mean anything. The authors show both are doing the same geometry: each learns a set of directions in activation space. And the allowed concepts are the nonnegative mixtures of those directions, a cone.

Supervision and sparsity then differ only in how the cone gets chosen. That shared picture builds a bridge: human-defined concept models supply reference cones, and an autoencoder can be graded by how well its cone approximates or contains them.
arxiv-2512-07955:
E. Cataldi, F. Belfiore, M. Curti, and many co-authors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on cosmic chemistry. The James Webb Space Telescope can now read the gas of very distant galaxies. Nitrogen, set against oxygen, records how those galaxies built their elements.

The sample spans hundreds of star-forming galaxies across cosmic time. Faint auroral lines in the deepest spectra give direct temperature-based abundances. Those anchor the first high-redshift calibrations of strong-line nitrogen diagnostics. One common diagnostic drifts mildly with era; another shows no clear drift. The team then charts nitrogen against oxygen across the full sample. Distant galaxies carry systematically more nitrogen at fixed oxygen than nearby ones. The excess grows stronger in the most metal-poor systems they measured. Bursty star formation and uneven metal loss are candidates. The work gives the most extensive confirmation yet of early nitrogen enrichment.
arxiv-2512-08055:
Honglian Wang, Haoyun Chen, and Aristides Gionis, computer scientists who study networks, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is PageRank, the classic algorithm that ranks the importance of nodes in a network from its link structure. They ask how PageRank can be made fair across groups without rebuilding the network itself.

Their approach reweights the transition probabilities on existing edges, leaving the network topology and restart vector untouched. They define a fairness loss between the actual group wise PageRank distribution and a target one, with a group adapted notion that accounts for homophily. Because the loss is not convex, they use projected gradient descent to find locally optimal edge weights. In tests, tiny changes to the transition matrix improved fairness a great deal against strong baselines. That makes the method attractive where adding edges or redesigning the network is not an option.
arxiv-2512-08355:
M J Plank, M Sushames, T Fisher Taylor, and colleagues, modelers in New Zealand and the United Kingdom, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They model pandemic response choices, where governments must pick between mitigation, suppression, and elimination with little information. Each option trades health harm against the economic cost of the controls themselves, and most earlier models counted only the health side.

Their framework counts both costs together and compares the three strategies across many disease and economic settings. For mild diseases, mitigation usually came out cheapest overall. For severe diseases, suppression won when spread was relatively slow, while elimination won when spread was fast. They anchor the model with New Zealand elimination response to COVID 19 in 2020, which the estimates placed near the point where elimination beats mitigation. The authors offer the framework as decision support for future pandemics, while noting that population differences still need adding.
arxiv-2512-08555:
Gilles Poncelet, Jonathan Lambrechts, Thomas Gillis, and Philippe Chatelain, computational scientists in Belgium, posted a methods paper on arXiv in December 2025. They present a solver for the Poisson equation, a workhorse of physics simulation that often eats most of the computing time in fluid flow studies. Their solver lives inside a framework that adapts grid resolution to where the action is.

The design mixes two ideas: multigrid, which attacks errors at several scales at once, and a Fourier based direct solver, which grants freedom in the boundary conditions. Any mix of unbounded and half bounded directions can be handled, the case many solvers avoid. Compact stencils keep accuracy up while cutting data exchange. Tests against exact solutions confirm the method, which scaled cleanly to more than sixteen thousand processor cores on leading European supercomputers. For open flows like wakes and plumes, that combination is valuable.
arxiv-2512-09355:
Junru Zhou, Yicheng Wang, and Pan Li study learning to branch, a machine learning approach to a key decision inside mixed-integer programming solvers. At each step the solver must choose which variable to branch on, and graph neural networks can learn that choice. Ordinary message-passing networks are fast but theoretically limited, while higher-order networks are powerful but far too slow.

The authors examine subgraph networks as a middle ground. They prove a sharper theory result: node-anchored subgraph networks, whose expressive power is strictly below a known benchmark, already suffice to approximate the strong branching scores solvers aim for. Practice tells a different story. On four benchmark datasets, the subgraph networks' cost per node created memory bottlenecks and slower solving than simpler networks and heuristics. The authors conclude that, for now, extra expressivity costs more than it earns, and future work must preserve efficiency.
arxiv-2512-09555:
Yuan Li and colleagues diagnose why vision-language models give unreliable quality judgments for photographs. Blind image quality assessment asks a model to score an image with no reference picture. Vision-language models seem ideal, since they can describe features and reason in words, but their descriptions often contradict their final scores. Scores also wobble between runs in ways human judgment does not.

The authors trace the problem in two steps. First, the predictions are weakly grounded in the visual features the model generated, so the reasoning chain is loose. Second, decoding the model's intermediate layers shows it leans on a set of candidate tokens, which drives instability. Their fix is a two-stage tuning method that separates seeing from judging: first the model learns features, then it infers quality from those features alone. On datasets the method cut instability nearly in half and improved agreement with human scores.
arxiv-2512-09855:
Andrew J. Shepherd, Daniel J. Blumenthal, and Ryan O. Behunin develop a theory of noise in large Brillouin lasers built on photonic chips. Such lasers serve precision tasks from atomic timekeeping to low noise microwave generation and quantum sensing. Making the resonator longer raises power and steadies the frequency, but then several optical resonances fit inside the Brillouin gain band. Existing models assume a single mode, so they cannot describe this regime. The authors build a coupled mode theory that allows many cavity modes to lase at once.

From the theory they derive the steady state behavior, the spontaneous spectrum, intensity noise, and frequency noise. The broad gain band produces unusual dynamics, with distinct features in the noise spectra that shift the standard fundamental linewidth. The analysis also shows that noise transferred from the pump laser can significantly widen the linewidth when phase matching is not ideal.
arxiv-2512-10555:
Gregory Nordahl, Rebekka Klemmt, and Espen Bøjesen clean up noisy data from four-dimensional scanning transmission electron microscopy, a technique that records a diffraction pattern at every point of a scan. Their trick is to record several sparse electron event patterns at each position, adding a local time dimension and turning the data into an effectively five-dimensional set.

Two cleaning pipelines are offered. One clusters the events with the DBSCAN algorithm and then applies multi-step thresholding based on persistence, while the other uses sparse principal component analysis with a single thresholding step. On simulated and real data, the cleaned images reached the same quality as raw data at a small fraction of the exposure, which means less damage to the sample. Defect detection grew far more sensitive to tiny shifts, and the method can also track how a material degrades under the beam.
arxiv-2512-11255:
Francesco Innocenti and El Mehdi Achour sharpen the theory of how transformers learn from cases placed in their input, a skill called in context learning. A recent result showed that an abstracted transformer block acts as if it were quietly updating its own feedforward weights based on the context it reads. That picture came from simplified models and settings.

The authors give a simpler proof that also generalises the result in three directions. It covers every sequence position rather than only the last, and deeper blocks rather than only the first. It also covers lifelike blocks that include normalisation layers. Tests on simple in context regression tasks confirm the theory. They also trace how the implicit updates from varied tokens relate within and between blocks. The work brings a promising explanation of in context learning closer to real architectures.
arxiv-2601-06655:
George Pasparakis and six co-authors guess shock states of stuff with far less data in 2026. A shock curve lists the states a stuff reaches when hit by a shock. Each point on that curve has cost a pricey run on a large machine.

Their frame is a chance-based curve fit bound by the laws of shocks. It learns from just a few runs and fills in the rest of the curve. A chance form of a Taylor sum builds the fit at its core. Jump rules at the shock front shape the fit so it stays true to the laws. The fit thus honors heat laws, not just the dots on a graph. Labs that study blasts and impacts can stretch small budgets much more. The way is built for work where each run costs a great deal.
arxiv-2601-07255: A team led by A. von Ungern-Sternberg Schwark posted a 2026 arXiv paper on a crystal called SmNiC2. The team asks how two states of the crystal act on each other. One is a wave in the charge of the crystal. The other is a state where the crystal acts as a magnet. A link through the shake of atoms in the grid ties the two states. The team probes the crystal with X-ray scattering. They add Raman spectroscopy, which reads shifts in light bounced off the crystal.
arxiv-2601-07655:
Lea Enzi and Stefan Thonhauser ask when an insured person should report a claim at all. Their 2026 preprint studies optimal claim reporting inside a bonus-malus insurance system. In such a system, reporting a claim moves the customer to a higher-premium class. Staying claim-free for a set period moves them down to cheaper premiums. Small claims may therefore cost more than they pay.

The authors model the contract as two regimes with transitions between them. The customer must weigh a payout now against years of higher premiums. Solving for the optimal rule gives a threshold for when reporting pays. The analysis serves actuaries who design bonus-malus schemes. It also explains rational customer behavior that insurers observe, such as hiding small accidents.
arxiv-2601-08055:
Daniil Karuzin, Zhiyu Dong, and Leonid Levitov study paired electrons in flat, curved electronic bands. Their 2026 arXiv paper starts from odd superconductivity found in rhombohedral graphene. They ask what bound states form when bands carry Berry curvature, a geometric twist in electron motion.

The authors solve a two-body problem and find chiral bound states with nonzero angular momentum. These are not the usual round s-wave pairs. With a Fermi sea present, the same forces lead to chiral pairing and several superconducting phases. Those phases break time-reversal symmetry, so the work links band geometry to new kinds of superconductivity.
arxiv-2601-08155:
Inpyo Song and four co-authors tackle explainable video anomaly detection with spatial grounding. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that anomaly detection matters for safety-critical uses. Yet many systems give explanations that cannot be checked against the video itself.

The gap grows in scenes with many interacting entities. Existing methods often produce incomplete or visually misaligned descriptions there, which lowers trust. The team proposes instance-aligned captions, where each caption ties to a specific object in the scene. Aligned captions let users verify what the system claims it saw. That verifiability is the point: an explanation should point at evidence, not float free.
arxiv-2601-08955:
Youwei Liu and four co-authors teach agents to look ahead in a fake world before they act. A world model is a learned sim of how a place changes when an agent acts. With it, an agent can plan with no risk to the real place. Past use was short: one step, or a fixed span of steps, no more.

Their method is called Imagine-then-Plan. The agent shifts its look span to fit the task at hand. Hard tasks get a long look. Easy tasks get a short one. A reader who builds agents gets a plan rule that bends with need. It may lift task scores while it keeps sim cost in check.
arxiv-2601-09455:
André Artelt, Martin Olsen, and Kevin Tierney study how hard it is to compute certain explanations of model decisions. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats counterfactual and semi-factual explanations in explainable AI. A counterfactual says what change would flip a decision; a semi-factual says what could change while the decision stays.

Clear explanations are essential when models are used in high-stakes settings. The authors bring complexity theory to the question, asking which explanation tasks are tractable at all. Hardness results draw a map of where explanation tools can be fast and where they cannot. That map helps practitioners pick explanation types their systems can actually deliver.
arxiv-2601-10255:
Jorge Olmos-Trigo sets an exact rule for how small grains bend light when a field is near. Such grains are named nanoparticles. Past rules bound how they can take and scatter light. Those rules are firm for plain and mixed grains. Magneto optical grains had no such rule.

These grains shift how light acts when a field is on. Olmos-Trigo works out the exact law for them. It covers grains with a line of symmetry. It holds for any light and any field. The law sets hard caps on what such grains can do. That guides the design of light tools at tiny scale.
arxiv-2601-10355:
Zhihao Xu and co authors mine text for fake tool use paths to train agents. An agent must learn to call tools in long chats. Real paths of such calls are hard to get. They are vast in kind and cost much to mark by hand. That gap slows agent work.

The team made a text based path to forge them. Plain text holds rich tales of tool use. From those tales, they forge paths that act like real runs. The paths span many tasks and tools. Models can then train on the forged paths. The aim is agents that learn tool use at scale.
arxiv-2601-10455:
Ruochen Li and co authors rethink how surgical plans by AI are graded. A plan for surgery must mix sight, long chains of thought, and craft facts. It is not clear that grades today test that mix well. A bad grade can pass a bad plan, or fail a sound one.

The team set a goal based test. A plan is right if it meets the goal of each phase. Goals are set by pro rules for each step of the craft. The tool is named SurgGoal. It checks if the goal is met, not if the words match a key. That is a more true test for safe use.
arxiv-2601-10655:
Carlo Cafaro and James Schneeloch take a symmetry-based look at quantum search. The continuous-time form of Grover's search uses a fixed Hamiltonian, an energy rule that steers the system. The search path stays inside a flat plane spanned by the start and target states. Within that plane, the motion has a clean shape.

The authors note a sharp limit: the search fails when start and target states are orthogonal, at right angles in state space. They frame the dynamics through Schrödinger's equation between such states. The view clarifies why some searches stall before they start. It gives quantum algorithm designers a geometric check on when Hamiltonian search can work.
arxiv-2601-10755:
Richard Evan Schwartz writes a personal, hands-on account of Boy's surface. Boy's surface is a famous immersed copy of the projective plane in three-dimensional space. It twists through itself in ways that defy easy mental pictures. Schwartz admits his own past tries to grasp it faded fast. The image would form, then slip away without a trace.

His paper is a fresh attempt to build the surface and hold it steady. The tone is that of a working geometer thinking aloud. Readers get both the construction and an honest record of struggle with a classic object. It suits anyone who has met a math shape that refuses to sit still in the mind.
arxiv-2601-11155:
Harald Garcke, Kei Fong Lam, Robert Nurnberg, and Andrea Signori model protocell growth. Their 2026 preprint uses a Mullins-Sekerka model with reactions. Protocells are simple cell-like drops from before true life. How they grew and split is a core puzzle of early life.

With reactions in play, drops can grow in the model. A grown drop can lose stability and then divide. The cycle of grow, split, grow can then repeat. Such cycles give chemical compartments, tiny walled spaces for reactions. Living systems rely on such compartments to stay organized. The team tests stability of the cycle and runs numeric trials. That checks when the grow-and-divide loop can hold up.
arxiv-2601-11255:
Yuling Shi and six coauthors improve search-based answers to hard questions. Their 2026 preprint is on multi-hop question answering with RAG. Multi-hop questions need facts chained across more than one source. Retrieval-augmented generation pulls texts in to help a model answer.

Most current methods let the model guide its own search path. The model plans each step and writes the next query. That self-guidance can break the chain of thought midway. Poor splits of the question let errors grow from step to step. The team's tree-based reasoning aims to hold the chain firm. A tree can keep more than one path in play at once.
arxiv-2601-11355:
Jagadis Nayak, Aviad Frydman, and Gopi Daptary join two exotic materials. Their 2026 preprint links a topological insulator to a disordered superconductor. The insulator is BiSbTeSe2, a known surface-current material. The superconductor is amorphous indium oxide, a messy film.

The pair forms a hybrid interface for the tests. Resistance and temperature runs show superconducting signs at low heat. The signs persist when the oxide sits in an insulating state. That hints that superconducting links survive the disorder. The effect is called proximity-induced superconductivity in the work. Such hybrids probe how surface states and pairing interact. They may guide designs for fault-tolerant quantum parts.
arxiv-2601-11555:
Triloki Nath, Manohar Choudhary, and Ram Pandey extend the Heron problem. Their 2026 preprint defines a generalized k, m Heron problem. The classical Heron problem seeks a shortest total path. A point must touch given sets with least summed distance.

The new form uses k feasible sets and m target sets. All sets are nonempty, closed, and convex in n-space. The task seeks an optimal configuration among them all. Optimality conditions state when a configuration cannot improve. An algorithm computes the optimum under those conditions. Heron-type tasks arise in facility siting and path design. More sets make the model fit real networks better.
arxiv-2601-11755:
Wenjing Chen, Yixin Chen, and Victoria G. Crawford study fair picks from large sets. In many tasks, data split by kind into groups that do not overlap. A good pick must stay fair or balanced across those groups, not just score well as a whole.

They build methods with two goals at once for this cover task. One goal is a good score, and the other is to meet the group rules well. Such two-goal methods are called bicriteria in the field. The work gives a way to trade a bit of one goal to gain much in the other, with proof of the bounds.
arxiv-2601-12055:
Lina Meyer, Felix Wissel, Tobias Knopp, and their co-authors set key choices for a label-free image cleaner in an automatic way. The cleaner, deep image prior, needs no training set. Its skill rests on net form and on when to stop its steps.

Tuning those choices by hand for each new image is slow. Their tool moves choices from past, like images to new ones. The test case is fluorescence microscopy, used in cell labs. Fast auto-tuning could let the cleaner run on large image batches.  Auto picks could also cut hand work for lab staff.
arxiv-2601-12155:
Xiang Gao, Xinmu Wang, Yuanpeng Liu, and their co-authors rebuild 3D objects from images with help from topology. Rebuilding is ill-posed, since shape, look, and topology can each be read in many ways from flat views. High-genus objects, with many holes, are the hard case.

They add persistent homology priors to inverse rendering. Those priors pin the hole count and shape class while views fit the rest. A firm topology prior can stop smooth but wrong rebuilds. The work targets meshes for design and scans.  High genus shapes test the prior more than plain shapes.
arxiv-2601-12355:
Beicheng Xu and four co authors aim to make machine learning easier for non experts. A key task is to pick a good algorithm and tune its settings. That joint task is known as the CASH problem. Tools that solve it can spare users a long trial and error search.

One classic tool is Bayesian optimization, but it can start cold with no good first guesses. Large language models can help here, since they bring prior sense of what may work. The team blends the two in a method called LB-MCTS. The mix is meant to make the search both fast and well guided from the start.
arxiv-2601-12855:
Yao Dong, Xin-Yao Huang, and Guo-Feng Zhang demonstrate nonreciprocal light transmission in an optomechanical system. Nonreciprocity means light passes one way but not the reverse. Their platform is driven by three mode parametric interactions. It handles both intense classical fields and weak quantum signals.

The platform is modular and reconfigurable. Each three mode optomechanical system serves as a fundamental building block. A single block already achieves nonreciprocity for classical fields. One way light control is key for isolators and circulators in photonics. Extending it to quantum signals serves quantum networks. Blocks that combine could build larger nonreciprocal devices on demand.
arxiv-2601-12955:
Premashis Kumar, Massimiliano Esposito, and Timur Aslyamov sort the ways a classic chemical model can go unstable. The model is the Brusselator, a toy system of two chemicals that react and spread. Their form of it is nonideal and keeps honest books on heat and energy. It adds the push and pull between molecules in both the spread and the reactions.

They then recheck a known scheme that sorts such instabilities into types. For each type, they ask if it can occur in this stricter model, and what it looks like. Push from entropy and pull from energy trade off to pick the winner. Spots, stripes, and waves in real chemicals start from such instabilities. A model that keeps its physics honest gives forecasts users can trust more.
arxiv-2601-13355:
Tawfiq Ammari and Samantha Gilgan study how folks with misophonia meet tech that can set off their traits. Misophonia is a state where set sounds, or cues tied to them, spark strong ill feels. It is still poorly known in clinics, yet it can shape a whole day.

The team ran sixteen semi structured talks with folks in the United States who live with it. They ask how such folks use, shun, or bend tech that boosts their trigger sounds. Shun is a key act, a form of non use by design. For tech teams, the finds call for sound picks and mute paths that do not force a hard pick of all or none.
arxiv-2601-13455:
Mohamed Moussadek Maiza builds a deformation theory that turns quasi Poisson forms into Poisson forms, and links it to 2D field theory. A deformation eases one math form into a next by a smooth path. His path starts with Hamiltonian quasi Poisson manifolds, a loose form used in gauge work.

It ends with Hamiltonian Poisson manifolds, the firm form, with worn cases let in. The theory also spans singular cases that spring from symplectic implosion, a cut down of a gauge space. Maiza shows the imploded cross section of a double deforms to the implosion of a cotangent form. Such bridges let tools proved on one side cross to the next.
arxiv-2601-13855: Jan Moser works on Jacob's ladders, a tool tied to the zeta function and prime counts, in work that assumes the Riemann hypothesis. The focus is the Ingham integral from 1932 and the point where its remainder term meets the Fermat-Wiles theorem. Moser proves that some increments of the integral exist with special traits. They yield new functionals and new forms of that famed theorem. The paper also adds fresh puzzles on sets of integrals.
arxiv-2601-14055:
Andrea Protani and co-authors locate brain tumors in multi-modal MRI with a new graph method in 2026. Modern vision backbones for 3D medical imaging process dense voxel grids. They use parameter-heavy encoder-decoder structures to rebuild space in detail. That design spends many parameters on spatial reconstruction rather than feature learning.

Their SVGFormer is a decoder-free pipeline for the task. A content-aware grouping stage partitions the volume into a semantic graph of supervoxels. Supervoxels are small, like-minded chunks of the scan. A graph neural network then reasons over that graph to find the tumor. Leaner models could scan faster while keeping accuracy.
arxiv-2601-14255:
Sangbeom Lim, Seoung Wug Oh, Jiahui Huang, and their co-authors present VideoMaMa in this 2026 paper. The topic is video matting, the task of cutting a subject out of each frame with soft, exact edges. The output is an alpha matte, a map of how clear each pixel is. Good matting models are hard to train for real-world clips.

The main block is a lack of labeled data. VideoMaMa starts from coarse segmentation masks, rough maps of where the subject is. It turns them into pixel-exact mattes. To do so, it draws on pretrained video diffusion models, which bring strong prior knowledge of how real scenes look and move.
arxiv-2601-14555:
Botong Ou and Baijian Yang work on Internet of Things security in this 2026 paper. IoT connectivity keeps expanding and brings quality-of-life gains around the world. It also introduces growing privacy and security concerns. One root problem is a lack of clear definition for managing shared and protected access to IoT sensors.

Without that definition, channels open by which devices can be compromised and sensitive data leaked. The authors present a WebAssembly based portable and secure sensor interface. WebAssembly gives a sandboxed, portable runtime for sensor access code. Readers get an interface design meant to let many apps share sensors without opening the door to leaks.
arxiv-2601-14755:
Lei Xie, Peilan Wang, and Guanxiong Shen study secure wireless links in this 2026 paper. They investigate movable antennas as a way to enhance physical layer security. The setting is a MIMOME system: multiple-input, multiple-output, with a multiple-antenna eavesdropper. Movable antennas can shift position to favor the true receiver over the eavesdropper.

The scenario is practical. The transmitter has imperfect eavesdropper channel state information. It knows only the instantaneous line-of-sight component, plus the statistical properties of the non-line-of-sight component. In plain terms, secrecy must hold with partial knowledge of the spy's channel. The work is a design, not a test on live air. It shows what can be kept safe when facts are thin. Readers get a security design that works under that honest limit.
arxiv-2601-14955:
Hanqi Jin, Gaoming Yang, and co-authors study how shoppers behave on e-commerce sites. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with recommendation, the art of guessing what a user wants next. A shopper may click, save, add to cart, or buy an item.

Each act means something different. The shifts between acts say a lot about intent and changing taste. The authors build a model that tracks these behavior sequences. A graph attention network in the model is made fully aware of the shifts between one small act and the very next act.
arxiv-2601-15055:
Isaac Baglin, Xiatian Zhu, and Simon Hadfield attack federated learning from a fresh angle. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with deep leakage, where a foe rebuilds private data from shared model updates. Most defenses try to block that rebuild.

The usual guards add noise, scramble data, or encrypt it. Yet they can still leak broad facts, such as class mixes or feature patterns. Strong denoising attacks often break them in the end. The authors present SpooFL here, a novel spoofing approach that takes a quite different path from pure blocking alone.
arxiv-2601-15255:
Prithak Bhattarai, Andrew Brandt, and a large collaboration lay out the design of a new accelerator experiment. Their 2026 arXiv white paper presents DAMSA, short for Dark Messenger Searches at an Accelerator. The experiment uses a short baseline at an accelerator site.

DAMSA hunts for short-lived processes in particle physics. Its targets include signs of a dark sector, a hidden family of particles. It also seeks well-motivated signals inside the standard model itself. As a conceptual design paper, the text sets out the detector, the main goals, and the physics case.
arxiv-2601-15355:
Anuj Bathla, Subrat Kumar Pradhan, and a large team photograph electric current inside a diamond transistor. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with field-effect transistors built on hydrogen-terminated diamond, layered with hexagonal boron nitride. Seeing the current's path helps engineers judge the device.

The team uses wide-field quantum diamond microscopy for the image. Nitrogen-vacancy centers inside the substrate act as tiny magnetic sensors. Their readings map the magnetic field of the flowing current. From that map, the team reconstructs how current moves through the transistor while it runs live in the lab.
arxiv-2601-15455:
Patrycja Balik, Szymon Jędras, and Piotr Polesiuk revisit a landmark algorithm from programming language theory. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the 1991 work of Jouvelot and Gifford. That work gave an algebraic way to reconstruct types and effects in a program.

A type-and-effect system tracks what a program returns and what side effects it may cause. The 1991 algorithm is a milestone in that area. It has inspired much later work in static analysis. The authors offer remarks on its algebraic structure, clarifying the firm foundations the classic 1991 algorithm rests firmly on.
arxiv-2601-15755:
Tristan Williams, Franziska Weeber, Sebastian Padó, and Alan Akbik critique how aligned language models are judged in a 2026 arXiv paper. Models are often steered to match the opinions of demographic groups. Most checks compare marginal response distributions. Each survey item is treated on its own. Matching item-by-item averages is essential, the authors grant. It may still miss deeper structure.

Real populations hold latent patterns that tie answers together. Cultural values theories describe exactly those patterns. A model can match every single item yet miss the whole worldview. The authors build a framework to test representativeness beyond marginals. For anyone using models as stand-ins for public opinion, that deeper check is the difference between a poll and a caricature.
arxiv-2601-15955:
Stacey Alberts and a large team present mid-infrared survey data in a 2026 arXiv paper. The data are part of JADES Data Release 5. They come from JWST's Mid-Infrared Instrument, MIRI, in coordinated parallel observations. The fields are GOODS-S and GOODS-N. Medium to ultra-deep mid-infrared imaging is reframing views of the early universe, the authors note. It reveals ultra-red dusty galaxies and quiet, quiescent ones.

The view extends to the epoch of reionization and the first galaxies. Mid-infrared light shows what near-infrared views miss. Dusty systems hide at shorter wavelengths. Coordinated parallels gather data while another instrument leads, doubling the science per hour. Data release papers document these sets so the whole community can use them well.
arxiv-2601-16355:
Suhong Moon and four coauthors study self, joint work and frame shifts in groups. Their 2026 preprint mixes real folk and fake folk in group games. Games are of the social trap type, where self gain clashes with group gain. Human acts rest on both clear thought and self and frame cues. The team asks if large models fake those human acts well.

They test model acts next to real acts in the same games. Like acts would back use of models as test folk. Split acts would mark where fakes break from real thought. The work helps teams judge sims of group life. It ties self cues to joint work scores.
arxiv-2601-16755:
Rohit Gheyi and a team of five co-authors hunt build flaws that hide in rare setups. Big software can switch parts on or off by flags. Some mixes of flags break the build at compile time. Tests oft miss those rare mixes. Their 2026 preprint pairs big AI models with this hunt.

The models scan code with its flag rules in view. They flag mixes that are apt to break. They then draft fixes for the breaks they find. This could save teams from late, costly build shocks. It suits cars, phones, and cloud tools with many flag paths.
arxiv-2601-16955:
Roman Poletukhin, Marcel Kollovieh, Eike Eberhard, and Stephan Günnemann build 3D molecules from stiff parts. Most AI builders place atoms one by one. Drug work oft thinks in chunks, not lone atoms. Their 2026 preprint treats chunks as stiff blocks. Each block keeps its shape as the build goes on. Flows then place the blocks in 3D space.

Their frame grows from frame-based work on proteins. It now serves plain molecules of all sorts. Block builds keep known good chunks whole. That speeds the hunt for new drugs and stuff. Labs can screen block-built forms for worth.
arxiv-2601-17355:
Yi Lyu, Shichun Yu, and Joe Catudal present Safeguard, a security layer for software defined networks. Such networks let apps set and change policy at line speed. Data can drive those changes as needs shift. That speed is a gain, but it holds a risk. Bad or odd data can push policy too far. Over-correction can cause harm no one meant.

Safeguard puts security controls at the network layer itself. Controls watch for shifts that go past safe bounds. The goal is fast change without loss of grip. Network teams gain a guard that moves at the same pace as policy. The work fits a world where networks re-shape themselves in real time.
arxiv-2601-17455:
Sagar Mahapatra and co-authors study a disordered crystal with a long chemical name, BaCu one-third Ta two-thirds O3. Copper ions carry spin one-half. They share a pseudo-cubic lattice with tantalum at random. X-ray tools map the local disorder in detail. They show tight structural limits on magnetic exchange paths. No magnetic order or spin freezing shows down to 0.1 kelvin.

That calm points to emergent random spin singlets. Spins pair up in random bonds rather than one set pattern. Such states test theories of quantum magnetism. They may host traits sought for new materials. The work shows how disorder can create order of a new kind. It guides hunts for like states in kin compounds.
arxiv-2601-17555:
Justin Downes, Sam Saltwick, and Anthony Chen use image salience to compress satellite photos. Satellites gather hundreds of terabytes of images each day. Storage and bandwidth costs climb with that flood. Most users care about small regions of each image. The rest can be stored with less detail. The authors preprocess images by salience to guide compression.

Saliency marks the parts viewers and tasks need most. Sharp storage there, lean storage elsewhere, saves space. Savings let archives keep more scenes in reach. They also speed image transfer to field teams. The industrial paper targets real pipelines. It weighs quality where it counts, not pixels in the abstract.
arxiv-2601-17655:
A. Madhav Sai Kumar and co-authors study instabilities in drying colloidal films. When suspensions dry, particles deposit in complex patterns. Cracks and delamination often spoil the film. The team tests sessile droplets with silica nanoparticles. They vary particle surface charge and substrate wettability together. Both traits shape how the drop dries.

They track evaporation dynamics and final deposit shape. Crack patterns are part of the record. Coupled effects matter because real coatings vary both at once. Paints, inks, and printed films all face these flaws. Knowing which mix cracks worst guides better formulas. The study gives makers a map of charge and surface effects.
arxiv-2601-17855:
Zixi Chen and co-authors name a hidden waste in how large language models are served. Their 2026 preprint reports that over forty percent of compute power can be lost to load imbalance. The loss is not a hardware limit. Serving systems run workers in lockstep, and each step waits for the slowest worker. Workloads differ and shift, so stragglers keep appearing while fast workers sit idle and draw power.

The authors propose a universal load balancing rule and apply it to model serving. A better split of work across workers cuts the idle time. The gain is free capacity in data centers that are already built. At the scale of modern AI services, that saving is large in both cost and energy.
arxiv-2601-17955:
Chandranathan Anandavijayan and Pallavi Bhat test a new story for how magnetic turbulence dies away. Their 2026 preprint studies systems where magnetic energy rules. Such turbulence shows a robust flow of energy toward large scales, even with no net magnetic helicity. That flow clashes with the standard picture of cascades to small scales. Recent work points to magnetic reconnection, the snapping and rejoining of field lines, as the driver.

The team probes that claim with two tools. They track how the spectrum evolves, and they study the current sheets where reconnection happens. Both tests check whether reconnection sets the pace of decay. The answer matters for plasmas in space, stars, and fusion devices.
arxiv-2601-18055: Christian Koke studies what happens when one term of an operator family is scaled up without bound. His 2026 preprint follows operators of the form A plus beta times B as beta tends to infinity. The family converges toward an effective operator defined on the kernel of B. The result shows how a strong constraint term forces the whole system onto a smaller space.
arxiv-2601-18155:
Aman Desai, Amelia Lovison, and Paul Jackson present a method to rebuild a fleeting bound state of two top quarks. Their 2026 preprint deals with toponium. Results from the ATLAS and CMS experiments at the Large Hadron Collider point to a top-antitop bound state near the threshold where pairs are born. The state decays almost at once, so its traces are faint. The authors use Recursive Jigsaw Reconstruction to piece the state back together from its decay products.

Jigsaw methods split a messy event into frames that can each be read more clearly. Rebuilding toponium tests our grasp of the heaviest known particle. It also opens a new window on how quarks bind at extreme mass.
arxiv-2601-18255:
Fei Meng studies how language models can keep learning without losing what they know. His 2026 preprint addresses continual learning. The core tension is between stability, holding old knowledge, and plasticity, picking up new tasks. Experience replay is a standard guard against catastrophic forgetting: old examples are mixed back into training. Yet its effects across the many skills of a large model remain underexplored, as Meng notes.

The title promises more than retention. It speaks of orchestrating structural safety alongside plasticity. That framing treats forgetting as a design problem, not just a data one. The study serves anyone who must update a deployed model over time.
arxiv-2601-18355:
Mauro Bonafini, Van Phu Cuong Le, and Riccardo Molinarolo study wave math in a space whose walls move with time. A wave in a fixed box is hard enough. Here the box can grow or shrink as the wave runs, and the wave must die at the walls at all times. The team asks when such a setup still has a sound answer that maths can trust.

They give two paths to the same end. One builds the answer step by step in small time hops. The next bends the rules with a soft fine that fades as the hops shrink. Both paths land on a weak but real answer under mild rules on how the walls may move. Work like this backs models of waves in tanks, tubes, and rooms that change shape in use.
arxiv-2601-18455:
Yihan Chen, Jialin He, and Tianying Xie work on a count task in the maths of large sparse sets. Take a set of points with a rule for which groups of points count as a full set. The set is called full when each new group you add breaks a banned shape. The task asks for the least count of groups a full set can hold.

The banned shape here is a tight knot of four points with all links among them, in a three-way form of the graph world. The team pin down that least count, or bind it tight, for the case at hand. Counts like these map the edge between sparse and dense. They show how thin a set can be while it still blocks the banned shape at each step.
arxiv-2601-18555:
Roberto Di Via and four colleagues teach a tool to find key points on hip scans in two kinds of image. Care for a hip fault rests in part on angles staff read off X-ray shots. Those angles flag a fault where the hip ball and its socket clash. But the full size and span of the clash need a three-dim view, which a deep scan can give.

A tool that finds the same points in both kinds of shot would let staff blend the two views. The X-ray gives the quick angles. The deep scan gives the span. The team test if their marks hold up when the kind of shot swaps. A firm cross test could cut hand work and make hip calls more even across clinics.
