It could also help plan cuts with both views in hand.
arxiv-2601-18955:
Ryan Flynn and Anders W. Sandvik study magnetism in two thin layers twisted against each other. When two sheets sit at a slight twist, a moiré pattern forms and the pull between the layers waxes and wanes across the sheet. That uneven pull can breed patchy magnetic textures.

The pair use a simple model of spins on the two layers, called a bilayer Ising model. The twist, or a slight strain in one sheet, sets the pattern of the pull. Their simple setup lets them map how the textures form without the clutter of a full material model.
arxiv-2601-19255:
Haoting Zhang and Shekhar Jain turn expert rules into anomaly detectors for supply chains. Spotting odd time series early lets managers act before shortages or gluts grow. Classic detectors learn from data alone and often flag patterns that clash with business sense, while hand review cannot scale to millions of products.

Their method uses language models to learn logic rules from human experts, then applies those rules at scale. The blend keeps the judgment of experts and the reach of software. Supply chains are the test case, but any field with scarce experts faces the same trade.
arxiv-2601-20255:
Yueyang Wang and four colleagues propose HE-SNR, a way to guide the mid-training of large language models for software tasks. SWE-bench is the standard test of model skill on real coding problems. The skills it tests are mostly built during mid-training, then drawn out by later fine-tuning.

The authors argue that good metrics to steer mid-training are missing. Their approach uses entropy to uncover latent logic in training data, and a signal-to-noise view to judge its value. Better mid-training guidance could raise coding skill without simply adding more data or compute.
arxiv-2601-20355:
Yue Liang and four colleagues present CURVE, a framework for scene understanding that resists spurious correlations. Scene graphs describe an image as objects and relations, a structured view that helps reasoning. But models overfit to patterns that happen to hold in training data, which harms them on new distributions.

CURVE is inspired by causality and joins variational uncertainty modeling with uncertainty-guided structural regularization. The design suppresses relations that vary a lot between environments, keeping those that look stable. More robust scene graphs would help robots and image systems act sensibly in places unlike their training data.
arxiv-2601-20455:
Thomas Eiter, Robert Lasarzik, and Marcel Śliwiński prove a new existence result for energy-variational solutions of evolution equations. Their result covers a general class of partial differential equations that change in time. Compared with earlier work on this solution concept, the advance is twofold, concerning weaker demands on the regularity weight and energies with merely linear growth.

They also discuss selection criteria for choosing among solutions. Applications include fluid dynamics systems such as the Euler-Korteweg system and binormal curvature flow. Broader existence results let modelers use this flexible solution concept for more physical systems. In plain terms, more flows now have a proof that a path through time exists at all. That is the ground on which the rest of the field stands.
arxiv-2601-20555:
Wadhah Zai El Amri and Nicolás Navarro-Guerrero present Vibro-Sense, a way for robot hands to feel touch through vibration. Rich contact sensing is crucial for manipulation, yet traditional tactile skins are expensive and hard to integrate. Their alternative localizes touch and tracks its path using vibro-acoustic signals.

Seven low-cost piezoelectric microphones are fitted to the hand. An audio spectrogram transformer decodes the vibration patterns made during physical contact. Cheap whole-hand touch could give warehouse and service robots the feedback they need to handle objects gently, without costly skins. The mics are cheap parts, not custom lab gear.
arxiv-2601-20655:
June Chen and four colleagues present OnePiece, a large distributed inference system with RDMA networking for AI-generated content workflows. AI generation now produces high-quality creative work across many domains. Yet existing systems waste throughput, resources, and scalability when many multi-stage jobs run at once.

OnePiece is optimized for those staged workflows, where the output of one model feeds the next. RDMA networking moves data between machines with low delay. Faster shared infrastructure would lower the cost of image, video, and media generation services as demand grows. The aim is more work done on the same racks of chips, with less time lost in line.
arxiv-2601-20855:
Sebastiano Monti and four co-authors test how well AI models plan far ahead. Their 2026 paper presents SokoBench, a benchmark for long-horizon planning and reasoning. The name nods to Sokoban, the classic box-pushing puzzle. Large language models have been tested hard on complex reasoning. Their long-horizon planning, though, has not been studied as closely. The team set out to assess it in a systematic way.

The benchmark targets state-of-the-art large reasoning models. Long-horizon tasks need many steps that stay consistent to the end. One early error can ruin the whole plan. SokoBench measures where models break down as plans lengthen. That gives developers a clear view of a weak spot. Better planning tests are a step toward agents that can carry out long jobs alone.
arxiv-2601-21155:
Oleksandr Tomalak and five co-authors extract a key nucleon property from antineutrino scattering data. Their 2026 paper concerns the nucleon axial-vector form factor. That form factor, called G_A, governs how leptons interact weakly with protons and neutrons. Processes it shapes include elastic antineutrino-nucleon scattering and muon capture by the proton. Knowing G_A precisely is critical for neutrino physics. Experiments worth billions depend on it.

The authors apply radiative corrections to the scattering data. Such corrections account for photons emitted during the interaction. Ignoring them biases the extracted form factor. From the corrected data they also derive the axial radius of the nucleon. That radius measures the size of the nucleon's weak charge. The work sharpens inputs for neutrino oscillation experiments. It is careful phenomenology in service of big detectors.
arxiv-2601-21455:
Yizhou Min, Yizhou Lu, Lanqi Li, Zhen Zhang, and Jiaye Teng question a standard way of grading uncertainty forecasts. Conformal prediction gives intervals with a promised coverage rate. Shorter intervals are usually judged better, since they look sharper while keeping the promise.

The authors show that interval length can be gamed. A trick they name the prejudicial trick makes intervals look shorter while coverage stays valid on paper. The catch is that the gain is not real sharpness. Their warning matters because these intervals guide medical, financial, and safety choices, where fake precision can do real harm.
arxiv-2601-21755:
Younoussa Sow, Nicolas Anquetil, Léandre Brault, and Stéphane Ducasse migrate a legacy language extension to modern Fortran by model transformations. Old Fortran still runs vital industrial code. Moving it to the two thousand eight standard is hard, and house extensions make it harder.

Extensions like Esope carry semantics rooted in old limits and domain logic that no manual records well. The authors transform models of the code rather than rewriting by hand. Automated transformation preserves meaning while updating the form. The approach offers industry a safer path to modernize code that plants and labs still depend on daily.
arxiv-2601-21955:
Fariba Afrin Irany explores whether generative language models can classify hospital patients from their records. Electronic health records hold vast amounts of unstructured clinical narrative. Those notes could support disease characterization, finding patient cohorts, and clinical decision support, if machines could read them well.

Long, specialized clinical text is hard to model, labeled examples are limited, and disease classes are heavily imbalanced. Irany's 2026 preprint presents a GPT-based architecture that moves from generative modeling to clinical classification of these notes. Success would help hospitals surface at-risk patients. It would help them build research cohorts. No armies of manual chart reviewers would be needed. Still, the stakes demand careful checks before any clinical use.
arxiv-2601-22055:
Yaxin Du and co-authors build a question answering system for long, mixed documents. Retrieval-augmented generation answers questions over long documents, but it stays brittle when text, tables, and figures are interleaved across many pages. Flat chunking, the usual preparation, breaks the document's native structure.

Chunks cut loose from their tables and figures become fragments that are hard to interpret alone. The team's 2026 preprint proposes a reader built on dual evolving graphs, structures that track both the document's layout and its meaning as reading proceeds. Reports, manuals, and papers are inherently multimodal, so a reader that respects that structure could answer with far fewer confident mistakes.
arxiv-2601-22355:
Binshuai Wang and Peng Wei add two new yardsticks for how far a data spread sits from a bell curve. Their 2026 preprint works in the frame of optimal transport, which prices the cost of reshaping one spread into another. They use the cone shape of that space to define an angle and a gap.

The angle tells how off-bell the spread leans; the gap gives its distance to the best bell fit. Both rest on the mean and spread of the data. Such tools help analysts judge when bell-based methods are safe. They give a clean, geometric read on shape.
arxiv-2601-22855:
Cécile Mailler and Zoé Varin study a math model of ants finding the shortest path to food. In the model, ants wander a graph between a nest and a food source, two marked points. They cannot talk to each other; they only leave scent trails as they explore.

The authors analyze this process on a family of graphs built from triangles in series and parallel. Such models show how simple local rules can solve a global search problem. The results inform both biology and the design of search algorithms that copy ant behavior.
arxiv-2601-22955:
M. Schubert and four co-authors study a cold gas of magnetic atoms squeezed into thin shapes. The atoms pull on each other over long range, and not equally in all directions. In such low-dimensional setups, the gas can form either solitons, lone stable waves, or quantum droplets, self-bound drops.

In one dimension the switch between those states can be abrupt or smooth, depending on conditions. The authors map how the crossover plays out in one and two dimensions. These gases are clean labs for studying matter that holds itself together.
arxiv-2601-23055:
Marek Kosiek and Krzysztof Rudol describe the spectrum of the bidual of a uniform algebra. A uniform algebra is a closed family of functions with a strong form of convergence. Its bidual is a larger algebra built by applying a duality step twice, and its spectrum is the set of its basic evaluation-like points.

They show that this spectrum is a quotient of the hyper-Stonean envelope of the original spectrum. The result links abstract algebra structure with topology. Such descriptions help analysts understand how function spaces behave under duality.
arxiv-2601-23155:
Powei Chang and a large team select training data for language models using information theory. Picking examples that maximize the log-determinant of Fisher information is attractive, because that objective is submodular. Submodularity lets greedy algorithms provably reach a large share of the best possible gain under a size budget.

Their SPICE method adds penalized conflict handling to that selection. The goal is efficient training: fewer, better-chosen examples for the same final quality. Careful data choice can cut the cost of instruction tuning sharply. A cardinality budget keeps selection honest: the method must choose a fixed-size set, not quietly use more data.
arxiv-2601-23255:
Ye Yu and four co-authors attack large audio-language models through spoken stories. These models take raw speech as input for assistants, education, and clinical triage. Moving from text to audio opens a new class of weaknesses that is still poorly mapped.

Their jailbreak converts text to audio and hides disallowed directives inside a narrative stream. A story format can slip instructions past filters tuned for plain text commands. The study tells builders that voice interfaces need their own safety testing. Narrative-style audio is the delivery vehicle, wrapping disallowed directives in story form to evade text-oriented safeguards.
arxiv-2603-01455:
Long videos are hard for AI models that can only hold a short span of facts at once. Niu Lian, Yuting Wang, Hanshu Yao, and colleagues propose a layered memory for video agents in this 2026 work. Dense image stores are slow and full of repeats, while text notes alone lose fine detail and can invent facts.

Their design, MM-Mem, sorts memory into three layers, from raw sense traces up to broad gist schemas. A training goal drawn from a theory of human memory keeps key facts while it squeezes out bulk. At query time, the system tries the broad layer first and digs deeper only when unsure. Tests on four benchmark sets cover both stored and live video, and the design held up well in both modes.
arxiv-2603-01855:
Hong-Bae Jeon, Kaibin Huang, and Chan-Byoung Chae estimate arrival angles for many users with a quantum receiver. Their 2026 work uses Rydberg atomic receivers, which sense radio signals through excited atoms, plus a radio lens front end. The task is to find each user direction from magnitude-only readings, with no phase data.

Their framework, Quantum-PROBE, models those readings as sums of angle-dependent power profiles shaped by the lens. That power-domain dictionary has clear structure, so user angles can be recovered without rebuilding phase. Two solvers follow: a sparse solver with a fast gradient method, and a cheaper canceller that peels off strong profiles one by one. Simulations beat representative atomic and radio benchmarks across many setups. The pair of solvers offers a clear trade between accuracy and complexity for quantum sensing gear.
arxiv-2603-01955:
Jifeng Xia, Ningyu Tang, Thomas Bisbas, and colleagues map atomic carbon across a nearby molecular cloud in this 2026 survey. Their work covers the Ophiuchus cloud regions L1688 and L1689 with a submillimeter telescope survey. Atomic carbon traces carbon chemistry in the interstellar medium, the gas between stars.

Combining the maps with photodissociation region models, they compare how carbon and carbon monoxide vary. In low-density, high-radiation zones, atomic carbon abundance swings less than monoxide does. That steadiness makes atomic carbon a more reliable tracer of molecular hydrogen there. Using it as a direct tracer, they estimate a large share of cloud mass that monoxide surveys miss. Line widths for atomic carbon also run broader than for a monoxide isotope, which hints at extra atomic contributions.
arxiv-2603-02155:
Kaixuan Ji, Qingyue Zhao, Heyang Zhao, and colleagues sharpen bounds for a choice problem in this 2026 paper. The problem is the multi-armed bandit, now with a penalty that keeps choices near a prior guess. That penalty is based on KL distance, a measure of how far apart two guesses sit. Past work hinted this setup could cut regret, the loss from wrong picks.

A fresh proof method gives the first strong bound that grows in a straight line with arm count. A matching floor shows the bound is nearly tight. When the penalty is weak, regret instead grows with the square root of time and arms. Together, the results map regret across all penalty strengths. The bounds are nearly best possible in arms, penalty, and time.
arxiv-2603-02355:
Faisal Muhammad and Muhammad Saif Ullah Khalid study self-starting in vertical wind turbines in this 2026 paper. Lift-driven vertical turbines often fail to start spinning on their own. Blade chord length and blade count shape both startup and steady running. The authors simulate freely rotating Darrieus rotors in two dimensions.

Two families are compared: one holds chord fixed across three and five blades. The other shrinks chord for five blades to keep total blade area matched. More blades speed early startup but lower the final spin rate, due to stronger blade-vortex clashes. Longer chords also aid startup through stronger unsteady loading. Yet they raise viscous losses and wake clashes, capping final speed. Torque splits into pressure and viscous parts clarify the trade-off for designers.
arxiv-2603-02655:
Anum Afzal, Yuki Saito, and Hiroya Takamura tackle live commentary for game videos in this 2026 paper. A good commentator must decide both what to say and when to say it. Recent systems using large multimodal models write strong text but mostly ignore timing.

The team tests whether prompting alone, with no extra training, can produce well-timed speech. They compare a fixed-interval method with a dynamic one that sets the next pause from the length of the last remark. On Japanese and English racing and fighting game data, the dynamic method matched human timing and content more closely. They also release data, models, and code.
arxiv-2603-02755:
Kazuyuki Hasegawa studies the still points of circle actions on quaternionic manifolds, spaces built on four-part numbers. His 2026 paper links those fixed-point sets to compatible complex structures living on the same space. The interplay between the two kinds of structure is delicate and only partly understood.

He derives an equation tying the first Chern classes, key shape measures, of the fixed-point set and of a flat quaternionic manifold. If the fixed set's class is not trivial, no richer hypercomplex structure can contain the given complex one near that set. He also works out the connected pieces of the fixed set for circle actions on quaternionic projective space. The results are then applied to a classic example due to Pontecorvo.
arxiv-2603-02855:
Tamara Grava, Robert Jenkins, Xiaofan Zhang, and Zechuan Zhang set up the scattering machinery for a classic wave equation with unusual edges. Their 2026 paper studies the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation, starting from waves that settle into different traveling patterns at far left and far right. Such step-like data model a front between two wave trains.

They formulate the direct scattering problem and establish the analytic properties of the resulting scattering data. The inverse problem, recovering the wave from that data, is then cast as a Riemann-Hilbert problem, and they prove it can be solved. A closing observation links their setup to the broader theory of soliton gases, dense crowds of interacting wave pulses. The framework opens the door to long-time behavior studies.
arxiv-2603-03055:
Jin Cao, Mohamed Elmi, and Hossein Movasati define a key invariant for Calabi-Yau varieties in two ways and bet they coincide. Calabi-Yau varieties are the curved spaces at the heart of string theory and much modern geometry. Their 2026 paper constructs the Hasse-Witt invariant, a number that captures subtle arithmetic behavior of such a space.

One construction uses the Cartier operator, a classic tool from characteristic-p geometry. The other uses a theory of Calabi-Yau modular forms developed by Movasati. The authors conjecture the two definitions always agree and back the claim with many worked examples. A proof would weld together two distant toolkits, arithmetic and modular, around one central class of spaces.
arxiv-2603-03155:
Joshua Steier asks what shapes the inner organization of models that predict molecular properties. Some models keep shape information cleanly separable from composition, others tangle the two. His 2026 paper introduces a probe method that strips out the composition signal and measures how much geometric signal a simple linear reader can still recover.

Across ten models from five families, recoverable geometry varied more than sixfold. The training target dominated: models trained on an energy-gap property kept far more geometry than energy-trained ones, whatever their architecture. Richer training data partly compensated for a mismatched target. Inside one model family, different symmetry channels specialized, vectors carrying dipole information and scalars carrying gap information. Nonlinear probes, he warns, can fake separation that is not there.
arxiv-2603-03255:
Alekhya Ghosh, Arghadeep Pal, Haochen Yan, and colleagues coax ultraviolet light out of a chip-scale ring for the first time. Silicon nitride microresonators lead integrated nonlinear photonics, but reaching ultraviolet wavelengths in a single resonator had never been done. Their 2026 paper reports fourth-harmonic generation spanning blue into ultraviolet light.

They map how input power shapes the wavelength ranges where second, third, and fourth harmonics appear, and track how the ultraviolet signal varies with power. The result stretches the platform to the lower edge of its transparency window, enabling on-chip ultraviolet conversion. Near-ultraviolet output around four hundred nanometers could excite quantum emitters in boron nitride, sharpen Raman spectroscopy, and power compact fluorescence imaging.
arxiv-2603-03555:
Brandon Yee and Krishna Sharma observe three quarters of a million artificial intelligence agents socializing without any humans. MoltBook, a coordination environment for autonomous language model agents, offers the first chance to watch emergent multi-agent behavior at population scale. Their 2026 study follows over ninety thousand active agents across three weeks and names the resulting phenomena Molt Dynamics.

Network clustering suggests six roles, but the pattern is mostly core and periphery: over nine in ten agents sit in one homogeneous peripheral mass, and real differentiation lives in the active minority. Information cascades across more than ten thousand propagation events follow a power law, and repeated exposure yields diminishing adoption returns. Collaboration is the weak spot. In the detected joint events, success rates were low and groups did worse than matched single agents. Cooperation, the authors conclude, is still nascent.

cia-0000049355: Dated June 2, 1982, declassified CIA document 0000049355 is a summary on El Salvador's performance on certification issues, noted for the Truth Commission. Its subject is how El Salvador measured up on the certification questions named in the heading. The file survives as a summary item, preserving the agency's framing of a review that its title describes only in general terms.
cia-0000096655: Soviet Defense Budget is the plain title of declassified CIA document 0000096655, dated October 4, 1978. The heading names the budget as the whole subject in three words. Readers find a short declassified item on Soviet military spending, its title giving no breakdown. It is preserved as one of the agency's recurring efforts. Each such effort tried to size up that budget.
cia-0000108155: National Intelligence Estimate Probable Economic Effects of a Severance of East is the heading, cut off mid-phrase, on declassified CIA document 0000108155, dated March 3, 1958. The title marks a formal estimate on the economic effects of a severance. What would be severed breaks off at the word East in the heading. The brief record preserves the break exactly as released.
cia-0000112355: Ufo Sighted Over Urumqi Evening of 6 Sep is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000112355, dated August 3, 1989. The title dates the sighting to the evening of September 6, a month after the file's own August date. That ordering stands on the face of the record itself. The brief record is a sighting item over Urumqi, in Xinjiang, China.
cia-0000115455: Guatemala: Prospects for the New Government -- National Intelligence Estimate is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000115455, dated January 6, 1986. The title marks a formal estimate on the prospects for Guatemala's new government. New is the heading's own word for that government in the title. The brief record is a government prospects estimate from the first week of 1986.
cia-0000117855: Title Deleted re: Answers to Questions Posed to Colonel Oliver North is the surviving heading on declassified CIA document 0000117855, dated August 3, 1985. The catalog notes the title was deleted, then names its subject: answers given to Colonel Oliver North. Questions and answers are the form named in the heading itself. The brief record preserves the deletion note with the subject as released.
cia-0000126955: A May 1961 CIA report gives the short-term prospects in Haiti. Francois Duvalier, known as Papa Doc, was tightening his grip on the Caribbean nation. The paper forecasts what Washington could expect as Haiti slid toward one of the hemisphere's darkest dictatorships. Prospects papers on Haiti recurred for decades because the country combined poverty, a feared police state, and a shoreline ninety miles from Florida in Washington's thinking.
cia-0000132455:
Communist influence in Cuba fills a CIA document dated February 2, 1960. By early 1960 communists sat inside the revolution's inner circle. The old question of whether they held influence had given way to a harder one: how much they held.

The document measures that influence across the government and its new bodies. For readers, it records the agency's answer at a key turning point. Within another year the revolution would declare its socialist character in public. The entry shows analysts reaching that conclusion in private well before the announcement was made. Their judgment came from watching posts, parties, and unions change hands.
cia-0000132655: Cuban communists telling foreign comrades how they won fills a CIA paper dated January 3, 1961. Victory had made Havana a classroom for the world's revolutionary left. Party men from Cuba were lecturing abroad on the road they had taken to power. The short paper reports what they said and the lessons they claimed others should draw from Cuba's case.
cia-0000132755: Multiple CIA briefings on Cuba share the date January 4, 1961, and this paper is one of that burst. The cluster followed the cutting of diplomatic ties on January 3, when the agency restated the island's situation from several angles at once. Now open to the public, the declassified text is preserved via the CIA Reading Room and the Internet Archive.
cia-0000134255: The man tipped as Cuba's next ambassador to Washington fills item 21 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated April 5, 1960. Within a year there would be no Cuban ambassador in Washington at all. For the moment Havana was still sending envoys in the normal way. The short item reports the name in prospect and the talk around it.
cia-0000135755: Dated 3 February 1961, this Spanish text belongs to the 2506 Brigade document set. The exile brigade was drilling under CIA supervision, its invasion of Cuba about ten weeks away. The catalog gives the item no subject of its own. It is kept in Spanish as released, one of the many dated records the brigade left from that February, and its content is a matter for the text, not the title.
cia-0000136255: From 6 May 1954 comes a CIA cable, since declassified, on special instructions for broadcasts following D-day, the aftermath scripted before the event. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136355: ODAYOKE's interests are in competent hands, LINCOLN assures CADICK in this June 1954 cable about the SKIMMER and SYNCARP basic agreement. That agreement committed support only to attain the objective of freeing the country, the station notes, not to any person for the top position. Placing CALLIGERIS on top is a policy matter above PBSUCCESS's jurisdiction. He must never assume unconditional backing, and limited concessions now may avert a greater tragedy.
cia-0000136755: The 2506 Brigade's Spanish files contain this document under an estimated date of 1 January 1961, flagged as estimated in the catalog. The brigade, Cuban exiles trained by the CIA, was in its final winter before the Bay of Pigs. No subject is recorded for the item. It survives in Spanish in the declassified release, one of the estimated New Year records that recur throughout this series.
cia-0000136855: Guatemala's white paper charges are a provocation, this January 1954 cable argues. The charges aim to disrupt hemisphere solidarity at Caracas. They also aim to win outside support. Officers worry about a Bogotazo-style disturbance at the conference. Headquarters asks for plans for counter propaganda. It also orders quick action. Articles should be placed in the publication Alerta. The cable is information war, planned ahead of the Tenth Inter-American Conference.
cia-0000137455: A Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade papers, dated only to 1960 and marked as estimated in the catalog. The brigade was the CIA-trained exile force that landed at the Bay of Pigs in 1961, so this record belongs to its training period. The catalog gives an estimated year and no subject. The document survives in the original Spanish in the declassified release, as part of the brigade's early archive.
cia-03003755: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1953/12/08, a CIA publication. Another December briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
cia-03017655: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1954/11/19, a CIA publication. The November briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
cia-03155155: CURRENT INTELLIGENCE BULLETIN - 1957/10/30, a CIA publication. The next day's briefing. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-03164655: March 13, 1946: the daily summary circulated in Washington. The postwar world's intelligence digest. The Cold War's infancy, on paper. Tomorrow's readers will find it. This file preserves that declassified summary. The archive guards it with care.
cia-03174755: February 25, 1955: the daily bulletin went to readers. The global intelligence summary for senior officials. The Cold War's late-winter brief. The library keeps the document safe. This declassified paper is stored. It is filed. The text is preserved.
cia-03184155: November 11, 1959 brought this intelligence bulletin. The daily briefing kept Washington posted on global developments. Veterans Day's classified reading. The file is now open to the public. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Kept for readers.
cia-03194455: April 24, 1955: the bulletin briefed Washington on global events. The intelligence analysts' daily product for senior officials. The Cold War routine continued. The archive guards it with care. This file preserves that declassified bulletin. Kept for readers.
commynes-memoirs-scoble-vol-1-1855:
Philippe de Commynes served Charles the Bold of Burgundy, then crossed to Louis XI of France and became his trusted adviser. His Memoirs, the first great political memoir of the modern kind, tell what he saw at both courts. Andrew Scoble translated the work, and this first volume, from 1855, holds books one through five.

Commynes watches the wars of Burgundy and France, the cunning of Louis, and the pride that ruins Charles at Nancy. He draws lessons on power with a cool, worldly hand: keep faith, buy peace cheap, fear your own anger. Kings read him for centuries as a handbook of rule. His voice, plain and knowing, still sounds modern.
commynes-memoirs-scoble-vol-2-1855:
The second volume of Andrew Scoble's Commynes, from 1855, holds books six through eight of the Memoirs. It adds the Scandalous Chronicle of Jean de Troyes, a Paris record of the same years. Commynes here follows the French court past the death of Louis XI into the reign of Charles VIII.

The young king invades Italy in 1494, and Commynes, sent as envoy, watches the old Italian order crack. He judges popes, dukes, and his own master with the same calm eye. Jean de Troyes adds the street view of Paris under Louis, its feasts, crimes, and court scandals. Together the two texts close the great memoir of the age. Commynes remains the first modern voice in political writing.
doe-osti-2997623-implementation-risks-of: RFID in TA-55 got its risk review, and this DOE report covers implementation hazards. The pages detail the risk analysis. The facility managers get their briefing. The site was TA-55. The analysis was risk. The managers got briefings. The hazards were implementation.
doe-osti-3017519-final-technical-report-: Climate extremes got structure-discovered, and this DOE final finds physical meaning. The pages detail the DE-SC0022255 findings. The climate folks get their closeout. The data were climate extreme. The closeout was climate. The meaning was physical. The structures were meaningful.
douglass-my-bondage-1855:
My Bondage and My Freedom, from 1855, is Frederick Douglass's second and fuller autobiography. By then he was a famed speaker, editor, and leader, legally free after British friends bought his liberty. He retells his early life with ten more years of thought behind it.

The bondage half gives the fullest account of his enslavement, his masters, and his escape. The freedom half traces his rise as an orator and his break with the Garrisonians. Douglass writes with open anger and sharp analysis of slavery as a system. Many readers judge it his greatest book. An introduction by James McCune Smith frames the enlarged edition.
euler-institutiones-calculi-1755:
Leonhard Euler orders the differential calculus in his Institutiones calculi differentialis, in Latin from 1755. No true textbook of the subject had existed before his. Euler takes the wild new math of Newton and Leibniz and sets it in teachable order, rule by rule, for every student to follow with profit.

Generations learned analysis from these patient, lucid Latin pages afterward. Functions, rates, and curves gain clear forms under his hand. Euler produced more math than any man of his century, perhaps of any century. This book shows his most useful gift: not discovery alone, but the power to make hard things plain for those who came after.
europmc-pmc10022855:
Morton and the FOxTROT trial group report mature results of a large randomized trial of chemotherapy before surgery for colon cancer, in a 2023 paper. Giving chemo first is standard in some cancers but needed formal testing in colon cancer. Patients with locally advanced tumors were assigned by chance to early chemo or to the usual surgery-first path.

The trial gave six weeks of chemo before surgery to the early-treatment group. The paper reports the long-term results on cancer return and safety. Surgeons and oncologists can use the findings to weigh a change in the order of care.
europmc-pmc10060155:
Issa and a large trial team report on revumenib, a drug that blocks the menin protein, in leukemia with certain gene changes, in a 2023 study. The target cancers carry either a rearranged KMT2A gene or a mutated NPM1 gene. Both forms depend on menin to keep cancer growth programs switched on.

The paper reports trial results in patients whose disease had returned or resisted other care. It describes responses to the drug and its side effects. The work supports a new class of targeted drugs for hard-to-treat acute leukemia.
europmc-pmc10166855:
Udeochu and a large team report that tau protein switches on an immune alarm in microglia that weakens the brain's resilience, in a 2023 study. Alzheimer's disease develops for years before symptoms appear. During that silent phase, some brains stay sharp despite building damage, a trait called cognitive resilience.

The team found that tau activates a DNA sensor, cGAS, in microglia, the brain's immune cells. That alarm lowers a protective protein, MEF2C, and resilience falls. The pathway may offer targets to keep minds sharp longer. It also helps explain why resilience varies.
europmc-pmc10191855:
Shalon and colleagues profile the human gut environment under normal, healthy conditions in a 2023 study. The gut's mix of microbes, proteins, and small chemicals changes along its length and over time. Those patterns shape digestion and health, yet most data came from stool alone, which gives only a partial view.

The team sampled directly from different gut regions in healthy volunteers. They mapped microbes and chemicals side by side at each site. The resulting atlas shows how much the gut's inner world varies by place, and sets a baseline for disease studies.
europmc-pmc10464255:
Sharkiya ran a rapid review in 2023 on how talk shapes care results for older patients. Clear talk helps doctors bond with patients and guides joint choices. The review hunted past work on patients aged 65 and over. Five data banks were searched for studies from 2000 to 2023.

Seven studies passed the screen. Sharkiya found that both spoken and unspoken signals lifted every patient outcome checked. Those outcomes covered how happy patients felt, how good their care was, and their health of body and mind. Talk styles ranged from word choice to tone and body stance. The studies had weak spots, though, in design and in small, narrow samples. The author calls for true trials with clear effect sizes next.
europmc-pmc11519755:
Goh and a large team run a randomized trial of whether a language model improves doctors' diagnostic reasoning in this 2024 study. Large language models had shown strong scores on medical test questions. Whether they help working physicians reason through cases was untested in a trial. Fifty physicians in family medicine, internal medicine, and emergency medicine took part.

Physicians were assigned to use a large language model or only conventional resources, such as reference texts. Diagnostic reasoning performance did not improve significantly with the model, the authors report. Scores with model access were statistically indistinguishable from scores with standard resources alone. The finding matters because the model itself scores highly when tested solo. The authors conclude that further development is needed to integrate such models into clinical practice effectively. Simply handing doctors the tool is not enough.
europmc-pmc1261155:
Tomfohr, Lu, and Kepler introduced a pathway-level gene analysis method in 2005. Single gene changes can hide broader biological shifts. Grouping genes by pathway can reveal clearer patterns. Their method scores each pathway activity level per sample.

Activity scores come from singular value decomposition of expression data. Tests used diabetes data and airway data from smokers. Smoker comparisons flagged nicotine metabolism and mucus production pathways. Glutathione metabolism, a defense pathway, also stood out. Tomfohr compares results with gene-set enrichment, a rival approach. Pathway scores give a more readable picture of cell state.
europmc-pmc1361355:
Negrete and co-authors tested whether a second cell protein can host Nipah virus in 2006. Nipah is a lethal emerging virus with no cure. Its known entry receptor is ephrinB2, a cell surface protein. Related ephrin proteins share overlapping body patterns.

Every known ephrin was tested for binding the viral attachment protein. Only ephrinB3 joined B2 in binding it. Binding strength was subnanomolar for both, though B3 released faster. EphrinB3 sufficed for entry of both test and live virus. Two key residues in B3 proved critical for that use. Negrete widens the known entry routes for Nipah.
europmc-pmc1621055:
A fading retina slowly steals sight in retinitis pigmentosa. Hamel reviewed the disease in 2006. Light-sensing cells die off, leaving pigment deposits in the eye. Night blindness comes first, then side vision narrows over decades until blindness.

About one in 4,000 people has the plain form. Forty-five genes or loci were known causes by then, making gene testing impractical for most. No therapy stops the disease or restores sight. Care aims to slow decline with sunlight protection and vitamins, treat cataracts and swelling, and support low vision. Hamel stresses genetic counseling for families.
europmc-pmc1797055:
Yip and Horvath extended in 2007 a network measure used to judge how tightly two genes are linked. In gene networks, direct links can be noisy or missing. The older topological overlap measure counted neighbors that two nodes share, since genes sharing partners often share a function or pathway.

Their generalized version, called GTOM, looks beyond immediate neighbors. It counts neighbors shared at two or more steps away and scales the result to fall between zero and one. Theory, plus tests on a yeast co-expression network and a fly protein network, backed the extension. Pairs with high generalized overlap were more likely to fall in the same functional class. The authors argue the broader view gives a sturdier and more sensitive read of interconnectedness.
europmc-pmc1802755:
Smith, Hay and co-authors recalculated in 2007 the basic reproductive number for malaria across Africa. That number, written R0, counts how many new cases one case can generate in a fully susceptible population. It gauges how hard malaria will be to control in a given place.

Their new method produced estimates for 121 African populations, expanding the known set about tenfold. Values ranged from near one to more than 3,000, a huge spread in transmission intensity. They also show that classic formulas overstate spread in small finite populations. Uneven biting, where some people are bitten far more than others, can raise some measures while lowering the true human-to-human count. Where R0 is highest, control will need several combined methods aimed at the most-bitten people.
europmc-pmc1865555:
Chandran and colleagues compared gene activity in 2007 between prostate cancers that had spread and those still confined to the gland. Spread, or metastasis, is the deadliest turn in prostate cancer, yet neither tumor shape nor blood tests reliably predict it. The team wanted the biology that sets spreading tumors apart.

They profiled 24 metastatic samples, resistant to hormone therapy, taken from four patients, and set them against a published set of 64 primary tumors. After stripping out genes from surrounding support tissue, the spread tumors proved highly varied. Still, 415 genes were at least twice as active in every patient's metastases, and 364 were at least half as active. The changed genes spanned multiple molecular pathways rather than one route. Those pathway sets offer candidate markers and drug targets.
europmc-pmc2124855: A medical paper comparing merits of various complements and amboceptors in serum diagnosis. The immune reagents. This article preserves that immunology. It awaits future readers. Its place in history is secure. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2125255: A medical paper with observations on the succus entericus. The intestinal juice. This article preserves that physiology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
europmc-pmc2125355: A medical paper with an immunological study of Bacillus influenzae. The flu germ's immunity. This article preserves that immunology. Future scholars will discover it. Its place in history is secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day.
europmc-pmc2128155: A medical paper with experimental studies on heteroplastic bone formation. The foreign bone. This article preserves that histology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. It waits for future eyes. The library keeps the document safe for everyone.
europmc-pmc2128355: A medical paper with studies based on a malignant tumor of the rabbit. The rabbit cancer. This article preserves that oncology. It awaits future readers. It holds its historical place. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2128455: A medical paper with an experimental study of mitochondrial changes in the thyroid gland. The thyroid's engines. This article preserves that cell biology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Time has kept the file intact through the years.
europmc-pmc2128555: A medical paper on the epidemiology of a rabbit respiratory infection, susceptibility of rabbits. The rabbit cold. This article preserves that epidemiology. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The file is now open to the public.
europmc-pmc2131155: A medical paper on the influence of ovariectomy on spontaneous mammary carcinoma. The spayed cancer. This article preserves that oncology. Future scholars will discover it. It retains its place in time. The library keeps the document safe.
europmc-pmc2131555: The germ-growing broth may look dead, but its chemistry tells a tale, which this paper captured. The team measured how the broth handled air and rust. The broth's hidden acts, noted. The article keeps that lab study.
europmc-pmc2292755:
Smith and Kruglyak asked in 2008 how genes and the environment interact to shape gene activity in yeast. They grew two yeast strains, called BY and RM, on glucose and on ethanol as food sources. Then they measured which genes were active in each strain and each food.

Most genes changed activity by strain, by food, or by both at once, and 2,037 genes showed a true interaction effect. By breeding the strains and profiling over 100 offspring, they mapped 1,555 genetic linkages tied to these effects. One hotspot traced to a variant in the gene IRA2, which controls a growth signal pathway. Local control variants stayed stable across foods, while distant ones often flipped direction.
europmc-pmc2361355:
Des Guetz and colleagues pooled studies on blood vessel growth in colorectal cancer in 2006. Tumors need new vessels to grow, a process called angiogenesis. Two measures reflect it: microvessel density, a count of tiny vessels in the tumor, and levels of VEGF, a vessel growth signal.

The meta-analysis kept 32 studies on vessel density, covering 3,496 patients, and 18 on VEGF, covering 2,050 patients. High vessel density predicted worse survival and faster relapse, with a risk ratio of 2.32 for relapse, but only when vessels were stained with CD31 or CD34 markers. High VEGF predicted poor relapse-free survival even more strongly, at a risk ratio of 2.84, and poorer overall survival as well. The authors urged standard ways to measure both markers in future trials.
europmc-pmc2522255:
Sheehan, Didelez, Burton, and Tobin explained in 2008 how a method called Mendelian randomisation can test cause and effect in observational health studies. Such studies often mislead. An exposure linked to disease may not cause it. Hidden factors can drive both. Genes offer a way out, since gene variants are assigned at conception roughly at random, like lots in a trial.

The authors use Katan's cholesterol example: people carrying the ApoE2 gene variant have lower cholesterol from birth without differing in lifestyle. If low cholesterol truly caused cancer, those carriers should show more cancer, and checking this tests causality directly. They set out the three assumptions a gene must meet to work as such an instrument, and review limits like pleiotropy, where one gene affects several traits.
europmc-pmc2588455:
McCurley and Callard tested in 2008 which housekeeping genes zebrafish researchers can trust as measuring references. Gene expression studies normalise results against a supposedly steady reference gene, but common choices wobble with conditions. The team measured eight candidate genes. They covered development stages and adult tissues of both sexes. They also covered embryos exposed to hormone-like chemicals and solvents.

Every candidate varied under some condition. Ranking stability picked 18s ribosomal RNA, beta-2-microglobulin, and elongation factor 1 alpha as most stable during development and across tissues. After chemical treatment a different trio won, while some reliable genes turned unstable. Sex differences appeared for certain genes in certain tissues. Choosing a poor reference even flipped the measured size of a hormone response. The authors urge checking references for each new experiment.
europmc-pmc2653555:
Hampson and co-authors studied in 2009 how rabies spreads among dogs in rural Tanzania, to test whether the disease could be wiped out worldwide. Rabies kills tens of thousands of people each year, mostly in Africa and Asia, and nearly all catch it from dog bites. Eradication would need proof that dog vaccination can break the chain of spread.

The team followed single rabid dogs in unusual detail, tracing whom each one bit. From those chains they estimated that each rabid dog infects only about 1.2 others on average. That is a low spread rate, well within reach of vaccination drives. The catch is speed: dog populations turn over fast, as puppies replace adults. Gains fade unless vaccine rounds return often. With steady effort, the authors argue, ending dog rabies is a realistic goal.
europmc-pmc2760755:
Paulmann and co-authors showed in 2009 that serotonin inside pancreatic beta cells modulates insulin secretion by a process called serotonylation. Serotonin is stored with insulin in beta-cell granules and released with it, yet its job there was a thirty-year mystery. Mice lacking peripheral serotonin, outside the brain, develop diabetes, which pointed to an intracellular role.

Serotonylation is the covalent binding of serotonin to small GTPase proteins by calcium-dependent enzymes, which switches those proteins on. In beta cells, that binding promotes the release of insulin granules when glucose rises. Blocking the process impaired secretion, while the brain serotonin system stayed intact in their model. The work reframes serotonin as an internal signal in insulin release, not just a brain messenger.
europmc-pmc2811155:
Narendra and colleagues worked out in 2010 how cells flag worn-out mitochondria, the cell's power units, for disposal. Two proteins in this system, PINK1 and Parkin, are faulty in some inherited forms of Parkinson disease. Parkin was known to gather on failing mitochondria, but the signal that calls it in was a mystery.

The team showed that healthy mitochondria constantly break down PINK1, keeping its levels near zero. When a mitochondrion loses power, PINK1 stops being destroyed and piles up on its surface instead. That buildup is what recruits Parkin, which then tags the unit for breakdown. Without PINK1's signal, Parkin never arrives, and damaged power units linger.
europmc-pmc2814855:
Lavasani and colleagues tested friendly gut bacteria in 2010 as a treatment for a mouse disease that mimics multiple sclerosis. The disease, called EAE, is an immune attack on nerve insulation. The team screened five Lactobacillus strains given daily to mice, looking for ones that calmed the attack.

Three strains cut inflammation in the brain and spinal cord and raised calming regulatory T cells. Given alone to already sick mice, each strain failed, but a mixture of all three halted the disease and reversed its signs. The benefit ran through a calming signal called IL-10, made by those regulatory cells, and transferring the cells to other mice carried the protection with them.
europmc-pmc2815955:
Luby and a large team combined records from every known Nipah virus outbreak in Bangladesh between 2001 and 2007. Nipah causes fever and brain inflammation and first erupted in Malaysia in the late nineteen nineties, spread there by sick pigs. Bangladesh instead saw repeated small outbreaks with varied virus strains, pointing to fresh spillovers from fruit bats.

Across the seven outbreaks and stray cases studied, more than half of the identified patients caught the virus from another person rather than from bats. That spread pattern sets Bangladesh apart from Malaysia, where person-to-person spread was never confirmed. The team traced how chains of cases build once the virus enters a community, which matters for hospital precautions.
europmc-pmc2846855:
Van der Worp and colleagues examined in 2010 why treatments that shine in animal disease models so often flop in human trials. The essay argues the failure splits into two broad sources. Animal studies themselves often carry design flaws that inflate apparent benefit. And animal versions of diseases can differ from the human condition in ways that doom transfer, however clean the experiment.

Systematic reviews of animal work can help pick the likeliest candidates, the authors contend, but hidden bias poisons that tool too. Companion work on stroke studies showed unpublished negative results inflate reported benefit by about a third. The piece closes with reporting recommendations so animal evidence can be judged honestly before patients are enrolled.
europmc-pmc2939055:
Lebouvier and colleagues tested whether routine colon biopsies can reveal Parkinson's disease damage in the gut nerves, in a 2010 study. Clumps called Lewy bodies, the hallmark of the disease in brain, also appear in gut nerve networks.

Biopsies from patients at different disease stages and from controls were stained for a marked form of alpha-synuclein, the clump protein. Lewy-type damage showed in most patient samples and in no controls, while patients also had fewer gut neurons per cluster. Damage levels tracked neuron loss and certain symptoms that respond poorly to the standard drug levodopa.
europmc-pmc3000155:
Peiris and colleagues reported on children hospitalised with breathing infections in Hong Kong in a 2003 study of the newly found human metapneumovirus. Over thirteen months they tested nose samples from nearly six hundred children.

The virus turned up in about one child in twenty, most often alongside pneumonia, asthma flare-ups, or bronchiolitis in infants. Compared with the better known RSV, these children were older and their wheezing more often reflected asthma than infant bronchiolitis. Activity peaked in spring and summer, all strains fell into known family lines, and admission rates for the virus were substantial.
europmc-pmc3004955:
Feinberg and co-authors unveiled a multiplexed scanning method that images the whole brain in under a second in a 2010 article. Standard echo planar imaging builds one slice at a time, taking seconds per brain volume and far longer for fibre mapping.

Their sequence stacks two tricks: firing several slice bands at once and refocusing echoes simultaneously, multiplying how many images land in one sweep. Whole brain functional scans at a common magnet strength ran several times faster, and fibre imaging sped up two to four times. At the stronger magnet the design also cut energy deposition and removed the need for fat suppression pulses.
europmc-pmc3018455:
Harr and French reviewed Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, two ends of one spectrum of severe drug reactions that strip the skin, in a 2010 article. Both are rare, striking roughly one or two people per million yearly, and both can kill.

Sore, blistering skin and mouth erosions deepen as the surface layer detaches, more extensively in the necrolysis form. Drugs cause most cases, with a known high-risk list spanning gout, seizure, and sulfa antibiotic medicines, though certain infections can trigger it too. Genetic susceptibility is real: one immune marker strongly predicts the reaction to a seizure drug in Han Chinese patients.
europmc-pmc3024255:
Langfelder, Luo, Oldham, and Horvath addressed a methods question in this 2011 paper: how can scientists tell whether a network module found in one dataset truly reappears in another? Modules are groups of genes that rise and fall together. Showing that a module survives in fresh data helps prove it is real and not a fluke of one study.

The authors compare several preservation statistics that need no module labels in the test data. Some work for any network, while others use correlation structure and prove stronger. Combining several measures into one summary score worked best. They show the methods on six gene network studies, from mouse tissues to human and chimpanzee brains. In one case, genes tied to cell death behaved differently between the two species.
europmc-pmc3101655:
Massy-Westropp, Gill, Taylor, Bohannon, and Hill published in 2011 reference values for hand grip strength from a large community study in Adelaide, Australia. Grip strength is a quick, reliable gauge of overall muscle function used in clinics and aging research. More than twenty six hundred adults without hand pain or arthritis squeezed a calibrated gauge, and results were sorted by age and sex.

Men outgripped women at every age, as expected. The link with body weight surprised: heavier bodies meant slightly stronger grips only in the youngest and oldest adults, and slightly weaker grips in between. The sample was heavier than most comparison populations, and its younger adults gripped less strongly than peers in published overseas data. The authors provide the full tables for local clinical use. They caution that international norms may misjudge Australian patients.
europmc-pmc3102055:
Church and colleagues documented in 2011 how the physical demands of American jobs collapsed over five decades, and how closely that collapse tracks national weight gain. Using labor statistics for private industry since 1960, they estimated how much energy each era's mix of jobs required. In the early nineteen sixties nearly half of jobs demanded at least moderate physical effort. Now fewer than one in five do.

Average daily energy burned at work fell by well over a hundred calories for both men and women. Feeding that drop into an energy balance model predicted the weight of forty to fifty year olds in each national survey era almost exactly, for both sexes. The authors do not claim work is the whole obesity story, since food intake matters too. But they show the disappearance of physical work alone can account for a large share of the nation's added pounds.
europmc-pmc3108955:
Doris Chan and colleagues published a 2011 pooled analysis in PLoS ONE of diet and bowel cancer. A major cancer report had already judged the link with red and processed meat convincing, so the team updated the evidence with newer long-term studies of adults. They combined results up to March 2011.

People eating the most red and processed meat had a clearly higher risk of bowel cancer than those eating the least. Risk rose in a near steady line with intake up to a moderate daily amount, then levelled off. Fresh red meat and processed meat each showed a link when judged apart. The authors support advice to limit both foods as one step toward lowering bowel cancer risk.
europmc-pmc3113855:
Meng-Chuan Lai and colleagues compared autistic men and women in a 2011 study in PLoS ONE. Autism is diagnosed far more often in males, yet whether the condition itself looks different by sex was unclear. The team tested matched adults with high-functioning autism or Asperger syndrome on thinking and behaviour measures.

Childhood symptom severity did not differ by sex, nor did scores for empathy, system-focused thinking, anxiety, or reading social cues. Adult women, though, reported more sensory symptoms and more autistic traits, while showing fewer current social and communication problems than men. The authors warn that this outward ease may help explain why autistic women are often recognised late or missed entirely by services.
europmc-pmc3133555:
Kim-Anh Lê Cao, Simon Boitard, and Philippe Besse presented a statistics method for sorting samples into groups using gene data in a 2011 paper in BMC Bioinformatics. Such datasets hold thousands of measurements for few samples, so picking the few genes that truly separate groups is the hard part. Their method trims a known grouping technique down to a small, readable gene set.

Tested on public cancer gene data and genetic marker data, the method classified samples about as well as rival tools while running faster. Its real edge is display: charts show which genes drive each group split and how samples arrange, making results easier to explain to biologists. The method ships in a free software package for large biological datasets.
europmc-pmc3156955:
David Kelley, Michael Schatz, and Steven Salzberg introduced a program that fixes errors in DNA sequencing reads in a 2010 paper in Genome Biology. Fast sequencers read DNA in short pieces with a small but troublesome error rate, worst near read ends, and those errors tangle genome assembly and hide real variants. Their program uses the machines' own quality scores plus per-letter error rates in a probability model.

Tested on realistic simulated reads, the program corrected errors more accurately than rivals. Cleaning reads first measurably improved both fresh genome assembly and variant detection. It scales to billion-read human projects and is free as open-source software. The work shows redundant coverage, cheap with modern sequencers, can be spent on accuracy before analysis even begins.
europmc-pmc3195755:
Randy Read and colleagues reported a task force plan to modernise how protein structures are quality-checked in a 2011 paper in Structure. The world archive of protein structures had grown massively since its checking rules were written. Mandatory deposit of the raw diffraction data opened new ways to verify the underlying experiment. A worldwide task force rethought validation from scratch.

They recommend a small set of quality indicators presented in an easy format, scored against both the whole archive and structures of similar sharpness, with detail available on demand. Most importantly, journal referees and editors should receive a concise quality summary when judging a structural paper. The aim is to catch weak structures before they mislead the many fields that build on the archive.
europmc-pmc3197655:
Melissa Harrison and colleagues published this 2011 study in PLoS Genetics on how the fruit fly embryo switches on its own genes. Early development runs on materials the mother deposits in the egg, and the zinc-finger protein Zelda helps start the embryo's own transcription. The team mapped where Zelda binds DNA before, during, and after that handover.

Using chromatin profiling at three early stages, they found thousands of Zelda binding sites already present in very young embryos. Many sat at promoters of genes not switched on until later, and at nearly all known enhancers used during the transition. Zelda binding alone predicted active regulatory regions well, suggesting Zelda prepares large parts of the genome for activation.
europmc-pmc3237355:
Virginia Rauh and colleagues followed a New York City birth cohort to age seven. They tested whether prenatal exposure to the pesticide chlorpyrifos leaves lasting cognitive marks. The paper appeared in Environmental Health Perspectives in 2011. Earlier work on the same children had found developmental problems at age three. Exposure was measured in umbilical cord blood at birth.

At seven, the children took a standard intelligence test. Each step up in prenatal chlorpyrifos exposure was linked to lower full-scale IQ. The link to lower working memory scores was stronger still. The pattern held after adjusting for the mother's education and IQ and the home environment. The authors note the pesticide remained in wide agricultural use, so early deficits could carry real educational consequences as children move through school.
europmc-pmc3241555:
Michael Keidar and colleagues reported that cold plasma can kill cancer cells selectively, in this 2011 paper in the British Journal of Cancer. Plasma is ionized gas, usually hot, but newer devices make it at near room temperature. Earlier laboratory and animal work hinted such plasma might attack tumors while sparing healthy tissue, and the team put that claim to direct tests.

In dishes, cold plasma eradicated cancer cells while leaving normal cells undamaged. In animals, it significantly shrank tumors. Measurements pointed to disturbed handling of reactive oxygen species and altered stress-response genes inside treated cancer cells. The authors argue that tumor ablation with cold plasma could transform cancer treatment. It would put another state of matter to medical use. They acknowledge, though, that the mechanisms of plasma-cell interaction remain debated.
europmc-pmc3284555:
Tommy Cedervall and colleagues followed plastic nanoparticles up an aquatic food chain and into fish, in this 2012 paper in PLoS ONE. Nanoparticles are entering cosmetics, detergents, and foods with little known about their effects on metabolism. The team fed algae exposed to manufactured polystyrene nanoparticles to zooplankton, and those to fish, then compared the top consumers with controls.

Exposed fish lost weight differently, carried an altered balance of blood fats, and distributed cholesterol differently between muscle and liver. In test tubes the particles latched onto a fat-carrying blood protein, offering a mechanism: properly used fat reserves become harder to mobilize. Behavior changed too; exposed fish took more than twice as long to eat the food offered. The authors propose their setup as a screening bioassay before new nanomaterials are manufactured at scale.
europmc-pmc3291455:
McDonald, Owings, and Jernigan measured infections from the gut germ Clostridium difficile in United States hospitals, reporting in 2006. The spore forming germ is the best known cause of diarrhea linked to antibiotic use, and severe cases can destroy the colon. Small hospital reports hinted that cases were climbing, but no national picture existed.

Using a national survey of hospital discharge records from 1996 through 2003, the team estimated how many patients left hospital with this diagnosis each year. Their analysis showed the rate rising over the period, confirming the warnings from single hospitals. They urged clinicians to watch for the disease more carefully and to work harder on stopping its spread between patients.
europmc-pmc3297555:
Huys and co-authors studied how people cut short their planning when a big loss appears, in a 2012 brain science paper. Planning ahead means weighing long chains of choices, and checking every branch is impossible. Volunteers played a new game of sequential choices for rewards and losses while the team tracked the shortcuts they used.

Players stopped weighing any path as soon as it contained a large loss, even when that habit clearly hurt their score. The reflex went beyond simple dislike of losses, acting like an automatic brake switched on by bad outcomes. People with more low mood symptoms pruned this way more strongly. The authors link this built in brake to theories of mood disorders and the brain chemical serotonin.
europmc-pmc3299755:
Vásquez and colleagues described the helpful bacteria living in the honey stomach of bees, in a 2012 study. Lactic acid bacteria are well known partners in the guts of humans and farm animals, but their roles in insects were largely unexplored. The team sampled every living honeybee species, along with related bees, and cataloged the bacteria in the crop where bees carry nectar.

They found a rich and ancient community, including many species new to science from two familiar bacterial genera. One species dominates the crop, and young worker bees pick up the microbes from nest mates and keep them in films lining the crop. Several of the bacteria kill germs that threaten bees. The authors suggest that feeding these bacteria could help protect pollinators, though some beekeeping habits may harm them.
europmc-pmc3364955:
Boissière and collaborators catalogued the bacteria living in the gut of Anopheles gambiae, the main African malaria mosquito, and asked whether that microbial community influences infection with the malaria parasite. They collected mosquitoes from natural breeding sites in Cameroon, challenged them with a wild parasite isolate, and sequenced their midgut bacteria.

The gut flora proved richer than previously described, yet most bacterial types appeared in only a few mosquitoes, and breeding site strongly shaped the community each adult carried. One pattern stood out: the abundance of Enterobacteriaceae in the midgut correlated significantly with whether the mosquito became infected. The authors suggest the natural gut environment helps decide transmission success.
europmc-pmc3367655:
Li and colleagues investigated a Japanese case of hepatitis E in 2005 that followed a meal of wild boar meat. Hepatitis E virus usually spreads through dirty water, but animal links had been suspected for years. The team tested both the patient's blood and the leftover meat from the animal eaten.

Both samples carried genotype 3 virus RNA, and the match gave direct proof of foodborne spread from boar to human. Earlier Japanese cases had been tied to raw deer meat and undercooked pork liver. europmc-pmc3416655:
Wang, Qu, and Zhao reviewed clinical uses of mesenchymal stem cells in 2012, a therapy that had drawn a decade of enthusiasm. Trials had already tested these cells in at least a dozen conditions. Completed trials in several diseases pointed to both safety and real benefit, with graft-versus-host disease and heart and vessel diseases singled out.

Four gifts explain the appeal, the authors argue. Injected cells home to injured, inflamed sites. They can mature into varied cell types, release helpful molecules that spur repair and calm inflammation, and tune the immune system itself. The review also tackles the practical hurdles of making clinical-grade cells and sets principles for moving the therapy from bench to bedside.
europmc-pmc3430255:
Chemat, Vian, and Cravotto set out six principles for green extraction of natural products in 2012, the pulling of valuable compounds from plants and other natural sources. Extraction hides inside perfumes, medicines, foods, and cosmetics, yet it eats at least half the energy of many production processes and floods of solvent for tiny yields. The principles rest on fresh technology, tighter processes, farm-based solvents, and energy savings. Examples run from a milliliter of rose absolute that costs a kilo of roses to large food and drug operations. The authors offer the concept as a working protocol, not just a wish. Cleaner extraction, they argue, is where the field's inventive effort is flowing.
europmc-pmc3465555:

Martello's group concludes Esrrb is both needed and enough to carry the signal.

faraday-experimental-researches-vol3-185:
Volume 3 of Faraday's Experimental Researches in Electricity appeared in 1855, holding Series 20 through 30. Michael Faraday's later series turned to magnetism's action on light and to the magnetic character of all matter. The volume completes the great run of his electrical papers.

Faraday showed that a magnetic field rotates the plane of polarized light, the first proof that light and magnetism are linked. He sorted materials into magnetic and diamagnetic kinds and mapped fields with iron filings. His lines of force, once doubted, here stand as a full way of picturing electric action. Maxwell built his equations on this ground. The volume closes a founding work of physics.
fielding-voyage-lisbon-1755:
Fielding's Journal of a Voyage to Lisbon appeared in 1755, months after his death. Dying of dropsy and gout, he had sailed for Portugal in 1754 seeking health, as his doctors advised. He kept a journal of the slow, painful crossing.

Storms, calms, bad food, and a bullying captain fill the record, told with wit that pain could not kill. Fielding also argues for reforms in how England fed and shipped its sailors. His farewell preface, knowing he would not return, is among his most moving pages. The little book closes the career of the novelist who founded a form and served as London's magistrate.
frus-1861-d155:
On 10 October 1861, William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton as the war moved to the coasts. The letter is document 155 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

October brought the war to the coasts, with expeditions fitting out in Northern ports. Paris watched those moves for signs of Union strength. Seward's letter guided Dayton's reading of the season for the French court. A port expedition sailed for the Carolina coast late that October month. A Carolina expedition that month gave Paris fresh proof of Union reach at sea. It sailed under Du Pont and struck Port Royal in the first week of November.
frus-1861-d255:
From his post abroad, James Shepherd Pike wrote to William H. Seward on 25 September 1861. It stands as Document 255 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d55:
A letter of 19 June 1861 went from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams in London. The letter is document 55 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's June letters mixed firm words with care not to push Britain too far. He knew a quarrel with London could doom the Union. This note to Adams keeps that balance, pressing the Union's rights while leaving the door open for British good will. Adams prized that balance and matched Seward's firmness with a cooler tone in person. A cooler tone in person let Adams press hard points without giving offense.
frus-1862-d155:
Writing from London on 3 October 1862, Charles Francis Adams sent a report to Secretary of State William H. Seward, preserved as Document 155 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Adams served as American minister to Britain through the whole Civil War.

October opened with British debate over the American war still unsettled. A report from Adams carried his read of ministers, newspapers, and public feeling in London, the raw material for Washington's next moves. Taken with the letters around it, this dispatch helps trace how the threat of British action rose and fell that fall. Southern agents worked London's clubs and press hard, and the legation tracked their moves.
frus-1862-d255:
On 27 February 1862 William L. Dayton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward from Paris, in a report printed as Document 255 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of two Paris papers under that date.

Dayton's mail sailed from French ports and took about two weeks to reach Washington, so his news was seasoned by the time Seward read it. Even so, his read on the French court set the frame for American replies. This report closes the February run of the Paris file, a month of Union wins and watchful quiet from France. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived.
frus-1862-d355:
A second Thouvenel instruction to Henri Mercier followed on 23 January 1862, printed as Document 355 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Edouard Thouvenel directed French foreign policy from Paris; Mercier carried it out in Washington.

Two instructions in five days suggest Paris was refining its guidance as news arrived from America and Mexico. The Atlantic lag meant such orders often answered month-old reports. Even so, the pair shows the machinery of French policy at work, and it helps explain the positions Mercier took with Seward that winter. France and Britain consulted each other often before either acted on the American war.
frus-1862-d455:
John Lothrop Motley, the American minister in Vienna, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 1 November 1861. It is Document 455 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the earliest Austrian paper in the file.

Motley had just taken up the Vienna post, and his first reports sized up an empire wary of republics and revolutions. Austria watched the American war through its own fears, yet it had little love for Britain's or France's games either. A new minister's first impressions mattered in Washington, where Seward was sorting Europe into friends, neutrals, and risks. The report opens the Austrian correspondence with a historian's eye for the forces moving under the surface.
frus-1862-d55:
On 1 May 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It stands as Document 55 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. It belongs to the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d555:
Four days after his last, on 10 May 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this instruction to Henry Shelton Sanford in Brussels. It is Document 555 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's record.

The short gap between orders reflects Sanford's habit of asking questions and Seward's habit of answering them. Brussels in 1862 was a crossroads of European gossip and intrigue, where Confederate agents also worked. A minister there needed fresh instructions often. The letter belongs to the busy spring file of the Belgian mission. In that file Washington treated a small court as a serious post. The man holding it had made it one.
frus-1862-d655:
On 15 November 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Robert H. Pruyn, the man picked to head the American legation in Japan. The letter is document 655 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. Pruyn would take over from Townsend Harris, the first man to hold the post.

Letters to an envoy on his way out carried the charge for his mission. It told what to seek, what to avoid, and how to speak for his government. Seward's note to Pruyn is part of that hand-over. It marks the point where the Japan post passed from its founder to the men who would hold it through the war.
frus-1863p1-d155:
On 13 April 1863, William H. Seward sent this second letter of the day to Charles Francis Adams in London. Adams was the American minister there. The letter is document 155 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet of Seward's 13 April pair held its own point, in the habit of the whole file. Such splits let Adams raise each matter with the British in its own time and words. This letter closes the day's work from Washington. It belongs to the steady stream that, by the spring of 1863, had made the London brief a model of its kind.
frus-1863p1-d255:
Writing from London on 30 July 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington.
