The dispatch is document 255 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d355:
Britain's side of the Washington exchange speaks in this note, sent by Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 January 1863. It is document 355 of the 1863 papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Lyons wrote as the voice of the British government in Washington. His notes carried protests, questions, and warnings that Seward had to answer with care. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d455:
Secretary William H. Seward sent an official note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 9 April 1863. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d55:
Christopher G. Memminger wrote this letter to Messrs. Fraser, Trenholm & Co. on 24 October 1862. Memminger ran the Confederate treasury. The firm, based in Liverpool with roots in Charleston, acted as the South's bankers in Britain. The letter is document 55 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Through Fraser, Trenholm & Co. flowed the South's money in Europe: cotton sales in, ships and arms out. A treasury letter to the firm dealt with the heart of the war's finance. This one is part of the Confederate group printed by the Union. It shows the South's cause resting, in no small part, on a Liverpool counting house.
frus-1863p1-d555:
A letter of 6 June 1863, from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, stands as document 555 in the printed record. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The State Department later published the letter in its 1863 foreign affairs volume, laid before Congress with the President's message. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d655:
From Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London to Secretary William H. Seward: a letter dated 5 November 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. Adams's task was to make the Union's case where it counted, inside the British capital, while Seward set the line from Washington. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d155: A third Churchill note to Roosevelt bears the date November 21, 1943, and it is Document 155 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Three messages in one day, hours before the gavel, close the letters section of the Cairo story in this run. The record names the parties and the date only. The note survives in the Foreign Relations series, a last word on paper before talk replaced writing.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d255:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 23 November 1943, at eleven in the morning, record a plenary session on Southeast Asia operations with the Chinese delegation present. President Roosevelt opened by welcoming Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek and Madame Chiang, calling the meeting historic.

Lord Mountbatten then laid out his Burma campaign. Two Chinese divisions were already moving from Ledo. British Indian corps would advance on the Arakan and Imphal fronts from mid-January. Wingate's long-range groups would thrust deep in February, with gliders ahead of the Yunnan forces. A parachute brigade would seize Indaw airfield in March for a division to fly in. Mountbatten stressed the brutal supply lines, jungle, and mountains facing the Allies, against Japan's easier river and rail routes.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d355: An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume records that this Tehran meeting appears in the President's Log, but that no record of the conversation has been found. The visit of the Soviet chargé d'affaires lasted at most twenty minutes. From its brevity and place in the schedule, the editors judge that it was presumably a courtesy call, and they print the note only to account for the entry in the Log.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d455: Document 455 offers guidance from the volume's editors, in note form. The State Department published the Cairo-Tehran volume as the official conference record. Its historians wrote notes to supply context and mark related files. The papers around the note date from the 1943 summit season. Leaders met in Cairo, flew to Tehran, then returned to Cairo. A short editorial note helps readers track that movement and its stakes.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d55: Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on October 25, 1943, and the letter is Document 55 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. That same day the volume also holds a memorandum by Secretary Hull, then still in Moscow. The record for the letter names the parties and the date only. It belongs, in the Foreign Relations series, to the last week of the Moscow Conference and the turn toward Cairo and Tehran.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d555:
A second message from Prime Minister Churchill reached President Roosevelt on March 3, 1944. Two Churchill messages in a day was no record, but it marks a crowded agenda between London and Washington. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Churchill used separate messages to keep subjects apart, giving each question its own paper and its own pressure. Paired messages let historians see what he thought could not wait and what he wanted answered together. For readers, this second text completes a day's diplomacy between the two leaders, three months before the Normandy landings, when every week carried decisions that could not be recalled.
frus-1944-quebec-d155:
Secretary Hull forwarded the British aide-mémoire on French participation in the Pacific war to Roosevelt on August 26, 1944. His covering memorandum is brief and points to the deadline: Eden wanted to answer the French before their envoy left London on August 29. Two proposals needed a yes or no from the president himself.

The first would attach a French military mission under General Blaizot to Southeast Asia Command headquarters. The second would establish in India a Corps Léger d'Intervention, apparently already formed at Algiers. Hull warned that although the suggestions looked military, they carried wide political implications. For that reason, he wrote, they were referred to Roosevelt for decision rather than settled by the department.
frus-1944-quebec-d255:
The Combined Chiefs approved Eisenhower's Scaf 78 proposals on September 12, 1944, and sent their approval from Quebec with two pointed additions. The message, Facs 78, was drafted at the 172d meeting, where Brooke had argued Eisenhower understressed the northern approach and the ports. Both points went into the text.

First, the chiefs drew Eisenhower's attention to the advantages of the northern line of approach into Germany over the southern, noting with satisfaction that he appeared of the same mind. Second, they stressed the necessity of opening the northwest ports, particularly Antwerp and Rotterdam, before bad weather set in. Approval, in other words, came with a clear statement of allied priorities.
frus-1944-quebec-d55:
Lester B. Pearson wrote again to Harry Hopkins on September 6, 1944. Pearson was Canada's ambassador in Washington. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume. It sits among the pre-conference staff papers.

Two Pearson messages in four days mark quickening Canadian arrangements. The conference was fast approaching by then. Quebec City would host Roosevelt and Churchill. Both leaders brought large staffs with them. Canada's diplomats smoothed the way from both capitals. For readers, the message underlines a summit's hidden labor. Host country envoys supplied that labor capably in 1944. Their work rarely reached the headlines.
frus-1945-50-intel-d155:
The meeting named in the title took place on 10 June 1946, and these minutes are its formal record. It is document 155 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

No speeches fill these pages; the form is a tight note of points made and ground covered, kept for later use. For a reader now, the draw is the nearness: this is the meeting as its own staff chose to keep it. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d255:
A memorandum from the Executive Secretary (Souers) reached the National Security Council on 16 December 1947. It survives in print as document 255 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. It was the first autumn of the new system: a fresh CIA, a fresh Council, and piles of first-year business.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d355:
Formal minutes cover a meeting of the Intelligence Advisory Committee, held on 3 December 1948. It survives in print as document 355 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. Three men — Dulles, Jackson, and Correa — were touring the CIA's work for the Council and taking notes for a report.

The pages give the meeting in the plain form staff used at the time: a topic, the sense of the talk, and the result. The brevity is the point: what the group did not settle, the minutes do not claim it did. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d55:
Minutes dated 11 December 1945 record a meeting held the day after Byrnes wrote to the two service secretaries. The December papers of the volume move at decision speed. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Meetings in the last weeks of a long fight tend to ratify what letters have already settled, and to park what they could not. These minutes belong to that stage of the intelligence contest. Readers can check them against the correspondence around them to see which questions still resisted answer. Within six weeks the president would issue his directive creating the new authority. The trail of paper in this volume leads straight to that act.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d155:
Roosevelt warned Stalin on 16 December 1944 that Washington might soon have to speak in public on Poland. His personal and top secret telegram, number 136, was sent from Warm Springs and is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Churchill's Commons speech and the pressure behind it frame the message.

The statement, if issued, would run on set lines. The United States stands without qualification for a strong, free, independent, and democratic Poland. Frontier questions should in principle await the general postwar settlement. Still, Washington would not object if those concerned settled them by mutual agreement, with Germany making up Poland's losses. The message also accepts that moving national minorities can, in some cases, serve security and calm.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d255:
Stalin laid out his Far East terms at a Moscow meeting, and Harriman reported them on 15 October 1944. Eden sat in for Churchill that day. General Antonov presented the Soviet estimate of Japanese strength in Manchuria, which ran higher than the allied figure. The report is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

To strike Japan, Antonov explained, Russia must first build up her Far East forces by thirty divisions. With the thirty already there, that makes sixty in all. The build-up would take two and a half to three months after Germany's collapse. Stalin then answered questions himself. He wants a two to three months' stock of food and fuel built up from now on, with rails and railroad gear among the needs.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d355:
Voting in the Security Council was the one big question left open after Dumbarton Oaks. This American statement of February 6, 1945, sets out the position. It reviews how the three delegations had studied the matter without settling it. On December 5, 1944, Roosevelt had sent Stalin and Churchill a proposed text for the voting section.

The statement reprints that proposal and builds the case for it. Under the American formula, each council member would have one vote. Routine matters would pass with seven votes. The paper is the brief Stettinius carried into the Yalta debate that finally unlocked the United Nations plan.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d455:
Do not let the Russians down. That is Harry Hopkins's plea in this note to the President, passed at the seventh plenary meeting on February 10, 1945. The Russians had given in so much at the conference, Hopkins wrote, that America should not abandon them now. Let the British disagree if they wished, and keep disagreeing at Moscow.

His advice on reparations was simple. Say the whole matter is referred to the Reparations Commission, with the minutes showing British disagreement about any mention of the ten billion. The slip shows Hopkins, ill and exhausted, still steering the President toward keeping Stalin inside the settlement.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d55:
Admiral William Leahy, the President's chief of staff, wrote to President Roosevelt at Hyde Park on 13 January 1945. His short note passes along the reply Roosevelt had just sent to Churchill about moving American ships into the Black Sea. The exchange appears in the Foreign Relations volume covering the Malta and Yalta conferences.

The reply directs the State Department to work through Ambassador Steinhardt in Turkey. Its goal is free passage for the naval auxiliary Catoctin, described as not a combatant vessel, plus four smaller ships that were really minesweepers. The same notice to the Turks would cover American planes flying the President's party and daily mail trips.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d155:
Admiral Leahy gave the Joint Chiefs' staff a list of study questions on June 15, 1945. His memorandum is document 155 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The subjects had been named to the President as likely to come up at the three-power meeting, and Leahy wants brief, useful recommendations as a matter of urgency.

The ten questions are mostly about Germany: dismemberment, the Ruhr and Saar, coal for Europe, trade between the zones, civil government, banking and money, and a single agreed propaganda line. The list also covers the German fleet, the treatment of war criminals, and the timing and terms of a peace treaty with Italy. Notes in the volume point to the papers each question produced, showing how Truman's briefing book was built.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d255:
A briefing memorandum urged settling the United Nations' first officers at Potsdam, dated July 4, 1945. The paper for the President is document 255 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The Preparatory Commission, set up to launch the new world organization, had left its two top posts unfilled at San Francisco.

The choice of a chairman for the Executive Committee and of an executive secretary should be settled when Truman meets Churchill and Stalin, the paper argues. The Executive Committee hopes to meet in London in the first week of August, so speed matters. The Soviet government attaches great weight to the chairmanship, the paper notes. Moscow will likely ask for the post itself, or propose rotating it among the Big Five as was done with the presidency at San Francisco.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d355:
Admiral Leahy, the President's chief of staff, reduced the Dutch flood question to a single proposal in an undated note. The Germans, during their occupation of Holland, had let salt water flood Dutch farmland. Leahy proposed that the Reparations Commission be directed to act on that wrong.

The Commission, he wrote, should recommend that Holland occupy, for a time, an area of German farm land next to its border. The area would equal the Dutch acreage the salt water had ruined. The note, kept with the Truman papers, shows how reparations thinking at the top could turn from money and machines to land itself.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d455:
Belgrade's press campaign over Macedonia is sampled in an extract from Shantz's telegram of June 25, 1945. The Yugoslav paper Borba carried a long editorial that day condemning what it called a Fascist reign of terror in Aegean Macedonia. The methods of EDES, the Greek resistance group, were compared to those of Hitler's SS troops.

The editorial also likened them to those of Greek reactionaries in the late nineteenth century. Greek slogans such as to Bitolj, and we want all of Macedonia, were cited as proof of Greek intentions. The campaign charged that Athens sought pretexts for a program to liquidate anti-Fascist forces in Greece. Shantz's extract shows Tito's press war warming up.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d55:
Churchill turned to practical matters in telegram number 82 to President Truman, sent from London on June 9, 1945. It is document 55 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. He had agreed in principle to the Berlin meeting on July 15, but he wanted the living arrangements settled in advance.

Churchill proposes that the British, American, and Russian groups each get separate quarters with their own guards, plus a fourth place set aside for joint sessions. He refuses to repeat Yalta, where the Western leaders were guests of the Soviet government. In Berlin, he insists, they should provide everything for themselves and meet on equal terms. He asks Truman where he stands on the idea.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d555:
Jefferson Caffery, the U.S. ambassador in Paris, wired Washington on July 10, 1945. His secret report is document 555 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It gives the views of Vladko Macek, head of the Croatian Peasant Party, who was then in France.

Macek called Yugoslavia a communist dictatorship with no democracy in the Anglo-Saxon sense. Of eleven men in the Croatian federal government, he said, nine are communists. He warned that peasant parties were being wiped out in Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, Rumania, and Poland. Subasic, he said, has no power, and the same fate awaits Poland's Mikolajczyk. Macek wanted to reach London to see King Peter, but the British were blocking his trip.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d655:
Ambassador Caffery reported French foreign minister Bidault's stand on the Tangier venue from Paris, June 25, 1945. His secret wire is document 655 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Venue had become a point of pride between Paris and London.

Bidault agreed that a decision on the meeting place was needed at once. He complained that he got almost no word of weight from London at that juncture. Churchill, he added, was too busy electioneering and trying to kick France out of the Levant. Bidault insisted the French would not go to London to discuss Tangier. He agreed that Moscow should be informed, as Washington proposed. He also agreed the host government might properly make that approach itself.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1055:
The Soviet delegation sent this aide-mémoire to the American delegation at Potsdam on July 25, 1945. The printed text is an extract, in translation. It complains of anti-Soviet activity by white Russian emigrants inside the western occupation zones of Germany. French military security men, it claims, actively back such work in the French army's zone.

In the British and American zones, the paper names a committee led by General Skoropadski and three others. It says the group set up Ukrainian Committees in several German cities in June 1945. Members carry printed certificates, sealed by a self-styled President of the Free Ukraine. They move freely among the zones and stir hostility in camps holding Soviet citizens.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1155:
Will Clayton wrote to McCabe, the Army-Navy Liquidation Commissioner, on 26 July 1945. McCabe's office wound down America's vast wartime supply machine. It sold off surplus goods and settled accounts with the allies who had received them.

Clayton, the State Department's chief for money matters, had to mesh that wind-down with foreign policy. What was sold, forgiven, or claimed abroad touched every ally's ties with Washington. A note between the two men joins the summit's money talks to the plain work of ending the supply programs. It shows the peace being priced at the working level.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1255: Ayers, the White House information officer, wrote to Ross, the president's secretary, on 27 July 1945. Both men handled the president's public word: what was said to the press, and when. Their channel served the traveling court at Potsdam. Ross spoke for Truman to reporters, and Ayers helped shape the daily flow of news. Their notes kept that flow in order.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1355:
Ambassador Jefferson Caffery in Paris cabled Secretary Byrnes directly on 21 July 1945. Byrnes was at Potsdam, so the cable went to the secretary at the summit rather than to Washington. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official American diplomatic record, prints it in the second volume on the Potsdam Conference.

Writing straight to the secretary abroad shows a matter Caffery judged too pressing for the home office queue. France, left out of the Potsdam room, pressed its claims through its friends wherever it could. This cable catches that pressure in motion. It also shows how the summit pulled the department's business toward Germany. With ambassadors aiming their reports at the men who could act on them at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-155: Printed in the unnumbered run after document 710, this note carries the voice of the Potsdam volume's editors. Editorial notes in the Foreign Relations series mark the join between papers. They tell readers what a file held and what it lacked. This one adds a measure of trust and order to the record it sits in.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-55:
Benjamin Cohen's notes on the plenary session of July 21, 1945, give the Polish assets debate in direct speech. They are an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Cohen's record begins with the foreign secretaries' report being read to the three leaders.

The report brought the Polish question up as the first item for decision. Byrnes named the first point of difference plainly. It was the transfer of the London Polish government's assets without any mention of its liabilities. Truman stated the U.S. position in law and in intent. When assets are transferred under U.S. law, liabilities must be transferred too. The United States did not intend to assume the old government's debts and hand the new government its assets. Churchill backed the President's proposals, and above all the rule of no release of assets without consideration of liabilities.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d755:
Document 755 is a proposal tabled by the United States delegation on July 23, 1945. The conference was then a week old. American drafts kept coming in a steady flow. Each one moved a topic from talk toward text. This proposal was printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

By the second week, proposals were written to be traded. A line offered here might buy a line elsewhere. Readers can sense that craft in a July 23 text. The document marks the point where the conference shifted from stating aims to swapping them. It is a working part of the machine that produced the final protocol.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d855:
The Central Secretariat recorded this memorandum on July 18, 1945, as document 855. The secretariat served the whole conference, not one delegation. It logged texts, kept records, and moved paper among three governments. This memo dates from the opening days. It was printed in the second Potsdam volume.

A secretariat memo shows the conference as a system. Someone had to know where every text stood. Readers gain respect for that invisible labor. The document also helps explain the record's completeness: the secretariat's habits are why so much survives. Its staff were the summit's memory, hired to forget nothing.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d955:
American staff set out these comments on July 30, 1945, on paragraphs 3, 5, and 6 of the Soviet reparations proposal. The paper is a fuller twin of the comments printed just before it. Its main target is the Soviet plan to express capital removals in tons.

Tonnage, the staff argues, says nothing about value or military importance. Machinery differs too widely for weight to serve as a measure. Quotas in tons would push indiscriminate stripping of working plants. The only sound basis is agreed productive capacity to be removed from war industries. On yearly deliveries, the staff accepts the Soviet product list as a starting point for discussion.
frus-1952-54v13p1-d455: A 1952-1954 FRUS document from the consul at Hanoi in the Indochina volume. France's war in Vietnam ground on. This entry holds that report. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
frus-1961-63v11-d155: A 1961-1963 FRUS letter from the Missile Crisis volume. The correspondence of the crisis. This document holds that letter. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. Its place in history is secure.
gao-gaoreports-b-296355: Burns and Roe Services took its July 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-298355: Glen/Mar Construction took its August 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Builders get the same full hearing as everyone.
gao-gaoreports-b-309955: A 2007 GAO ruling on a contract fight from Nautical Engineering, Inc. The marine firm said the agency's pick broke the rules of fair bidding; the ruling puts each claim to the test. Published rulings like this guide the next round — they tell agencies and bidders alike where the legal lines are drawn.
gao-gaoreports-b-310155: This 2007 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by SAGE Systems Technologies, LLC. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. The ruling sets ground rules for future federal contract contests. Its full text is kept in the library next to this description.
gao-gaoreports-b-400255: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Murray-Benjamin Electric Company, L.P. The August 7, 2008 ruling examines how the agency evaluated the bids. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-255: The Navy's new littoral ships needed proving time in 2005, and GAO's report says the plans had to allow enough time to demonstrate capability. The review pumps the brakes. The first ships deserved the sea trials. The time had to be allowed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-555: DOD's use of VA's mail pharmacy could save money in 2005, and GAO's report says the switch could produce savings and benefits. The findings do the math. The report warns that the troops' prescriptions deserved smart buying. The savings had to be seized.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-955: Judges' family pensions got a GAO cost look in 2005, and the report prices the survivors' payouts. The findings do the math. The report warns that the judicial widows deserved honest accounting. The judicial widows deserved honest accounting. The payouts had to be priced.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1055: Foreign worker programs got a GAO survey in 2006, and the report shares selected countries' experiences. The findings gather the lessons. The report shows the world wrestled with the same labor questions. The experiences had to be studied. The labor lessons crossed borders.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-55: Health professions education programs got a GAO review in 2006, and the report examines the training pipeline. The findings take the measure. The report warns that the nation's healers needed good training. The programs had to be sound. The healers needed good training.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-655: Expedited hurricane aid was a fraud magnet in 2006, and GAO's report says FEMA's weak controls exposed the government to abuse. The findings document the looting. The report warns that the storm's victims should not compete with thieves. The controls had to be fixed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-955: The Pentagon's radio overhaul was less risky but still troubled in 2006, and GAO's report says the restructured program cut risk, though challenges remained. The findings balance credit and caution. The report warns that the troops' radios still needed work. The program had to deliver.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-255: The bank insurer's people programs looked sound in 2007, and GAO's report says the human capital and risk efforts appeared solid, though evaluation lagged. The findings credit the design. The report's nudge: good programs still need proof they work. The proof had to follow the promise.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-355: Employers were trimming health and pension perks in 2007 — GAO's report tracks the cost-cutting and what it meant for workers. The findings map the squeeze in detail. The report's warning: the shrinking benefit was the quiet pay cut of the decade.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-455: Homeland Security's many networks were talking past each other in 2007 — GAO's report says the federal systems needed to be better joined up. The findings demand the wiring be linked. The report's point: a homeland split in its data cannot stand secure.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-555: Poor seniors were missing their drug discount in 2007 — GAO's report says Social Security needed to push harder on outreach for the low-income drug subsidy. The findings measure the enrollment gap. The report's plea: the cheapest benefit is the one people actually claim.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-655: The fire agencies were fighting blind in 2007 — GAO's report says no clear goals or strategy guided the costly war on wildfire. The findings describe big spending without a compass. The report demands what every campaign needs: know what winning looks like before you pay for it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-355: GAO published its findings on bank Secrecy Act: Increased Use of Exemption Provisions Could Reduce Currency Transaction Reporting While Maintaining Usefulness to Law Enforcement Efforts in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-855: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at post-Government Employment Restrictions and Foreign Agent Registration: Additional Action Needed to Enhance Implementation of Requirements. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-955: The Government Accountability Office dug into medicare: Covert Testing Exposes Weaknesses in the Durable Medical Equipment Supplier Screening Process in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gesner-historia-animalium-lib3-1555:
Birds take the stage in the third volume of Gesner's Historiae animalium, published in 1555. Gesner sorts the birds of Europe and beyond, from eagles down to sparrows. The volume carries the fine woodcut portraits that made the whole series famous in its own century and ours.

Each entry gives names in many tongues, then habits, food, and human uses. Gesner reports country lore beside the reports of ancient writers. He judges what he can and marks what rests on hearsay. The result is the ornithology of the Renaissance in one great tome. Bird lovers still open it for the pictures alone, then stay for the learning.
hare-experimental-investigation-spirit-m:
Robert Hare was a US chemist of note who built lab gear. His Experimental Investigation of the Spirit Manifestations came out in 1855. Hare had set out to mock the spirit craze of his day. His tests with his own gear, the spiritoscope, turned his mind round.

The gear was made to bar fraud: the medium could not touch the dial. Yet the dial moved, Hare says, and spelled out words of sense. He came out in print as a convert to the new creed. The book is the first of its kind to bring lab craft to the seance.
heptameron-turner-1655:
The Heptameron is a seven-day book of spirit conjurations ascribed to Peter de Abano, the medieval Italian physician. Robert Turner Englished it in 1655, printing the Latin alongside his translation. For three centuries afterward, Turner's version stood as the standard English Heptameron for workers in the art.

Each day of the week has its angels, hours, perfumes, and prayers. The magician follows the planet that rules the day and calls its spirits in order. Circles, robes, and conjurations are specified with care. The book's weekly rhythm makes it a working calendar of magic. Turner's plain English brought a Latin classic within reach of English practitioners.
history-of-the-catholic-church-from-the-: This edition of James MacCaffrey's church history covers the Renaissance to the French Revolution: reformations, councils, and the Church under siege. Fair-minded and thorough, it remains a reliable guide. The Catholic story, told with balance.
hutcheson-system-moral-philosophy-vol1-1:
Hutcheson's System of Moral Philosophy appeared in 1755, eight years after his death, published by his son from the Glasgow lectures. Hutcheson had been the most beloved teacher of the Scottish Enlightenment. The System was meant as his summa, the full statement of the moral thought he had taught for years.

Volume 1 opens with human nature: the senses, the passions, and above all the moral sense by which we approve virtue. Hutcheson argues that virtue is discerned by feeling rightly trained, not by cold reason alone. His famous standard, the greatest happiness of the greatest numbers, appears here in an early form. The volume made the teacher's fame permanent and set the agenda for his student Adam Smith. It remains the foundation book of the moral-sense school.
hutcheson-system-moral-philosophy-vol2-1:
The second volume of Hutcheson's System of Moral Philosophy followed the first in 1755, completing the posthumous work. Volume 1 had grounded morals in the moral sense. Volume 2 puts that system to work on the questions of law, rights, and government.

Hutcheson treats the rights of individuals, the grounds of political authority, and the duties that come with each station in life. He defends a right of resistance when rulers destroy the ends for which government exists, a doctrine with a long afterlife in America. Property, contracts, marriage, and war all receive careful, humane treatment. The closing book turns moral thought into political thought. Readers have called the System the charter of the Scottish Enlightenment, with liberty rooted in the moral sense itself.
inigo-jones-stone-heng-restored-1655:
Architect Inigo Jones surveyed Stonehenge for King James and gave his verdict in Stone-Heng Restored. The book appeared in 1655, after Jones's death. Jones had reshaped English building with classical design.

He argues the stones are a Roman temple, built to a sky god. His drawings impose neat geometry on the rough circle. The theory is wrong, as later work has shown. Yet the survey counts as a pioneering act of field study. Jones treated the ruin as architecture to measure, not magic to fear, and that shift mattered. Bold error can still move a field forward.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lowenthal-natha:
Nathan Löwenthal, a Russian histologist born in 1856, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Isidore Singer. Histology is the study of body tissues under the microscope. He was educated at St. Petersburg, Kiev, and Geneva, worked as assistant to Schiff at Geneva, and became professor of histology at Lausanne in 1890.

The article is mainly a long list of his studies, published in German and French journals between 1883 and 1903. They cover degeneration after injury, pathways in the spinal cord and brain, cell structure, and the making of sperm and eggs in animals. It also names two books, a histology volume printed at Paris in 1901 and an atlas of vertebrate histology printed at Berlin in 1904. The entry works best as a period bibliography of a laboratory scientist’s output.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magdeburg-10255:
Magdeburg, capital of Prussian Saxony on the Elbe, receives a community history in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. About two thousand of its 229,633 people were Jews when the article was written. Jews lived there as early as the tenth century. Their district, the Judendorf, lay outside the city and answered to the archbishop.

The article opens with two imperial documents. In 965 Otto the Great placed Magdeburg's Jews and traders under the archbishop's sole control. A similar document of Otto II followed in 973. From these the writers infer a community already large and vital to the town's trade. They note the Jewish traveler Ibrahim ibn Ya'qub, who appeared at Otto's court that same year. Jews mourned publicly at an archbishop's funeral in 1012. Yet the First Crusade is said to have driven them from the Judendorf. The entry frames a typical German pattern of protection and expulsion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mandelstamm-max:
Max Emanuel Mandelstamm, a Russian eye doctor and Zionist, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born in Zhagory in 1838, he studied medicine at Dorpat and Kharkof, graduating in 1860. In Berlin he trained under Graefe and Virchow. He settled in Kiev in 1868 and still lived there in 1904.

The article joins his medical fame to a blocked career. He ranked among Russia's leading oculists and lectured at Kiev University for twelve years. Three times he was chosen professor there. Each election was voided because he was a Jew. He headed the university eye clinic for four years and founded his own hospital in 1880. In Jewish life he led emigration aid after the 1881 riots. He also pled the Jewish cause before the official commission on the riots. A leading figure at the Zionist congresses, he wrote for their papers as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-maryland-10455:
Maryland was one of the thirteen original American states. Cyrus Adler and J. H. Hollander survey its Jewish history in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. They divide that history into three periods: the colonial years from 1634 come first. The second runs from the decades before the Revolution to the removal of Jewish political disabilities in 1826. The third covers the era of German immigration and congregational growth that followed.

The opening sections stress how quiet the colonial record is. Unlike New York or Charleston, Maryland saw no single wave of Jewish settlement. Jews seem to have drifted in one by one. Names such as Mathias de Sousa appear as early as 1639. The one clearly documented figure is Jacob Lumbrozo, an early medical practitioner and a busy man in the province's economic life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-megillat-ta-ani:
Megillat Ta'anit, the “Scroll of Fasting,” is a calendar of Jewish holidays. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach examine it in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. It lists thirty-five days of glorious deeds and joyful events on which fasting was forbidden. On fourteen of them public mourning was banned as well. The work has two layers: terse Aramaic notices, and Hebrew scholia, or comments, explaining them.

The days run by the calendar, Nisan to Adar, not by the order of the events, and the article sorts them into five ages. They run from before the Maccabees through the Hasmoneans and the Roman period to days admitted after the destruction of the Temple. It also insists the compilers invented nothing. These feasts were kept by the people long before anyone wrote the list. The work of the scroll was to grade them, assigning the lesser days a ban on fasting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendel-10655:
Mendel is the name of a Hungarian family of Buda. Its three known generations supplied Hungary's Jews with their official chief. Gotthard Deutsch and Ludwig Venetianer tell the story in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jacob, Israel, and Isaac Mendel held the chief office in succession. They held it between 1482 and 1539. The office was styled Princeps, Supremus, or Praefectus Judaeorum. That last title means prefect of the Jews.

King Matthias created the post, the article explains. The Jews would thus have an accredited representative at court. That man was answerable for their taxes. The prefect could fine and otherwise punish Jews. As an official of the crown, he alone was exempt from wearing the Jews' hat. The office seems to have existed only in those decades. The entry ends with the family's run in it. It rests on Hungarian histories of the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyer-leopold-1:
Leopold Meyer, a Danish physician born in Copenhagen on November 1, 1852, receives a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, written by Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer. He took his medical degree in 1880, studied obstetrics abroad, and came home to teach gynecology at his own university.

In 1897 Meyer was made professor of obstetrics and children's diseases at Copenhagen. His Danish books covered normal pregnancy and childbirth, the process of menstruation and its disorders, and the care of infants in their first year. Since 1890 he had also served as associate editor of Bibliothek for Læger, described here as the leading Danish medical journal of its day.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-minkovsky-phine:
Phinehas Minkovsky was born at Byelaya Tzerkov in April 1859. He was the Russian cantor who joined a hereditary gift to conservatory training. Herman Rosenthal and Benzion Eisenstadt write about him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His father Mordecai was cantor of the town's great synagogue. Mordecai was a descendant of the Talmudist Lipmann Heller, and the boy sang in his choir.

Minkovsky studied Talmud on his own in the bet hamidrash. He taught himself Russian and German at eighteen. He trained his voice under Nisan Spivak and then Robert Fuchs at Vienna, taking a singer's diploma. From 1888 his posts ran Kishinef, Kherson, Lemberg, Odessa, and New York. Then Odessa called him back in 1892 to its Broder Synagogue. He also wrote a history of synagogue liturgy, published in 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-montalban-10955:
Montalban in Aragon is not the Castilian town of the same name. It had a Jewish community by the fourteenth century. Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling record it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. In 1306 its governor was permitted to admit ten Jewish families expelled from France. He was given charge of the Jews, with power to settle all their lawsuits.

At the great disputation of Tortosa a century later, the community was represented by one Abu Ganda. The entry's last fact leaps to Italy. A certain Jacob of Montalban died a martyr at Ancona in 1556. Three glimpses — admission, disputation, martyrdom — are the whole surviving outline of the community's story.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-abrah:
Moses ben Abraham ha-Kadosh, called the martyr, was a Lithuanian rabbi of the seventeenth century. Herman Rosenthal and Bernhard Friedberg wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Born probably at Brest-Litovsk, he studied in the yeshiva of his grandfather, Rabbi Höschel, and later led a yeshiva of his own there.

In 1673 Moses became chief rabbi and head of the yeshiva at Grodno. He sat in the Lithuanian Council at Khomsk in 1679, and a year later he declined a call to Cracow. He died at Grodno in 1681. His comments on the Yoreh De'ah, the Tif'eret le-Mosheh, were printed by his grandson at Berlin in 1776.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-solom:
Moses ben Solomon of Salerno was an Italian philosopher and commentator of the thirteenth century. Joseph Jacobs and J. S. Raisin wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Between 1240 and 1250 he wrote a commentary on Maimonides' Guide of the Perplexed, and later revised part of it.

Only a small portion of that commentary survives, with notes added by his son Isaiah. The work is mostly a paraphrase, and it renders the technical terms into Italian. Moses also knew Latin, and in that language he read the Guide with Nicola da Giovenazzo, a nobleman. The entry shows Maimonides crossing the language line in Italy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naaman-11255:
Naaman was the Syrian general whose cure from leprosy is told in the fifth chapter of Second Kings. Emil G. Hirsch, M. Seligsohn, and Wilhelm Bacher wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on him. A captive Israelite girl in his house told him of the prophet Elisha. Her king's letter, sent to Israel's king, caused alarm before it caused a cure.

Elisha would not come out, but sent word: bathe seven times in the Jordan. Naaman raged at the slight, let his servants talk him down, bathed, and was healed. He confessed Yhwh and begged two mules' loads of Israelite earth for an altar at home. The rabbis add that Naaman was the archer who had killed Ahab, struck with leprosy for his pride.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-b-isaac-:
Nathan b. Isaac Jacob Bonn was a rabbi in Germany. Gotthard Deutsch and S. J. Levinson wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served first at Mayence and later at Hamburg. His work dates from the middle of the seventeenth century. Little else of his life is recorded here.

Bonn wrote a book called Shikhat Leket. It was a supplement to the Yalkut Hadash, printed at Prague in 1652. The supplement gathers legends and cabalistic notes on the Pentateuch. Those passages had been left out of the Yalkut itself. The book was reprinted at Amsterdam in 1700. That edition added a preface and new material by another editor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nisibis-greek-h:
Nisibis was a city of northeastern Mesopotamia. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A rich Jewish community lived there in Herod's time. Temple gifts from abroad were stored in its treasuries. Strong escorts then forwarded them safe to Jerusalem.

Its college was famed under Judah b. Bathyra. Rabbis read a Bible verse as pointing to his school. Under Trajan its Jews resisted Rome most stubbornly. The city fell only after a lengthy siege. Lucius Quietus laid it waste and massacred its Jews. Corpses, the record says, strewn its streets and roads. Benjamin of Tudela found a thousand Jews there later. Three synagogues stood there in Pethahiah's visit after that.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ochs-adolph-sim:
Adolph Simon Ochs was an American newsman and press owner. Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born on March 12, 1858, at Cincinnati. He was schooled at Knoxville, in Tennessee. As a boy he worked in a news office there.

Ochs learned the trade of the press from the ground up. He worked as a boy who bore the paper to homes. He then worked as a printer in more than one city. In 1878 he gained a half share in a Chattanooga daily. Two years later he owned the whole of that paper. In 1896 he took the chief share in the New York Times. He then bought two Philadelphia papers as well. He helped found the Associated Press, a news group.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paks-conference:
The Paks Conference was a meet of rabbis in Hungary. Gotthard Deutsch and Eduard Neumann wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It met at Paks on August 20 and 21, 1844. Talks in the Hungarian parliament had stirred the air. Those talks dealt with full rights for the Jews there.

Such talks raised calls for reform of faith and rite. Jews were to be drawn close to their Christian fellow folk. One chief call was for a school for rabbis in Hungary. Paul Horwitz, rabbi of Papa, sought to head off that plan. He planned a meet of rabbis to set a fixed rule. That rule would bind all Hungarian flocks in one frame. He sought to guard the old faith from state decreed change. He wrote to strict and free men alike for the meet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pesak-lit-decis:
Pesak is an Aramaic word that means a decision. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Julius H. Greenstone wrote the article. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The word also suggests a cutting off of debate.

A pesak is a ruling given without fresh argument. It may be spoken or put in writing. Joined with din, it forms a judicial decree. A writer who states bare law is called a posek. All such writers together are the Posekim. They split into the early and the later authorities.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pimentel-sara-d: Sara de Fonseca Pina y Pimentel was a poet of Spanish descent. Joseph Jacobs and Israel Cohen wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She lived in England in the early eighteenth century. Her known work is Espejo Fiel de Vidas, printed at London in 1720. The book holds Spanish verses of praise. They honor Daniel Lopez Laguna's Spanish Psalms in meter. Little else about her life has come down.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-polna-affair-12:
Polna is a town in Bohemia where a murder led to a charge of ritual murder. Gotthard Deutsch wrote the full account for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Agnes Hruza, a seamstress of nineteen, left her work on March 29, 1899. She never reached her home village that night. Her body was found in a forest three days later.

Her throat had been cut and her clothes were torn. Blood and blood-stained stones lay near the body. A rope lay there as well. Suspicion first fell on four vagrants seen near the forest. Among them was Leopold Hilsner, a Jew of twenty-three. The case grew into the famed Polna ritual murder trial. The article follows the charge and the court fight step by step.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pribram-richard:
Richard Pribram was an Austrian chemist born at Prague in 1847. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied at Prague and then at Munich. He took his doctorate at Munich in 1869. More study at Leipsic followed before he went home.

Back in Prague, Pribram helped in the chemical rooms of the university. He taught there as a private lecturer for two years. In 1874 a new trade school at Czernowitz made him its chemist. A university opened in that town a year later. He taught there too, and rose in its ranks. The entry traces his posts step by step.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-quadratus-ummid:
Ummidius Caius Quadratus was the Roman governor of Syria. Isidore Singer and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He held that post from the year 50 to 60. In his time the procurator Cumanus caused a sharp strife. Cumanus took the side of the Samaritans in their quarrel. The Galileans stood on the other side of it.

Both parties laid their claims before Quadratus in appeal. In the year 52 he went down to Samaria in person. He put down the rising with a hard hand. The rebels of both peoples were crucified by his order. Five Galileans were named as the men who stirred it up. Josephus gives their count as eighteen in one work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ram-b-hama-1255:
Ram b. Hama was a Babylonian amora of the third generation. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied under R. Hisda and learned beside Raba. He later married Hisda's daughter.

The article praises his sharp mind but notes a flaw. Raba said Ram reached answers too fast at times. He liked to decide points on his own reasoning. One pupil left him for a teacher who checked texts first. The entry also records his early death. Raba then married his widow. Readers see both the gift and the risk of quick thinking.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reform-advocate:
The Reform Advocate was a Jewish weekly first issued on February 20, 1891. Herman Rosenthal and Isidor Warsaw wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It was published at Chicago. Charles E. Bloch founded it.

The article says the paper spoke for progressive Judaism. Emil G. Hirsch ran it from its start. He was its sole editor at first. T. Schanfarber served as associate editor from 1901 to 1903. The writers call it the boldest champion of Reform Judaism. A short note cites the paper's own first issues. Readers learn who founded, printed, and edited a leading Reform voice. Its home city and founding date anchor the record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reichenheim-leo:
Leonhard Reichenheim was a German manufacturer and politician born on May 3, 1814. Isidore Singer and Gotthard Deutsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Bernburg. He died at Berlin on January 26, 1868.

The article says he entered his father's business at fourteen. In 1846 the firm bought a large Silesian woolen mill. It soon employed twenty five hundred workers. The mill ran a school and an orphan asylum for workers. Reichenheim won honors and entered the Prussian Diet in 1859. Voters returned him at every election until his death. He spoke with authority on finance and industry. He also directed Berlin's Jewish hospital. The entry joins factory reform with public service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenhaupt-mori:
Moritz Rosenhaupt was a German cantor born at Offenbach on the Glan on March 14, 1841. Isidore Singer and Julius Frank wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His father was a rabbi and teacher in the town.

Rosenhaupt trained under Cantor Löwe at Strasburg and Salomon Sulzer in Vienna. He served as cantor and teacher at Kochem, then at Speyer from 1864. In 1881 he became cantor at Nuremberg, following Josef Singer there. His Shire Ohel Ya'akob gathers synagogue songs in three parts. He also set the Forty-second Psalm to music as a concerto.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samael-13055:
Samael is the prince of the demons in Talmudic and later Jewish literature. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Ludwig Blau wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He appears there as accuser, seducer, and destroyer of men.

His name is read as the venom of God, the entry says. He is one with the angel of death, who slays with a drop of poison. Yet he is also a great prince in heaven, ruling angels and powers. As evil embodied, he patrons the sinful empire of Rome. He bears twelve wings and commands a whole army of demons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-zarfati-:
Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Samuel Ẓarfati. He was court physician to Popes Alexander VI and Julius II. He died about 1519. His name shows he came from France, most likely the south. At the crowning of Julius II, Samuel spoke for the Jews. He asked that their privileges be continued.

A papal bull of May 14, 1504, confirmed Samuel's own rights. He could treat Christian patients. He need not wear the Jews' badge. The pope took him and his family under direct protection. King Louis XII of France gave him safe-conduct as well. In August 1511 the pope fell gravely ill. Every physician but Samuel gave him up for dead. Samuel proved right, and the pope lived two more years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scheid-elie-132:
Isidore Singer and S. Mannheimer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Elie Scheid. He was a French communal worker and writer. Scheid was born at Hagenau, in Alsace, on October 24, 1841. A failing voice ended his plan to become a rabbi. He went into business instead. Bad memories of his parents' funerals moved him to act.

In 1863 Scheid founded the Ḥebra 'Am Segullah, a burial society run on modern lines. Other Alsatian societies soon copied it. He also wrote histories of the Jews of Haguenau and of Alsace. In 1883 Baron Edmond de Rothschild called him to Paris. Scheid became inspector of the new colonies in Palestine. Over sixteen years he made twenty-two journeys there. He supervised the settlers' work until he retired in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-scranton-13355:
Cyrus Adler and A. S. Anspacher wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Scranton. The Pennsylvania city is the third largest in the state. It is the capital of Lackawanna county. Jews settled there while the place was still called Slocum's Hollow. The name Scranton came about 1850. Joseph Rosenthal was the town's first policeman, in 1860.

Scranton's first congregation formed in 1858. It was reconstituted in 1860 as Anshe Ḥesed. Its Linden street synagogue rose in 1866. That was the county's first building raised only for Jewish worship. A new temple on Madison avenue was dedicated in 1902. About 5,000 Jews live in Scranton in 1905. They support five congregations and two daily Hebrew schools. One Jew long led the board of education. He later became director of public safety.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-severus-julius-:
Julius Severus was a Roman general who became consul in 127. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He governed provinces including Dacia, Moesia, and Britain. Rome then sent him from Britain to Judea on a hard task.

His task was crushing the revolt led by Bar Kokba. Severus avoided open battle with the rebels. Instead he hunted them through caves, ravines, and strongholds, one by one. The fighting ground on until the revolt was wiped out. Rome's Senate granted him a triumph for success in Judea. The entry shows the method behind one of Rome's most brutal victories in the province.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shemana-semana-:
Shemana was a scholarly, prominent family of Tunis in North Africa. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the family. Samuel ben Joseph Shemana served as rabbi of Tunis. His family later settled in the town of Susa.

Samuel wrote a commentary printed at Leghorn in 1835. Solomon Shemana wrote on Talmud tracts and on Maimonides. His book appeared after his death, paid for by his brother. It was printed at Leghorn in two parts in 1809. Another Solomon, Samuel's son, wrote on the great ritual codes. His grandson published that work in 1866. The entry traces three generations of Tunisian Jewish learning in print.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sihon-13655:
Sihon was the Amorite king of the land east of the Jordan. Emil G. Hirsch, Jacob Zallel Lauterbach, and Wilhelm Bacher wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. His realm ran from the Arnon to the Jabbok. The Jordan bounded it west and the desert east.

His capital was Heshbon, captured from the king of Moab. Five Midianite kings owed him allegiance as vassals. When Israel asked passage through his land, he refused flatly. He gathered his army at Jahaz to block them. There Israel defeated and killed him in battle. His whole kingdom passed into Israelite hands after him. Psalms rank Sihon with Og as a great mighty king. The entry sets his fall within Israel's march to Canaan.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simonsen-david-:
David Jacob Simonsen was a Danish rabbi and author born in Copenhagen in 1853. Isidore Singer and Frank Cramer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied Talmud and Hebrew letters from boyhood. In 1874 he won a prize for a treatise on Arabic philology. He then studied at the rabbinical seminary at Breslau.

Simonsen was called to Copenhagen as assistant to Chief Rabbi Wolff. He was the first Danish-born rabbi of that congregation. At Wolff's death in 1891 he succeeded him as chief rabbi. He resigned in 1902 and received the title of professor. He wrote much for Danish and foreign Jewish journals.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-edward-:
Edward S Solomon, also spelled Salomon, was an American soldier and jurist. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Sleswick on December 25, 1836. He emigrated to the United States and settled in Chicago. In 1860 Chicago voters elected him an alderman there.

At the Civil War's outbreak he joined the Illinois infantry. He rose from second lieutenant to major by 1862. He then helped organize the Eighty-second Illinois Infantry regiment. He fought at Chancellorsville, Gettysburg, and Chattanooga with distinction. In 1865 he was brevetted brigadier-general for his service. Grant later made him governor of Washington territory.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spicker-max-139:
Max Spicker was a German musician born at Königsberg on August 16, 1858. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was educated at the Conservatorium at Leipsic in Germany. In 1878 he toured Germany and Russia with violinist Miska Hauser. He then conducted opera at Heidelberg, Cologne, and Ghent.

In 1883 Spicker became conductor of the Beethoven Männerchor in New York. In 1889 he led orchestral concerts at Brighton Beach as well. In 1891 he became musical director of Temple Emanu-El, New York. His works include an Anthology of Oratorio in 1890. He also issued an Anthology of Opera in 1895. With William Sparger he prepared The Synagogal Service for use.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-symbol-14155:
A symbol is a visible sign of an object or idea. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. The Hebrew word for it is ot. In early Judaism an ot meant a religious token too. It marked the bond between God and his people.

Israel held two founding symbols of the covenant. The Sabbath was a sign for ever, says Exodus. Circumcision was the token of Abraham's covenant. Other symbols sort into eight wide groups. They cover the Temple, sacrifices, and the priests. Numbers, metals, and colors form further groups. Cherubim, festivals, and prophetic visions close the list. The entry then reads the Temple as a symbol of man. It shows how things carried meanings beyond themselves.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-takkanah-plural:
A takkanah is an enactment that updates Jewish law for new times. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. It can revise an ordinance that no longer fits. Or it can stand as a new rule drawn from scripture. The term also names the institution it creates.

Such enactments began in Second Temple times. Later ages kept issuing them across Jewish history. Many early ones were ascribed to Moses himself. They include reading the Torah aloud on Sabbaths. Festival days, new moons, and half-festivals joined that list. The first blessing of grace after meals is one. Priest watches and wedding week customs are others. Widows' wedding feasts later shrank to three days. The entry shows law bending without breaking across centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tarsus-14255:
Tarsus is a Turkish town on the River Cydnus. Joseph Jacobs and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. It lies twelve miles from the Mediterranean Sea. Under Rome it was the capital of Cilicia. Its trade, textiles, and rhetoric schools won fame.

The city's first people were Semitic in origin. Phoenician coins often called the place Taraz. Josephus identified Tarsus with biblical Tarshish. He believed Jonah meant to flee there. A monument to Jonah surfaced there in 1876. Hellenic influence spread from Alexander's time onward. Seleucids settled Jewish colonists at Tarsus about 170 B.C.E. Their revolt under Antiochus touched Jewish history. The entry links a Cilician port to scripture and settlement.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-theft-and-stole:
Theft and stolen goods under Jewish law are covered in full here. Wilhelm Bacher and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Stealing breaks the commandment against theft, the article begins. Even stealing as a joke is forbidden. So is stealing with plans to return the goods.

Buying stolen goods ranks as a grave sin too. Without buyers, the rabbis reasoned, thieves would stop stealing. Herdsmen and watchmen face special limits as sellers. Goods should not be bought from servants or children. A seller who whispers to hide the goods gives himself away. The article then turns to punishment and double repayment. Law and daily caution blend throughout.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tortosa-14455:
Tortosa, a city in Catalonia, had Jews owning land in Roman times. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its community ranked among Spain's richest in the 1200s and 1300s. Old privileges were confirmed again and again until 1328.

Jews of Tortosa lent the crown large sums in wartime. They helped fund the conquest of Urgel county. In 1323 they manned two ships for a royal fleet. Tax relief rewarded that service for years. Farming, wine, trade, and dyeing filled their working lives. The Astruc brothers ran big dye works there. Marriage rules required ten men and set officers present. The terror of 1391 broke the community's wealth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tyria-or-tireh-:
Tyria, or Tireh, a city of Asia Minor near Smyrna, had an ancient Jewish community. Gotthard Deutsch and Abraham Galante wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Its Jews arrived before the Spanish expulsion of 1492. Disasters later shrank the community badly. Its laws have followed Smyrna's model since 1825.

Most Tyria Jews came from Constantinople, Brusa, or Salonica. They speak Turkish, Greek, and Judaeo-Spanish among themselves. Three synagogues serve them, the newest from 1887. A gravestone of Jehiel Caro dates to 1488. Their Talmud Torah became an Alliance school in 1895. Chief rabbis included Hayyim Benveniste of the Keneset ha-Gedolah. About 1,600 Jews lived among 20,000 residents.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wahrmann-israel:
Israel ben Solomon Wahrmann was a Hungarian rabbi and Talmudist. Isidore Singer and Eduard Neumann wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Altofen. He died at Budapest on June 24, 1824. In 1799 he became rabbi of Pesth. He was the first rabbi the state officially recognized there.

Under Wahrmann the Pesth community grew fast. Its first statutes were drafted at his urging. His lasting work was the Nationalschule, an elementary school. It opened on September 8, 1814. Its lessons joined Hungarian and modern science with Hebrew. The school raised the community's learning for years. Only one of his sermons was ever printed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-weisz-berthold-:
Berthold Weisz was a Hungarian deputy and industrial leader. He was born at Budapest in 1845. Isidore Singer and Ludwig Venetianer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He studied at Budapest's gymnasium and commercial academy. Political economy was his special focus. In 1876 he joined the Budapest exchange's arbitration board.

Weisz helped found Budapest's suburban railroad in 1879. He took part in framing the industrial code. He built factories for preserves, brassware, and cartridges. Textile mills rose under him across Hungary. He also started the Danubius Dockyards. Since 1896 he has sat in parliament. In 1903 he received the title of court councilor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wise-leo-14955:
Leo Wise (born 1849) was an American journalist and publisher, the son of Isaac Mayer Wise. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He studied at colleges in Cincinnati and Hartford and took a law degree in Michigan.

His youth held two bold side trips. He served a short term in a Union river fleet in 1863. In 1872 he prospected in the South African diamond fields. There he opened a digging that later grew into the famed Kimberley mine area. Back home he ran Jewish papers for years. He published Die Deborah and the American Israelite of Cincinnati. He also brought out most of the books his father wrote.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yakkar-ben-samu: Yakkar ben Samuel ha-Levi the First was a German scholar of the 1000s. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived for a short time at Speyer. He was a pupil of Kalonymus of Rome. Some of his queries to that teacher still survive in print. They treat a custom found among the Jews of Speyer alone. The same theme is treated by the scholar Mordecai as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zalmunna-15155: Zalmunna was a king of Midian slain by Gideon in the Bible tale. Emil G. Hirsch and Bernhard Pick wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He is named in the Book of Judges in five places. One verse in the Psalms names him as well. He is always named with Zebah at his side. Zebah was a king of Midian like him in rank. The pair fell in the war told in the eighth part of Judges.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zidon-sidon-152:
Zidon, or Sidon, is a name of a man and of a famed old town. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. As a man, Zidon was the first son of Canaan. As a town, it was the most old town of that land.

One Greek scribe calls it the most old of all there. It lies twenty miles south of the town of Beirut. Its lands ran from the Lebanon slopes to the sea coast. In its prime it held a port for each time of year. Both ports now lie choked with sand from the sea. Its name may come from the rich fish trade of its folk. Kings of its own ruled the town in the old days. Its king wed his girl to Ahab of Israel in time. The seers of Israel oft name its great trade in verse.
kant-critique-pure-reason-meiklejohn-185:
Immanuel Kant first published the Critique of Pure Reason in 1781, the founding work of his philosophy. The English text here is J. M. D. Meiklejohn's translation of 1855. Kant asks what human reason can know and where its limits lie. He argues the mind shapes experience through forms like space, time, and cause.

Kant distinguishes what appears to us from things as they are in themselves. He tests reason's claims about God, the soul, and the world as a whole. The book set the terms for later thought about knowledge and metaphysics. It is famously hard to read. Few works of philosophy have had a deeper or longer influence.
king-henry-vi-part-2-pg2255:
In Shakespeare's King Henry VI, Part 2, a court scene turns on one man's defence of himself. Gloucester insists his foes have laid their heads together against him. He claims notice of their secret meetings to make away his life. An old proverb, he says, finds a staff to beat a dog.

The Cardinal answers that such railing cannot be borne by loyal men. Suffolk charges Gloucester with twitting the Queen in clerkly words. The Queen replies that a loser may be given leave to chide. Buckingham urges an end, and the Cardinal claims Gloucester as prisoner. Guards are told to take the Duke away and keep him sure.
king-s-cutters-and-smugglers-1700-1855:
E. Keble Chatterton wrote this history of British revenue cutters and smugglers. Published in London in 1912, it covers the years 1700 to 1855. Chatterton had already written several books on ships and the British navy.

Early chapters trace the earliest smugglers and the growth of smuggling. Later ones follow the fast cutters that chased them along the coast. The book carries thirty-three pictures, including a revenue cruiser chasing a smuggling lugger. It suits readers who like sea history and true tales of pursuit. Chatterton writes as a historian of the sea, not as a novelist. Still, the chases and seizures give the facts a strong pulse.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
The March 1876 Lippincott's reviews past expositions. Its century series reaches a third paper on earlier festivals. Sketches of India continue with a third installment. Rebecca Harding Davis reports on life-saving stations.

Mrs. Linton advances Leam Dundas through chapters twenty-five to twenty-eight. Lady Blanche Murphy describes convent life and work. Kate Hillard contributes Love's Sepulchre, a poem. Sidney Lanier addresses a poem to actress Charlotte Cushman. Love's sepulchre, South African letters, and a sylvan search follow. Ellis Yarnall remembers Charles Kingsley for the same issue. Lady Barker's South African letters run through this whole season of issues.
longfellow-hiawatha-1855:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow published The Song of Hiawatha in 1855, and it sold faster than almost any poem of the century. Longfellow built his hero from Ojibwe legends gathered by the ethnographer Henry Schoolcraft, blended with a Finnish epic's driving meter. The result became America's most-read long poem.

Hiawatha, a culture hero of the lake country, grows from a miraculous childhood to manhood among the Ojibwe. He fasts, wrestles the corn spirit, builds a birch canoe, and woos Minnehaha of the Dakotas. Their wedding feast, her death in a famine winter, and his final departure west fill the closing cantos. The trochaic rhythm is unmistakable and endlessly parodied. For better and worse, the poem fixed the national myth of the noble savage.
macaulay-history-england-vol-3-1855:
Thomas Babington Macaulay published Volume 3 of his History of England in 1855. This volume covers the first years of William and Mary after the Glorious Revolution of 1688. War with France, the siege of Londonderry, and the Battle of the Boyne fill the narrative. Scotland and Ireland receive long, vivid treatment.

Macaulay presents 1688 as the founding moment of English liberty and progress. His Whig faith shapes every judgment. The volume was left part of an unfinished work at his death. Even so, its sweep and detail set a standard for narrative history. Readers still enjoy Macaulay's confidence and color, even when they question his conclusions.
macaulay-history-england-vol-4-1855:
Thomas Babington Macaulay published Volume 4 of his History of England from the Accession of James II in 1855. Macaulay, a famed essayist and politician, set out to tell England's story from 1685 onward. His history sold hugely and read like a novel.

William III's reign fills this volume, with war in Ireland and Europe, plots at home, and battles over money and power. Macaulay praised the settlement of 1688 and the growth of liberty, and he judged its enemies harshly. His confident Whig view shaped how Victorians saw their past. The volume shows his gifts at full stretch: clear narrative, vivid scenes, and strong opinions on every page.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-louis-xiv-and-of:
Book one of the Duchesse d'Orleans's memoirs opens with a preface. Elizabeth Charlotte of Bavaria kept a vast correspondence for years. Near eight hundred of her letters came to light in 1767.

De Praun, a Brunswick councillor, was ordered to extract the best. The 1788 French set cut her bold phrases and hid most names. A Strasbourg set of 1789 kept far more of her true voice. Later sets added a life of her that read like a village sermon. The 1807 reprint strayed no further than its flawed parent set. Her letters, salt and all, drive the fame of this book.
more-antidote-against-atheism-english-16:
Henry More, the Cambridge Platonist, published An Antidote Against Atheism in 1655. His title states his strategy plainly. If spirits and witches are real, he argues, then matter alone cannot explain the world, and atheism fails at its root.

More appeals to apparitions and witchcraft as living proofs of spirit. His cases come dressed in elegant philosophy rather than courtroom Latin. The tone is that of a poet-philosopher reasoning in a garden. His book is the philosophical demonology of the 1650s, the decade's most graceful case for the unseen world. It shows Cambridge Platonism turning ghost stories into metaphysics, with full seriousness and considerable charm.
nerval-aurelia-french-1855:
Gérard de Nerval wrote Aurélia in the last months of his life, and it appeared in 1855, the year he died. The text here is the French original. Nerval called it a descent into dream, an account of his own mental illness and the visions that came with it.

In Aurélia a lost love merges with figures of myth and faith. Dreams open doors between the living, the dead, and the divine. Nerval moves between lucid reflection and wild, haunted imagery. Later French writers, above all the surrealists, prized the book as a map of the dreaming mind. It stands beside his tale Sylvie as his most loved prose work.
openalex-w1999954155:
Jesse Read, Bernhard Pfahringer, Geoffrey Holmes and Eibe Frank wrote about computer labelling tasks. Their paper appeared in Machine Learning in 2011. Some items need several labels at once, not just one. A common simple method treats each label on its own. That method ignores links between labels.

The authors proposed classifier chains, a method that links the label tasks. Each step can use the labels predicted before it. They also built a group version that combines many chains. They tested the methods on many datasets. The chain method matched strong rival methods in accuracy. It also stayed fast enough for large datasets. The paper argues that simple base methods deserve more credit.
openalex-w2008384755:
Camila Gonzalez, Ophelia Wang, Stavana Strutz and colleagues modelled future risk of leishmaniasis. Their paper appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases in 2010.
