Leishmaniasis is a disease spread by sand flies. It already occurs in Mexico and Texas. The team asked if climate change could push it north.

They built habitat models for two sand fly species. They also modelled three rodent species that carry the parasite. The models used place records plus climate and land data. The team tested how well the models predicted known sites. They then ran the models under future climate scenarios. The scenarios covered 2020, 2050 and 2080. Results showed where suitable habitat could expand in North America.
openalex-w2084301655:
Wenquan Wang, Binxiao Feng, Jingfa Xiao and colleagues sequenced cassava genomes from wild and farmed plants. Their paper appeared in Nature Communications in 2014. Cassava feeds millions across the tropics. It yields well on poor land and in dry spells. Comparing wild and farmed genomes shows how domestication changed it.

The team produced draft genomes for both forms. Each form carried genes the other lacked. Millions of small DNA differences separated them. Genes for starch storage bore signs of selection. Genes for toxic compound production were reduced in farmed types. Small RNA differences may help explain starch gains. The genomes offer tools for breeding better cassava.
openalex-w2121361055:
Carlos Alberto Quesada, Oliver Lawrence Phillips, M. Schwarz, and colleagues published this study in Biogeosciences in 2012. They asked whether soils or climate best explain why Amazon forests differ in height, growth, and tree turnover across the basin. Earlier work noted an east-west pattern that matched changes in soil richness and rock type.

The team took soil samples from fifty-nine forest plots across the Amazon and linked them to climate and tree records. Both soil and climate mattered strongly. Soil physical traits shaped how fast stands turned over, while total soil phosphorus best predicted wood growth. The study shows basin-wide forest differences rest on ground and weather together.
openalex-w2162497755:
Reyazul Mir, Mainassara Zaman-Allah, Nese Sreenivasulu, and colleagues published this review in Theoretical and Applied Genetics in 2012. They lay out how genomics, plant physiology, and breeding can join forces against drought in crops. Drought is among the worst limits on world farming, and climate change is expected to make it harsher.

The review stresses precise measurement of drought responses before gene hunting begins. Gene discovery routes include trait mapping, gene cloning, candidate genes, and gene activity studies. Breeding tools then carry the gains into fields: marker-guided backcrossing, repeated marker selection, and genome-wide selection. Combined this way, the authors argue, science can deliver drought-tolerant varieties that protect food security in a shifting climate.
openalex-w2263420555:
Michael Zemp, Holger Frey, Isabelle Gärtner-Roer, and colleagues published this study in the Journal of Glaciology in 2015. They reviewed the world's glacier monitoring records, coordinated internationally for over a century. Their question was simple and grave: how unusual is the glacier decline of the early twenty-first century?

The World Glacier Monitoring Service holds about forty-two thousand records of glacier front positions since 1600. They show retreat over centuries as a truly global pattern, with brief readvances never regaining Little Ice Age maxima. Mass measurements since 1850 tell a sharper story. Recent loss rates are without precedent in the observed period, and likely in recorded history, so further loss looms even if climate stabilizes.
openalex-w3039666655:
Khalid Alam, Jaeyoung Jung, Matthew Verosloff, and colleagues posted this preprint on bioRxiv in May 2019, before peer review. It presents a rapid, low-cost way to detect contaminants in water using regulated in vitro transcription. The senior team works in synthetic biology at Northwestern University and partner institutes.

Standard water testing needs a laboratory, time, and money, which many communities lack. The authors build their test on cell-free reactions, where gene transcription is switched on outside living cells. A contaminant in a water sample can trigger that switch and produce a readable signal. Such a design aims at tests that are cheap, fast, and usable in the field. The preprint lays out the approach for fellow researchers to judge.
openalex-w4220656655:
Catherine Arsenault, Anna Gage, Min Kyung Kim, and colleagues studied how health systems in ten countries held up during COVID-19. Their study appeared in Nature Medicine in 2022. When the pandemic hit, visits for many other health needs fell sharply. Missed vaccinations, births care, and chronic treatment can harm health long after the virus fades. Resilience means keeping such services running through a shock.

The team used routine health information systems and administrative data from the ten countries. They tracked how service use changed as the pandemic unfolded, facility by facility. Comparing countries shows which systems bent and which broke. The work gives governments evidence for protecting everyday care during the next crisis, not only emergency care.
openalex-w4221093155:
Malcolm Mistry, Rochelle Schneider, Pierre Masselot, and colleagues compared two kinds of temperature data for health research, in a paper published in 2022. Studies of deaths linked to heat and cold usually rely on weather stations. Stations give exact local readings but cover the globe unevenly. Climate reanalysis, which blends observations into a complete grid, offers full coverage in space and time instead.

The team ran the first broad, multi-region test of the newest reanalysis data sets for health impact work. They weighed reanalysis performance against traditional station records. The question matters because global mortality studies need exposure data everywhere, including places with few stations. Their comparison guides researchers choosing data for temperature and health analyses.
openalex-w4310852955:
Sarthak Pati, Ujjwal Baid, Brandon Edwards, and colleagues show how federated learning can pool brain tumour data without moving it. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2022. Rare cancers give each hospital few cases to train detection software. Pooling scans centrally is hard: privacy law, ownership, and sheer file size stand in the way. Federated learning instead trains models at each site and shares only model updates.

The team applied the method to glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer, focusing on detecting the tumour's extent in scans. Models trained this way can match centrally trained ones, the authors note from prior work. Learning from larger, more varied data should sharpen boundary detection. The approach also opens collaboration to hospitals that could never share raw patient data.
openalex-w7171682655: Muscles fade with age, and doctors need better ways to spot it. This paper proposes a four-gene panel for detecting aged, senescent cell states in muscle tissue. The authors targeted sarcopenia diagnostics. A geroscience study of reading aging in genes.
openalex-w7204642155: Heart surgery stopped and restarted at Brasilia's main public hospital, right as COVID hit. This article profiles 188 patients who had heart operations there from late 2019 through 2022, covering the service's revival and the pandemic years. The authors map who was treated and how they fared. A rare institutional portrait of cardiac care under extraordinary strain.
openalex-w7204999855: Kids who move more tend to be healthier in body and mind, yet inactivity keeps rising. This paper reports on a project that set out to teach young people why exercise matters, connecting physical activity to chronic disease, obesity, and mental well-being. The authors describe the awareness effort and its reception. Simple in premise and earnest in execution, it makes the case for movement as preventive medicine.
openalex-w7205008855: University life tests more than intellect; it tests how students handle people, pressure, and independence. This study examines the link between social skills and mental health in college students, asking whether students with stronger interpersonal repertoires cope better. The authors frame social skills as a resource for navigating academic and personal demands. Relevant to counselors, educators, and anyone who remembers freshman year.
openalex-w7205015755: Tired doctors make more mistakes. This study looks at how lack of sleep harms the thinking, focus, and split-second choices of health workers on long shifts. The authors review the effects on medical errors and on the workers' own mental and physical health. A sobering reminder that the people who care for patients around the clock pay a price in their own bodies and minds.
openalex-w7206185255: Robotic exoskeletons, wearable frames that help people move, are advancing fast in Brazil. This article reviews a decade of development, with special attention to rehabilitation uses and to biosensors like EMG electrodes that read muscle signals to guide the device. The authors explain how sensor integration is making these machines more responsive to the wearer's body. A survey of a technology that is moving from labs toward clinics and workplaces.
openalex-w7212423455:
Joao Henrique Rolde leads a team that reviews a gel made from a patient's own blood, used to help dental implants take hold. The gel, rich in platelets, is spun from blood with no added drugs and set where bone must grow. The team read trials and past reviews from 2019 to 2026 in four databases. The lens spans socket care, sinus lifts, and the gum round the post.

The gel, the work shows, helps the post sit firm. It also helps new bone grow in sinus lifts. In socket care, it cut gum shrink more than grafts from a bank. Doubts stay on two points: slow bone loss at the rim, and how long gains hold. Each lab makes the gel its own way, which clouds the tale. The team backs its use, with a call for one set method.
openalex-w7212446055:
Rayane Priscila Leal Leite and Arejacy Antonio Sobral Silva test green ways to feed crops the nitrogen they need. Farm-made nitrogen feeds most fields, but it costs much to make, leaks from the soil, and rides a world mart prone to shocks. Beans and kin pull nitrogen from the air and store it in their roots. The pair tried two paths with a sunn hemp crop grown ahead of sorghum.

In one path, the hemp was cut and left on the field, or dug in, ahead of the sorghum. In the next, its mass was made into a plant feed to spread by hand. The aim was to see how much farm-made feed each path could spare. The work is part of a wide hunt: food grown with less gas burned and less cash sent abroad.
openalex-w7216402655:
Marcos Vinicius Pereira Gonçalves and Juliana Araújo Santos Martins tested a mineral particle film on sweet corn in a 2026 field experiment in Uberlândia, Brazil. Sweet corn suffers leaf diseases more than common maize, because its tissues are tender and its breeding favors sugar, and few pesticides are registered for it. The team sprayed the aluminum silicate product, sold as Surround WP, at several rates up to above the manufacturer's recommendation, in a replicated block design.

No statistically clear differences appeared among treatments for either of the two diseases tracked, a leaf blight and white spot. A trend toward lower disease severity showed at the higher rates, however. The authors conclude the product has potential as a complementary tool for managing leaf diseases in sweet corn, especially at higher rates. They call for further studies under more stable experimental conditions before its effectiveness can be confirmed.
openalex-w7221131555:
Alice Viera da Silva and two co-authors reviewed literature from 2013 to 2025 on eating habits across a lifetime. Their 2026 review asks how those habits shape healthy aging. With chronic diseases tied to poor diet widespread among older people, they ask which patterns protect function and independence in old age.

Balanced diets rich in fruit, vegetables, whole grains, and quality protein were linked to fewer chronic diseases and preserved capacity. Ultra-processed food, smoking, and heavy drinking pointed the other way, toward lost autonomy. Aging itself complicates eating through sensory and chewing changes, while income, schooling, and isolation also weigh in. Lifelong food education, the authors conclude, is a tool for autonomy.
phrenologische-bilder-zur-naturlehre-des: Phrenologische Bilder, 1855. Another edition. This book preserves that work. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it. It holds its historical place. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Those who study the era will use it in their work.
plos-pbio-0020055:
Jerel C. Davis and Dmitri A. Petrov examined gene copying across eukaryotic genomes in PLOS Biology in 2004. Gene duplication is a main source of new traits. When a gene is copied, one copy can keep the old job while the other is free to change.

Not all genes get copied and kept at the same rate. The authors found that proteins conserved over long spans of evolution are copied more often than others. That runs against a simple guess that the most vital genes would resist change. Their result suggests that proven, stable proteins make good raw material for new functions. It reshapes how genome scientists think about where novelty comes from.
plos-pbio-0020155:
Susan E. Ptak, Amy D. Roeder, Matthew Stephens, and their team compared a DNA hotspot in humans and chimps for PLOS Biology in 2004. Hotspots are short DNA stretches where genetic shuffling during reproduction happens far more than average. One human hotspot, called TAP2, has no match in chimpanzees.

That absence is striking, since chimps share most of our DNA. It shows hotspots can appear and vanish fast in evolution, much faster than the DNA around them. The finding changed how scientists model recombination, the shuffling that creates new gene mixes each generation. Chimp data can no longer be assumed to mirror our own hotspot map.
plos-pbio-0020355:
Ryan B. Rountree, Michael Schoor, Hao Chen, and a large team studied joint cartilage in mice in PLOS Biology in 2004. Cartilage caps the ends of bones and lets joints glide. Signals through BMP receptors help build it before birth, and the team asked whether those signals still matter after birth.

They do: without BMP receptor signaling, adult cartilage breaks down and joints suffer. That means cartilage is not a set-and-forget tissue. It needs constant upkeep signals through life. The finding matters for arthritis, where cartilage loss is the core problem. A signal required for upkeep is a natural place to look for treatments that protect joints.
plos-pone-0000055:
Hendrik Bonarius, Frank Baas, Ester Remmerswaal, and co-authors built a finer lens for watching the immune system in a 2006 paper. Each T cell carries a receptor that fits one target, and the full set of receptors, the repertoire, is a fingerprint of a person's immune state. Older methods blurred that fingerprint into broad families.

Their method monitors the repertoire at single-clone resolution, following individual T cell clones as they rise or fall. That precision matters in infections, transplants, and vaccines, where a few expanding clones may carry the whole response. Watching one clone at a time turns a crowd scene into a set of trackable stories.
plos-pone-0000155:
Felix Zajitschek, John Hunt, Susanne R. K. Zajitschek, and colleagues published this cricket study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It tests intra-locus sexual conflict, the idea that a gene good for males can be bad for females, or the reverse. The authors measured reproductive fitness and ageing in field crickets.

As the title states, they found no such conflict over fitness or ageing in these crickets. A negative result still counts: it trims a popular theory down to the cases where evidence supports it. The study is a useful check on how widespread sexual conflict really is in wild populations.
plos-pone-0000255:
Rani E. George, Edward F. Attiyeh, Shuli Li, and colleagues published this cancer genomics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Neuroblastoma is a childhood cancer of nerve tissue. The authors scan tumors genome-wide using high-density SNP arrays. These chips read hundreds of thousands of DNA markers, revealing the gains and losses that mark the cancer's genome.

Patterns of deletion and duplication point to the genes driving a tumor. A genome-wide survey gives an unbiased map of those changes in neuroblastoma. The results guide the search for outcome predictors and drug targets in a cancer that behaves very differently from child to child.
plos-pone-0000355:
Leonor Saiz and Jose M. G. Vilar published this theoretical biophysics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Inside living cells, DNA loops bring distant sites together, and proteins bound on the loop change gene activity. The authors carry out a multilevel deconstruction of the in vivo behavior of these looped DNA-protein complexes, breaking their behavior down across scales.

Loops behave differently inside a crowded cell than in a test tube. A multilevel account connects molecular forces to the loop's actual dynamics in vivo. The work guides the modeling of gene regulation, where looping is a central mechanism.
plos-pone-0000455:
Irmgard Amrein and colleagues checked whether bats make new brain cells as adults, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. In many mammals, the hippocampus, a memory center, keeps producing neurons throughout life, a process called adult neurogenesis. The team examined bats, order Chiroptera, and looked for signs of that production.

They found adult neurogenesis in the bat hippocampus to be absent or at a low rate. That exception is informative: if some long-lived, big-brained mammals manage without it, the process is not a universal requirement. Comparative findings like this keep theories about why new neurons matter honest, by testing them against animals that break the pattern.
plos-pone-0000555:
Laurent Pélozuelo and colleagues studied mate choice between two forms of a crop pest moth, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. European corn borers come in pheromone races: females of each race release a different scent blend, and males follow their own race's scent. The team examined assortative mating between the races, going beyond assortative meeting.

Meeting is about being in the same place; mating is about actually choosing. If the races meet but still mate within their kind, the barrier is preference, and the races may be splitting into species. Pest evolution matters practically too, since control methods often exploit the very pheromones that divide the races.
plos-pone-0000655:
Cheryl A. Stoddart, Cheryl A. Bales, Jennifer C. Bare and co-authors validated a mouse model of HIV infection in PLOS ONE in 2007. The SCID-hu Thy/Liv model implants human thymus and liver tissue in mice that lack their own immune systems. HIV-1 can then infect the human tissue. The model serves preclinical tests of antiviral drugs before human trials.

To validate it, the team used representatives of all four classes of licensed antiretrovirals. A model that answers known drugs correctly can be trusted more with unknown ones. Their endpoint analyses measured viral quantities to judge each drug. Animal models live or die by such checks.
plos-pone-0000755:
Birte Kretschmer, Katja Lüthje, Andreas H. Guse and colleagues adjusted an immune protein and watched antibody output fall, in PLOS ONE in 2007. CD83 is a membrane glycoprotein known as an important regulator of T cell maturation in the thymus and of T cell responses in the body. The team had recently reported a function on B cells too: forcing CD83 expression everywhere interfered with antibody production.

Working in vitro, they report that B cells carrying extra CD83 raise IL-10, a calming immune signal, and reduce immunoglobulin secretion. CD83 thus modulates B cell function directly. Fine control of antibody output matters in vaccination, allergy, and autoimmune disease alike.
plos-pone-0000855:
Carl Troein, Dag Ahrén, Morten Krogh and colleagues asked whether the standard way microbes control their metabolism is truly the best way. Transcriptional regulation of metabolic pathway genes is an approach that works well, nearly universal in microorganisms. The lac operon of E. coli is one example: cells make enzymes and transporters only when a nutrient is present, so cells do not waste resources.

Their 2007 PLOS ONE question is whether that strategy is optimal for fitness, or merely good and historically locked in. Such tests split what evolution perfected from what it merely settled for. The answer shapes how engineers should design synthetic microbes: copy nature, or improve on it.
plos-pone-0000955:
Kira Makarova and co-authors studied the genes behind radiation survival in a second hardy bacterium, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Deinococcus bacteria withstand radiation, UV light and drying that would kill most life. The first of the group to be fully sequenced was Deinococcus radiodurans.

Here the team analyze Deinococcus geothermalis, a heat loving relative. Their title reports that the pool of extreme resistance genes shrinks under comparison. Shared toughness across species may rest on fewer genes than single genome studies suggested. Narrowing that pool focuses the search for how these bacteria repair shattered DNA so well.
plos-pone-0001055:
Saliou Fall and colleagues argued that gene transfer rules in bacteria may be a side effect of DNA repair. They published the work in PLOS ONE in 2007. Horizontal gene transfer, genes moving between unrelated bacteria, is the major force in bacterial genome evolution. Open questions remain about which genes move, and how often.

The authors focus on genetic transformation, uptake of loose DNA from outside. They suggest its regulation rides on the machinery that repairs DNA, a spandrel, a feature that exists because of another feature. That reframing changes where to look for controls on gene swapping, a process behind antibiotic resistance spread.
plos-pone-0001155:
Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is among the most aggressive and deadly cancers. Marina Pasca di Magliano and co-authors examined a signaling pathway in this cancer in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The pathway is Wnt signaling, a system embryos use to organize growth, and most of these tumors also carry mutations in the Kras gene.

The authors report common activation of the canonical Wnt pathway in pancreatic adenocarcinoma. A growth pathway borrowed from development, switched on in most tumors, is a possible point of attack. The paper adds to the case that this cancer leans on embryonic programs to sustain itself.
plos-pone-0001255:
In survival analysis, researchers often ask whether the time until failure and the cause of failure are independent. Isha Dewan and Sangita Kulathinal study that testing problem when some causes of failure are missing, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Missing causes are common in practice, when a failure is recorded but not classified.

The authors base their test on the conditional probabilities of failure from a specific cause, given no failure up to a fixed time. Their method aims to stay valid even with incomplete cause data. The paper is a contribution to statistical theory for reliability and medical follow-up studies.
plos-pone-0001355:
Cre recombinase is a tool that lets researchers delete or switch genes at chosen sites in experimental animals. Controlling when it acts, however, has been inefficient. Nicolas Jullien and colleagues present a solution called DiCre, dimerizable Cre, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The concept: split Cre into two inactive halves that join only when a drug brings them together.

Conditional transgenesis using this system gives efficient temporal control over Cre activity. Timing matters because deleting a gene early in development can mask its adult role. DiCre became a widely used tool in mouse genetics after this report.
plos-pone-0001455:
Pierre Gladieux and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on apple scab, a fungus ill that hurts orchards world wide. The fungus has spread to near all apple growing lands. To predict how well control steps will work, labs must know where it came from. The team traced its spread with gene data.

Their data point to a start in Central Asia, the home of the wild apple. From there the fungus moved out with farmed apples. A clear origin tale helps growers plan for new strains. It also shows how a crop disease can ride trade and planting across the globe in a short span.
plos-pone-0001555:
Bashar Ibrahim and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study that models the cell division checkpoint in a computer. This checkpoint holds a cell back until all chromosomes are locked to the split frame in the right way. Only then may the cell part its copies. Faults here seed cancer and birth ills.

Their model rebuilds the checkpoint's web of signals step by step in code. A working model lets labs test faults no bench test could reach. It also shows which links in the web matter most. Such maps help drug teams find the checkpoint's weak points in tumors.
plos-pone-0001655:
Nicholas A. Lesica and Benedikt Grothe listened in on the hearing pathway of mammals in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. They asked how well the system keeps up with the timing of natural sounds, such as animal calls. Their recordings came from neurons in the inferior colliculus, a midbrain hub for hearing.

From the cells' responses to vocalization sounds, the authors derived temporal receptive fields, maps of which time patterns each cell prefers. They then judged how the pathway adjusts its timing strategy to fit natural stimuli. The full text gives the recordings, the maps, and the measures of timing accuracy. Hearing aids and speech processors copy this pathway's tricks, so knowing how it handles real-world sound timing has both basic and applied value.
plos-pone-0001755:
Sizolwenkosi Mlotshwa, Gail J. Pruss, Angela Peragine, and their co-authors studied how plants spread gene silencing in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Dicer-like enzymes cut long double-stranded RNA into the small RNAs that mediate silencing. Silencing can then amplify and spread along a gene, a process called transitive silencing.

Working in Arabidopsis, the team reports that the enzyme DICER-LIKE2 plays a primary role in transitive silencing of transgenes. The full text gives the plant mutants and the silencing spread measurements. Transgene silencing is both a tool and a nuisance in plant science. It lets researchers switch genes off, but it can also shut down engineered traits that farmers want kept on.
plos-pone-0001855:
Nicaise Tuikue Ndam and co-authors analyzed gene expression of the malaria parasite in pregnancy in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Malaria in pregnancy causes anemia in the mother and low birth weight. It is one of the many forms of Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Red blood cells carrying the parasite can gain sticky traits that drive how severe the malaria gets.

Their gene activity analysis shows which genes the parasite switches on in pregnancy, linked to binding in the placenta. The full text gives the gene lists and comparisons. Pregnancy malaria needs its own vaccine, and the genes specific to it are the leading vaccine parts.
plos-pone-0001955:
Connie Wong and co-authors sharpened a lab trick that turns adult cells back toward an embryo-like state, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Fusing an adult cell with a stem cell can reprogram the adult nucleus. But the process is slow, and the steps behind it were poorly known. A faster assay would let labs hunt the genes that drive the change.

The team tuned stem cell fusion to work at high efficiency, then used it as a test bed. With it, they report that a gene called Sall4 acts as an enhancer of reprogramming. Tools like this speed the search for safe ways to make patient-matched stem cells.
plos-pone-0002055:
Hugh Cahill and Jeremy Nathans promoted a simple eye reflex as a lab test for brain function in mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The optokinetic reflex steadies a moving image on the retina by turning the eyes to follow it. It needs no training, can be evoked again and again, and draws on diverse brain circuits.

Those traits make it a fine quantitative test of nervous system function. The pair applied it to variation caused by genes and by drugs. A cheap behavior test that reads out deep circuitry can screen mutant mice and drug effects far faster than anatomy can.
plos-pone-0002155:
Arthur Bikbaev and co-authors studied a receptor that links learning and memory in the hippocampus, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The hippocampus is a brain region vital for forming memories. A receptor called mGluR5, which senses the messenger glutamate, strongly shapes both lasting changes at synapses and learning itself.

The team blocked mGluR5 for a long period with a drug called MPEP and traced what happened next. They looked at late-phase LTP, the long-lasting strengthening of synapses tied to memory, and at how network activity changed. Their results help map the steps between one receptor and the act of learning.
plos-pone-0002255:
Rien van Haperen and co-authors tested how a fat-moving protein in blood cells affects artery disease, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Phospholipid transfer protein, or PLTP, rides on HDL, the so-called good cholesterol particles. In engineered mice, high PLTP lowers HDL and raises atherosclerosis, the buildup of artery plaque, and PLTP is found in human plaques too.

The team raised PLTP levels in bone marrow derived cells and watched the effect on disease. Their results show this source of PLTP alone can drive atherosclerosis. The finding sharpens the case that how fat is shuffled in blood helps decide whose arteries clog.
plos-pone-0002355:
Collin Elsea and co-authors tested whether blocking a stress signal can ease a harsh side effect of chemotherapy. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Patients on systemic chemotherapy often suffer deep fatigue like the sickness behavior that follows infection. That state is driven by inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1 beta, TNF-alpha, and IL-6, released when drugs damage tissues.

The team inhibited the p38 MAPK pathway in their models. Blocking it suppressed the cytokine surge caused by etoposide, 5-fluorouracil, and doxorubicin, without weakening the drugs' tumor-killing activity. Separating a cancer drug's benefit from its misery is a prize worth chasing for patient care.
plos-pone-0002455:
Wood-Kaczmar led the team behind a 2008 research article in PLOS ONE. Named on the byline are Alison Wood-Kaczmar, Sonia Gandhi, Zhi Yao, among others. Its subject is pINK1 Is Necessary for Long Term Survival and Mitochondrial Function in Human Dopaminergic Neurons. Parkinson's disease (PD) is a common age-related neurodegenerative disease.

The authors lay out their aims in clear terms and keep the focus on the work itself. Readers finish with a clear sense of the problem, the approach, and why the question was worth the team's time. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002555:
Santos and other authors present their study in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Named on the byline are Nuno R. dos Santos, Maryvonne Williame, Stéphanie Gachet, among others. Its subject is relB-Dependent Stromal Cells Promote T-Cell Leukemogenesis. The Rel/NF-κB transcription factors are often activated in solid or hematological malignancies.

In most cases, NF-κB activation is found in malignant cells and results from activation of the canonical NF-κB pathway. The writing stays close to the facts the team had in hand when the work was done. It stands as one careful step in a longer line of work, with its question and approach laid out in full.
plos-pone-0002655:
Janyce A. Sugui and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was genes differentially expressed in conidia and hyphae of aspergillus fumigatus upon exposure to human neutrophils. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Janyce A. Sugui, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Aspergillus fumigatus is the most common etiologic agent of invasive aspergillosis in immunocompromised patients. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002755:
Pu Zhang and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was expression analysis of the NLRP gene family suggests a role in human preimplantation development. The catalog record names Pu Zhang first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. The NLRP (Nucleotide-binding oligomerization domain, Leucine rich Repeat and Pyrin domain containing) family, also referred to as NALP family. It goes on to note a further point. Several NLRP s have been indicated as being involved in reproduction as well. The piece stands as a short, open record of the research question and the grounds on which the authors pursued it.
plos-pone-0002855:
Claire Gaillard and co-authors reported work in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was a High-Sensitivity method for detection and measurement of HMGB1 protein concentration by High-Affinity binding to DNA hemicatenanes. Authorship is credited in the record to Claire Gaillard and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract states the starting point plainly. Protein HMGB1, an abundant nuclear non-histone protein that interacts with DNA and has an architectural function in chromatin. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002955:
Sakshi Shrivastava and Sharmila Mande searched bacterial genomes for parts of the type VI secretion system in 2008. That system, a needle-like device bacteria use to export proteins, had lately been reported in cholera and two other disease bacteria. Eighteen genes had been tied to it in Vibrio cholerae.

The authors set out to identify and characterize the system's gene parts across bacterial genomes by computer analysis. Finding the parts widely would suggest the device is a common weapon. Published in PLOS ONE, the survey helps microbiologists spot this system in new genome sequences.
plos-pone-0003055:
Helen Burgess and Louis Fogg examined full melatonin profiles in a large sample in 2008. The study's aim was to map individual differences in how much melatonin people secrete and when, using profiles not suppressed by light. Lifestyle variables were then checked for links to amount and timing.

Melatonin is the hormone that signals night to the body clock. Published in PLOS ONE, complete profiles across many people show the normal human range, which single samples cannot. Sleep medicine uses such ranges to judge delayed or advanced clocks and to time light and melatonin treatment.
plos-pone-0003155:
Nicholas P. Vyleta and Stephen M. Smith report a fast effect of caffeine on glutamate signals in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Caffeine is known to trigger calcium release inside many cell types. In neurons it acts before the synapse and can change how transmitters are released. The team used the whole-cell patch-clamp method to record currents in detail.

They found that caffeine quickly and reversibly changed the frequency of events tied to glutamate-activated currents, and the title reports fast inhibition of those currents. Readers get a precise cellular account that differs from caffeine's better known actions. It adds nuance to how a common drug affects brain signalling.
plos-pone-0003255:
Christian B. Gocke and Hongtao Yu study a chromatin repressor complex in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Marks on histones in chromatin control which genes are on. A transcriptional co-repressor complex containing LSD1, CoREST and HDAC1 represses transcription. It does so by removing histone modifications associated with transcriptional activation, thereby switching genes off.

The title reports that ZNF198 holds this LSD1-CoREST-HDAC1 complex steady on chromatin through its MYM-type zinc fingers. Readers learn what holds a silencing machine in place. Drugs could target such anchors in cancers where gene silencing goes wrong. The details matter for drug work on gene silencing.
plos-pone-0003355:
Alex J. Cadotte, Thomas B. DeMarse, Ping He and colleagues measure causality in neural networks in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. A major goal of neuroscience is to understand the relationship between neural structures and their function. Recording of neural activity with arrays of electrodes is a primary tool employed toward this goal. However, relationships among neural activity recorded by these arrays are hard to interpret as causal.

The authors present causal measures of structure and plasticity in simulated and living neural networks. Readers get methods tested first where the true wiring is known, in simulation. Validated measures can then be trusted more when applied to living brain circuits.
plos-pone-0003455:
Manabu Ato and co-authors asked why invasive strep beats first responders in this 2008 paper. Group A streptococcus usually causes simple sore throats. Invasive strains instead cause flesh-destroying disease and toxic shock. Neutrophils, the first white cells on scene, fail against these strains.

The team traced that failure to a broken regulator in the germ. With the regulator off, the germ switched on several virulence factors at once. That combined attack left neutrophils unable to control the infection. The study shows how one control fault can arm a common germ. That burst of weapons helps explain the speed of the worst invasive cases.
plos-pone-0003555:
Tomokazu Konishi and co-authors compared gene chip platforms in this 2008 methods paper. Microarrays read the activity of thousands of genes at once. Several rival platforms of chips compete in labs. Results from unlike platforms were often doubted.

Their parametric framework yielded matching results on two platforms. The same data gave coincident gene lists under that analysis. Biological truth can survive a switch of machines, given sound statistics. The work reassures labs comparing older and newer chip data. Gene chips remain a workhorse even as direct sequencing grows cheaper each year.
plos-pone-0003655:
Corinne E. Griguer, Claudia R. Oliva, Eric Gobin, and colleagues published this cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. CD133 is a protein often used to pick out supposed stem cells in glioma, a brain tumor. Glioma cells also suffer weak energy supply and low oxygen.

The team tested whether energy stress itself switches CD133 on. They found CD133 marks glioma cells under bioenergetic stress, not a fixed stem cell class. That shift in meaning matters, because it changes what researchers think they are isolating when they sort tumor cells by this protein.
plos-pone-0003755:
Maria B. Ospina, Jennifer Krebs Seida, Brenda Clark, and colleagues published this systematic review in PLOS ONE in 2008. Behavioral and developmental therapies for autism spectrum disorder are widely used and widely debated. Claims about how well they ease core symptoms vary a lot. The team set out to summarize the clinical evidence.

They gathered and weighed studies of these interventions for children with autism. The review sorts which approaches have real support and which rest on thin evidence. For families and clinicians, it separates supported care from hype in a field full of promises.
plos-pone-0003855:
Mikael Le Clech published this cell biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Centrioles are cylinders built from nine triplets of microtubules. They are needed to form centrosomes, flagella, and cilia, yet how they are built is poorly understood. Duplication of the centrosome begins as the cell readies to copy its DNA.

Le Clech studied the protein CAP350 and its place in that process. He shows CAP350 keeps centriolar tubules stable and helps centrioles assemble correctly. The finding fills in part of how these nine-triplet organizing centers get built right.
plos-pone-0003955:
Joshua M. Epstein, Jon Parker, Derek Cummings, and co-authors modeled fear spreading beside disease in 2008. Classic epidemic models assume people keep their contact habits fixed. Real outbreaks show people do change, often from fear. They distance themselves, stay home, or flee affected places.

Their PLOS ONE article couples two contagions, fear and disease, in one model. Each spread shapes the other's course through the population. Math and computer runs explore how the pairing changes outbreak size. Public health plans can use such models to foresee behavior-driven turns. The study ran in PLOS ONE, an open journal read by labs around the world.
plos-pone-0004055:
Emily J. Capra, Sonja M. Skrovanek, and Leonid Kruglyak compared development gene programs in two worm strains in 2008. Gene activity changes across development in C. elegans. It also varies between genetically distinct strains. Earlier time-course studies of worm development were incomplete.

Their PLOS ONE article profiles two C. elegans isolates side by side. Comparing strains shows which developmental patterns are universal or strain-specific. Such variation is raw material for evolution within a species. It also warns model-organism labs that one strain cannot speak for all. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004155:
Aviad Levin and colleagues published this HIV study in PLOS ONE in 2009. HIV-1 integrase is the viral protein that stitches viral DNA into the host cell's genome. Its first job is to trim the ends of the viral DNA, snipping off a small piece to ready it for insertion.

The team studied short peptides, protein fragments, taken from integrase itself that bind a second viral protein called Rev. They report that these peptides stimulate the integration of the viral genome. Finding fragments that change how the virus inserts its DNA may point to new ways to interfere with HIV's life cycle.
plos-pone-0004255:
Marie Garnier-Lhomme and colleagues published this cell membrane study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The inside of a eukaryotic cell is in constant motion, with membranes splitting and fusing to move cargo and rebuild compartments. The nuclear envelope, the double membrane around the DNA, is one such structure, and it breaks down when cells divide.

The authors describe remnants of that envelope that persist as fluid membranes. These remnants are enriched in sterols and polyphosphoinositides, two classes of membrane lipids. Characterising what is left of the envelope helps explain how cells rebuild their nucleus after division.
plos-pone-0004355:
Serena Battaglia and colleagues published this liver cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chronic hepatitis C infection and the resulting cirrhosis are major risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma, the main liver cancer. TGF-beta is an important driver of liver scarring and cancer, but its actual impact on human cancer progression was still poorly defined.

Working with hepatitis C core proteins derived from liver cancer, the team show these proteins shift TGF-beta responses. Instead of tumour suppression, the signal now drives epithelial-mesenchymal transition, a change that helps cancer spread. The virus thus twists a guard into an accomplice.
plos-pone-0004455:
Blocking a survival protein made pancreatic tumors less invasive in mice, report Jeffrey Hager, Danielle Ulanet, Lothar Hennighausen, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Cells die by a built-in program that members of the Bcl-2 family control. Tumors often raise the levels of family members that block death, which helps them survive.

The protein studied here is Bcl-x, one of those death blockers. The team removed it genetically in a mouse model of pancreatic neuroendocrine cancer. Surprisingly, tumor growth and cell death barely changed, but the tumors became much less invasive, as the title reports. That split result matters: a drug target need not shrink a tumor to be useful if it stops the tumor from spreading into new tissue.
plos-pone-0004555:
Three glowing voltage probes are compared on how faithfully they report electrical signals, by Hiroki Mutoh, Amelie Perron, Dimitar Dimitrov, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The probes are genetically encoded: cells are given genes to make fluorescent proteins that change brightness with voltage. They promise a way to watch electrical signaling in chosen nerve cells inside intact brain tissue.

The three most advanced probes of this class are built by fusing voltage-sensing parts with fluorescent proteins. Their responses differ by color, or spectrally. The team measured those spectrally resolved response properties side by side. A fair comparison helps labs pick the right probe for watching brains at work, and shows builders where the next gains lie.
plos-pone-0004655:
Skin cells from Alzheimer's patients carry a varied pattern of stress signaling flaws, report Graziella Mendonsa, Justyna Dobrowolska, Angela Lin, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Alzheimer's disease is a growing burden for individuals and society. Big questions loom: could a test forecast long-term risk, and do all patients share the same cell defects?

The team used skin fibroblasts from patients whose Alzheimer's was highly penetrant, meaning strongly inherited and certain to appear. Molecular profiling revealed diversity of stress signal transduction cascades among these cells. In other words, the same disease arrived by different signaling routes even in skin. That diversity argues against one blanket test or one single mechanism for Alzheimer's.
plos-pone-0004755:
Mandy Lehmann and colleagues showed that anthrax lethal toxin harms lung lining by breaking its inner scaffold, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lethal toxin is a key factor in anthrax disease and drives much of its harm. Its active part is a cutting enzyme that snips most forms of a signaling relay inside cells.

The team asked how that snipping injures the lung lining that keeps air and blood apart. They traced the harm to loss of scaffold integrity that needs the relay. A broken lining lets fluid flood the lung. Blocking that step could help treat inhaled anthrax.
plos-pone-0004855:
Grégory Jubelin and colleagues showed cycle inhibiting factors are a growing family of cyclomodulins in microbe pathogens, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The factor produced by enteropathogenic E. coli was the first cyclomodulin found injected via type III secretion. It provokes cytopathic effects with cell cycle arrest at multiple phases. Homologs now appear in invertebrate and mammal pathogens beyond the original Escherichia host range.

A broad family suggests conserved host manipulation strategy. Blocking cycle arrest could reduce virulence. Comparative genomics reveals new members rapidly. Shared targets simplify countermeasure searches. Future studies can use these results to refine both methods and theory. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field.
plos-pone-0004955:
Parkinson's disease is hard to study directly. Brain tissue from patients with confirmed diagnoses is scarce. Greg Sutherland and colleagues took a different route in PLOS ONE in 2009. They combined gene-activity data across many existing studies. Some of those studies used tissues outside the brain.

This cross-study analysis hunts for patterns single studies miss. Small studies lack the power to see shared signals. Peripheral tissues are easier to sample than brain. Shared signals there could become accessible disease markers. By pooling the evidence, the authors test which changes are consistent. Consistent changes are the ones worth trusting.
plos-pone-0005055:
Caspases are the executioner enzymes of cell death. They snip target proteins to carry out the death order. Emma Creagh and colleagues studied one target, Bicaudal. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They compared fruit flies and mammals. Bicaudal turned out to be a conserved substrate for caspases in both.

Cutting Bicaudal is part of the death program across species. Yet Bicaudal is also essential for cell survival. That dual role is unexpected. A death-enzyme target keeps cells alive day to day. The finding reveals how death machinery and life machinery overlap. It warns against simple stories about executioner proteins. Their targets may be load-bearing parts of living cells.
plos-pone-0005155:
Babies starved of oxygen in the womb face heart risks later. Growth restriction in utero is linked to adult cardiovascular disease. Andrei Tintu and colleagues modeled the link in chick embryos. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. Chronic low oxygen altered the embryos' cardiovascular development. The team examined mechanism, intervention and long-term consequences.

Hypoxia induced dilated cardiomyopathy in the embryos. The heart's chambers stretched and weakened. Interventions could blunt part of the damage. Effects persisted beyond the low-oxygen period. The embryo model shows how early oxygen shortage scars the heart. It connects womb conditions to adult disease in a controlled system. Such models help test protective treatments before human trials.
plos-pone-0005255:
Molluscum contagiosum is a contagious skin virus that causes small raised spots and large outbreaks. Despite how common it is, its pattern in the United States was largely unknown. Reynolds and colleagues estimated its incidence among American Indians and Alaska Natives in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Population-based estimates describe who gets the virus and how often in these communities. The numbers fill a basic data gap for a directly spread infection. Public health teams can use them to plan clinic resources and watch for outbreaks. Counts like these also help clinics spot an outbreak early, when a few cases in one town can still be stopped with care and hygiene.
plos-pone-0005355:
Botulinum neurotoxins are among the most potent toxins known, able to cause death or long respiratory failure. Treatment needs antitoxins matched to the toxin type, given early. Kalb and colleagues tested lab-made antibodies against three A-type toxins in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The panel of monoclonal antibodies could extract the toxins and inhibit their enzyme activity. The toxins tested were subtypes A1, A2, and A3. Antibodies that both capture and disable the toxin could speed diagnosis and improve treatment of botulism. Fast tests for this toxin must work in a clinic tent or a lab far from help,. A set of matched antibodies is the core part such a test is built from.
plos-pone-0005455:
Isabelle Defourny and co-authors reported a large food program for children in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Around the world, vast numbers of young children weigh too little, and poor food plays a part in many child deaths. In the worst-hit areas, clinics cannot treat each child one by one.

The program handed out fortified spreads made with milk to large numbers of children at once. The team checked whether this broad approach reached children and helped them. Their evidence supports giving ready food aid widely in places where severe hunger is common, rather than waiting for clinic visits.
plos-pone-0005555:
Melis Karaca and co-authors studied variety among insulin-making cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The pancreas makes more insulin cells when the body demands more insulin. Workers think that not all of these beta cells are alike; groups within them may do different jobs.

Using a surface marker, the team separated two groups of beta cells in living animals and compared how they work. The groups differed in ways that could matter for how insulin output rises. Knowing the groups may help efforts to grow replacement cells for diabetes. Groups that differ before illness could also explain why some pancreases cope with demand longer than others.
plos-pone-0005655:
Ju Lu, John Fiala, and Jeff Lichtman presented a method for tracing nerve fibres from many microscope images in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Mapping how nerve cells connect requires following thin fibres through stacks of images. Doing that by hand for a whole muscle or brain region is painfully slow.

Their semi-automated method follows glowing fibres labelled in transgenic mice, with a person checking the machine's work. It handled both fibres entering a whole muscle and the branches of cells in the cortex. Faster tracing brings true wiring maps within reach.
plos-pone-0005755:
Qunying Hong and co-authors reported in 2009 that a complement protein can wake a tumor suppressor in prostate cancer cells. Body fluids around tissues carry low levels of complement, part of the immune system's tag-and-attack kit. Its effects on prostate cancer growth were largely unknown.

The team found the complement piece C1q switches on WWOX, a suppressor that works with the famous guard p53. Once on, WWOX pushes the cancer cells toward programmed death. That is a surprising, helpful role for an immune protein better known for attack tagging. It suggests new angles for prostate treatment research.
plos-pone-0005855:
Jasen Wise and co-authors screened in 2009 over five hundred apparently healthy people for hidden chromosome-end rearrangements. About five percent of unexplained intellectual disability traces to unbalanced rearrangements at the tips of chromosomes. Half of those are inherited from a parent carrying a balanced form.

Using fluorescent markers, the team also found mosaic patterns on the X chromosome in their sample. Rates in healthy people set the baseline for judging patient results. Without that baseline, clinics can misread normal variation as disease. The study supplies those reference numbers from a large, careful screen.
plos-pone-0005955:
Some cell signals feed each other in a loop, each one raising the next. Anjali Bheda, Wei Yue, Anuradha Gullapalli and colleagues found such a loop in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper pairs UCH L1, an enzyme that trims ubiquitin tags, with the beta-catenin and TCF pathway, a well-known growth signal in cells.

Each side boosts the other, the team reports, a pattern called positive reciprocal regulation. UCH L1 has links to brain disease and to cancer, so its partner pathway matters beyond one lab result. A loop like this can lock a cell into a state, which helps explain stubborn disease and suggests two points where a drug might break in.
plos-pone-0006055:
Stress often buys a longer life at the price of later breeding. William Ratcliff, Peter Hawthorne, Michael Travisano and colleagues asked in 2009 when that trade pays. Their PLOS ONE paper models a gene pool that stress is shrinking, a setting where food limits or toxins raise lifespan in creatures from yeast to rats while delaying reproduction.

In a shrinking pool, trading early young for a longer life can raise fitness, even when total young fall, the title reports. Timing, not just count, decides who leaves descendants. The model helps explain why the lifespan trade shows up so widely in nature, and it gives the classic life-history debate a crisp, testable claim.
plos-pone-0006155:
A cell pulls itself along by contracting, and that squeeze needs a cleanup crew. Yuval Cinnamon, Oren Feine, Helfrid Hochegger and colleagues found the dependency in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies cellular contractility, the actomyosin squeeze governed by the kinase ROCK and the myosin light chain, and the part played by microtubules and the RhoA switch.

Contractility requires ubiquitin-mediated proteolysis, the tagged destruction of proteins, the title states. Breaking proteins down is thus part of pulling forward, not just housekeeping. The link matters for cancer spread and wound healing alike, since both ride on cells that can squeeze and move through tissue.
plos-pone-0006255:
Cells rebuild their internal scaffolding each time they divide, and timing is everything. Yuen Chyao Ling, Aleksandar Vjestica, and Snezhana Oliferenko studied a scaffold organiser called Mia1p, or Alp7p, in fission yeast in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The protein belongs to a conserved complex that organises microtubules, the cell's rails.

Mia1p must shuttle between nucleus and cytoplasm for the microtubule arrays to be remodelled properly. Stopping the shuttle breaks the rebuilding schedule. The finding shows location is a form of regulation: a protein can be present yet useless if it is in the wrong compartment. Division depends on such traffic control.
plos-pone-0006355:
The viruses behind many common colds are more varied than their mild symptoms suggest. Ting Huang and colleagues studied human rhinoviruses in children with acute respiratory infections in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Rhinoviruses fall into at least three species, sorted by genome regions such as VP4 and VP2.

The team found evidence of recombination, where viruses swap genetic material, plus rich genetic diversity. Recombination scrambles family trees and can create new variants quickly. Tracking that diversity improves surveillance of childhood respiratory illness. It also complicates vaccine hopes for the common cold.
plos-pone-0006455:
Jaehong Kim, Mei Swee, and William Parks found a second workplace for a known protein, in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is SYT, also called SS18, first found through a synovial sarcoma gene swap. It is made in two forms and was thought to work in the nucleus, helping switch genes on. Using form-specific antibodies, the team found a sizable pool outside the nucleus.

In the cytosol, the liquid part of the cell, SYT forms bind to actin, a core building protein. There they function in adhesion that depends on the matrix around the cell. A gene-switch helper thus also helps cells grip their surroundings. The dual role reshapes ideas about this cancer-linked protein.
plos-pone-0006555:
Myoung Sook Kim and co-authors found a new marker for colon cancer in PLOS ONE in 2009. In addition to genetic changes, epigenetic alterations accumulate as cancers develop. The team studied promoter DNA methylation of the oncostatin M receptor beta gene. Methylation can silence a gene without changing its code.

Their title calls this methylation a novel diagnostic and therapeutic marker in colon cancer. A methylation mark detectable in tissue or stool could aid early diagnosis. If the silenced gene restrains tumors, restoring it might help treatment. The study links an epigenetic change to a common cancer.
plos-pone-0006655:
Tamás Czárán and Rolf Hoekstra modeled bacterial cooperation and cheating in PLOS ONE in 2009. An increasing body of empirical evidence suggests cooperation among clone-mates is common in bacteria. Bacterial cooperation may take the form of excreting public goods, molecules that benefit the whole group. Quorum sensing, bacteria counting their neighbors, coordinates such cooperation.

The authors model how quorum sensing drives evolution of cooperation, and how cheating threatens it. Cheaters enjoy public goods without paying costs. Theory shows when cooperation can survive that threat. The model speaks to real systems from infections to soil communities.
plos-pone-0006755:
Tahir Hakami and his team blocked a key brain receptor in rats in PLOS ONE in 2009. The receptor is called NMDA. Drugs such as ketamine block it. Those drugs blur thought and can mimic psychosis. They also make the signs of schizophrenia worse. In rats, the drugs cause odd acts and an odd brain state.

The team focused on gamma waves, the fast rhythms of brain activity. With the receptor blocked, gamma waves turned abnormal across the brain. The change was strong and it lasted. It showed up awake or asleep, at rest or on the move. Such a firm link ties gamma waves to this receptor's health. It backs gamma waves as a sign of the brain faults seen in schizophrenia.
plos-pone-0006855:
Peter J. Dodd and Neil M. Ferguson brought field theory tools to population biology in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many ecology and epidemiology models are stochastic, meaning chance-driven. Some also track space explicitly. Techniques from quantum field theory have served similar systems before. They were used mainly to study critical behavior.

The authors argue for a many-body field theory approach. They apply it to stochastic models in population biology. The approach can handle fluctuations that simpler methods average away. Epidemics near their threshold are exactly where fluctuations matter. The work gives theoretical biologists a heavier mathematical tool for such problems.
plos-pone-0006955:
Sudha Jayaraman, Jacqueline Mabweijano, Michael Lipnick, and colleagues evaluated trauma training in Uganda in PLOS ONE in 2009. Kampala had no formal emergency system at the time. Lay people there carried a heavy burden of injuries. The team had earlier shown a basic prehospital trauma course for lay people was feasible.

Here they tested whether the course worked and could scale up. Trained lay first-responders were the first link in trauma care. Programs like this matter where ambulances are scarce. Teaching bystanders simple bleeding and airway skills can save lives before a patient ever reaches a hospital.
plos-pone-0007055:
Ming Li, Jamie Mangold, Chamindi Seneviratne, and colleagues studied nicotine dependence genes in PLOS ONE in 2009. The GABA B receptor helps control neurotransmitter release in the brain. It also regulates ion channels and signaling enzymes. Whether natural variants in its two subunit genes affect addiction was unknown.

The team analyzed the genes GABBR1 and GABBR2 in two populations. Participants were European-American and African-American. They tested single genes and gene interactions for links to nicotine dependence. Brain calming circuits are plausible players in addiction. Confirming them could guide new treatments for smokers trying to quit.
plos-pone-0007155:
Yi Han, Aaron Miller, Julie Mangada, and colleagues screened drugs for a stem cell cleanup tool in PLOS ONE in 2009. Stem cells differ from other dividing cells in basic ways. The team reasoned a screen of approved drugs might find one that kills stem cells selectively. They compared human embryonic stem cell derived neural stem cells with dopamine neurons.

An automated screen found a small molecule matching that profile. It eliminated the neural stem cells but spared the dopamine neurons. Such a compound could purge risky leftover stem cells from cell therapies. That safety step matters before any transplant into patients.
plos-pone-0007255:
Agron Plevneshi, Tomislav Svoboda, Irene Armstrong, and colleagues tracked serious pneumococcal infection among homeless adults in Toronto in 2009. Finding high-risk groups for Streptococcus pneumoniae infection helps target prevention programs. Homeless adults face crowding, poor nutrition, and limited care, all raising infection risk in daily life.

The authors ran prospective, population-based surveillance in Toronto. They counted invasive pneumococcal disease and lab-confirmed pneumococcal pneumonia in homeless adults. Their PLOS ONE results quantify a burden that is easy to miss in routine statistics. The data support focused vaccination and outreach for this population.
plos-pone-0007355:
Stephen J. McGregor, Michael A. Busa, James A. Yaggie, and colleagues tested wearable motion sensors in runners in PLOS ONE in 2009. High resolution accelerometers, called MEMS devices, can be worn during exercise. The authors ask whether their signals validly estimate oxygen use, known as VO2, and running speed on a treadmill.

They compare highly trained inter-collegiate runners with untrained runners. They assess validity and reliability of the accelerometer signals against measured oxygen use. They also compare running mechanics between groups. Reliable wearable estimates could let coaches monitor training load outside the laboratory.
plos-pone-0007455:
Nicholas Graves and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on older patients returning to hospital as emergencies. Repeat admissions are common in this group and costly for health systems. A program existed to reduce re-admissions among high-risk older people. The question was whether its benefits justified its price.

The team built a cost-effectiveness model using data from a randomized trial. The model weighed the program's costs against hospital stays avoided and health gained. That balance is what policymakers need before funding a service widely. The analysis gives hard numbers rather than impressions. It shows how economic modeling can guide decisions about care for older patients.
plos-pone-0007555:
Jeffrey Hall and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on bird flu in the American kestrel, a small North American falcon. The highly pathogenic H5N1 virus had spread across Asia and Europe, worrying health officials worldwide. Raptors could plausibly carry it across continents. The team experimentally infected kestrels with H5N1 to learn what the virus does to them.

Whether the birds sicken, die, or carry the virus quietly changes how risk is judged. A raptor that survives infection could spread the virus along migration routes. One that dies fast is a warning sign instead. The controlled infection gives facts where speculation stood before. Such data guide surveillance of wild birds during outbreaks. The kestrel, common across North America, is a sensible sentinel to test.
plos-pone-0007655:
Hideki Hayashi and colleagues published a methods study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on screening drugs against enzymes inside cells. Intracellular proteases, which cut other proteins, are promising drug targets. Screening methods against them were mostly limited to test-tube assays. Those assays have technical limits and miss the biology of a living cell. The team built versatile assays that run inside cells instead, suitable for high-throughput screening.

Cell-based assays can test both activators and inhibitors of the proteases. They also capture the enzymes' cellular regulators, which test tubes leave out. A compound that works in a cell has passed a more honest test. Drug pipelines lose many candidates at exactly that gap. The study supplies screening tools meant to close it. Protease drug hunters gain a more realistic first filter.
plos-pone-0007755:
Navneet Aujla and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It measures depression in people with early blood sugar problems. Depression and diabetes are clearly linked, though which one leads is unclear. Very little work had compared ethnic groups on this question.

The team studied White-European and South-Asian people side by side. Their groups included impaired glucose regulation and screen-detected type 2 diabetes. They counted how common depression was in each group. The results can help clinics screen for low mood when they find blood sugar problems, especially in mixed communities.
plos-pone-0007855:
Lorna Harries and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It compares three related genes across species. The genes, HNF1A, HNF1B and HNF4A, form a self-regulating network. That network acts in the pancreas, liver, kidney and gut.

The network's layout looks similar in rodents and humans. Yet switching a gene off produces divergent effects in each species. The authors measured expression differences that may explain the mismatch. Their warning is practical: mouse results on these genes may not transfer directly to people. That matters because the genes are tied to diabetes.
plos-pone-0007955:
April Chan and colleagues studied a protein where bone meets blood in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein, Id1, calms the work of osteoclasts, the cells that break bone down. Bone and marrow sit side by side, and the cells there shape each other's lives.

The team showed Id1 holds back the gene program that osteoclasts use, and that this affects both new bone and new blood cells. One switch thus helps run two systems at once. The finding may guide care for bone loss and for blood diseases that share this border zone.
plos-pone-0008055:
Mana Parast and colleagues studied a master switch for building the placenta in PLOS ONE in 2009. The switch is PPAR gamma, a protein switched on by fat-like signals. Mice without it die before birth for want of a working placenta, the organ that feeds the fetus.

The team showed the switch steers placenta stem cells as they multiply and split into the organ's layered cell types. One layer line in particular needs its guidance. Faults in this system underlie grave pregnancy ills, so a clear map of the switch's orders may lead to better care.
plos-pone-0008155:
Xin He and colleagues built a physics-based model of how gene switches cooperate in PLOS ONE in 2009. Transcription factors are proteins that bind DNA and turn genes on or off, often in teams. Genome-wide binding maps show where they land, but not how they help or hinder each other.

Their model starts from the physical chemistry of binding and predicts team behavior from the maps. It can say which pairs attract, which compete, and how spacing between their sites matters. A model with true mechanics, not just pattern fitting, should hold up as new data arrive.
plos-pone-0008255:
Ryan D. Kitko and colleagues studied acid stress in a bacterium in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Bacillus subtilis meets a wide range of acidity in its environment. The bacteria keep the pH inside their cells within narrow limits. Permeant acids such as benzoate can slip inside and release protons there. That acidifies the cytoplasm and triggers a response.

The team mapped which genes switch on or off under benzoate stress. This transcriptome view shows how the cell defends its internal balance. Understanding acid response matters for food safety and industry. It also reveals basic rules of bacterial survival.
plos-pone-0008355:
Joel N. Glasgow and colleagues targeted gene therapy vectors in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Successful gene therapy requires delivery vehicles that find the right cells. Antibodies can guide such vehicles, and small single chain antibody fragments work too. Pairing them with adenovirus vectors is an attractive route to cell-specific targeting. The team built a strategy using a secreted single chain antibody.

A secreted guide can redirect the virus from outside the cell. That avoids rebuilding the virus for each new target. Flexible targeting would speed development of gene therapies. The study tests that concept in practice.
plos-pone-0008455:
Wook Kim and co-authors hunt for missed genes in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on Pseudomonas fluorescens Pf0-1, a soil germ. Genome maps are first drawn by computer programs. They predict coding parts and then match them to known proteins. That method can miss real genes, in germs and in larger species alike. The team use protein data to check the map.

They detect proteins from genes the map had not marked. Each such find is proof the gene is real and active. Fixing the map improves all later work on this germ. The method also shows how protein surveys can correct genome notes.
plos-pone-0008555:
Hanna Kelker and co-authors propose a vaccine strategy against HIV in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. New strategies are needed to elicit broadly neutralizing antibodies. Such antibodies must target the HIV envelope glycoprotein, gp120. Some potent epitopes on gp120 are cryptic, meaning hidden in its normal shape. They are also conserved and depend on that folded shape. Combos of broadly neutralizing antibodies can protect animals from challenge in studies.

The team's strategy aims to expose those hidden epitopes to the immune system. Presenting them in the right shape may train antibodies that block many strains. That is a central challenge for an HIV vaccine. The work offers a design route worth testing.
plos-pone-0008655:
Elizabeth Cooper and co-authors test species boundaries in columbine flowers in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Aquilegia formosa and Aquilegia pubescens are two closely related columbine species. Despite morphological and ecological differences, they are highly intercompatible. Prior studies revealed little sequence divergence between them. The team examine genetic variation at nuclear loci across both species. They ask if those loci can distinguish the two forms.

They find nuclear variation fails to distinguish the two species. Gene flow and recent divergence blur their genetic boundary. Distinct looks and habitats thus persist without deep genetic splits. The case challenges simple genetic definitions of plant species.
plos-pone-0008755:
Muriel Priault, Erika Hue, Fanny Marhuenda, and colleagues compared two survival proteins in colon cancer cells. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Autophagy lets cells eat their own parts to survive hard times. Two proteins, Bcl-2 and Bcl-xL, can each restrain that process. Both act through a partner called Beclin 1, or so it seemed. The HCT116 cell line gave a controlled test bed.

Removing each protein showed they do not rely on Beclin 1 equally. One leans on the partnership while the other works around it. That split matters for drugs aiming to starve cancer cells. It warns against treating the two proteins as interchangeable.
plos-pone-0008855:
Osigwe Esue, Laura Rupprecht, Sean Sun, and colleagues watched a bacterial filament that bends a cell into a crescent. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Crescentin is a protein filament inside the germ Caulobacter crescentus. It spans the cell's length along one side. That placement forces the cell's curved shape. How the filament assembles and moves was poorly known.

Experiments in dishes and in living cells tracked crescentin dynamics. The filament grows, shrinks, and remodels in patterned ways. Those motions explain how a cell holds a stable curve. Bacterial shape turns out to be actively maintained, not set once.
plos-pone-0008955:
Ana Sanz and co-authors traced how a signal molecule stirs inflammation in kidney cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The molecule, TWEAK, belongs to a family of signals that can injure kidney tissue. It acts on tubular cells, the cells lining the kidney's tiny urine-making tubes. Earlier work showed TWEAK switches on one inflammatory pathway in these cells.

The team found it also wakes a second, slower pathway, called the non-canonical NF-kappaB route. Through that route it changed levels of CCL21, a signal that draws immune cells. The two pathways firing in sequence may shape how kidney inflammation develops. Blocking the signal is one idea for protecting kidneys in chronic disease.
plos-pone-0009055:
Jennifer Cropley and co-authors examined a famous coat-colour gene whose settings half-pass to pups, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The agouti allele Avy makes genetically identical mice range from yellow and fat to brown and lean. A stray piece of DNA inserted near the gene acts as a control element. Methyl tags on that element decide how strongly the gene speaks.

The team measured those tags carefully in the silent state. Methylation turned out incomplete, patchier than expected. Feeding mothers extra methyl donors did not firm the tags up. Diet, in this case, could not rewrite the inherited setting.
plos-pone-0009155:
Marlou De Kroon and co-authors followed Dutch children from the Terneuzen birth cohort into adulthood, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The harms of overweight grow with age, and damage begins in childhood. Prevention works best when it is aimed at the most sensitive age window. The study weighed how children's BMI changes across the early years.

Weight gains between the ages of two and six mattered most of all. BMI change in that window correlated strongest with being overweight as an adult. Gains earlier or later in childhood carried noticeably less weight, literally. Preschool years look like the prime moment to prevent lifelong overweight.
plos-pone-0009255:
Ceiridwen Edwards and co-authors published this ancient DNA study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Today's cattle descend from the aurochs, a huge wild ox now extinct. Archaeology and genetics point to the Neolithic Near East as where domestication began. Still, the details of that origin remain open to testing.

The team produced a complete mitochondrial genome from a Mesolithic wild aurochs. Mitochondrial DNA passes down the mother's line, making it a clean tracer of ancestry. A full sequence from a truly wild animal gives a baseline for comparison. It helps separate the wild heritage from changes that came with domestication.
plos-pone-0009355:
Howard Yang and co-authors published this epigenetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. DNA methylation, chemical tags on genes, varies between people and between body tissues. Earlier work showed genes and chromatin patterns run in families. Whether methylation across the whole genome also follows inheritance was less clear.

The team measured methylation patterns genome-wide across genetic backgrounds and tissue types. They separated how much of the pattern comes from a person's genes. They also measured how much comes from the tissue itself. That accounting helps anyone reading methylation data know whether they are seeing ancestry, anatomy, or disease.
plos-pone-0009455:
Yuan-Hao Hsu and Jolinda Traugh studied a protein switch called Pak2 in PLOS ONE in 2010. Pak2 belongs to the kinase family, proteins that add phosphate tags to other proteins. Its action is held in check by a built in brake part. A phosphate tag on one spot can release that brake.

The pair gathered hundreds of human kinase sequences to compare them. A method that tracks pairs of building blocks that change together flagged pairs that matter for Pak2. Those coupled pairs help control whether Pak2 is on or off. Knowing them can guide work on drugs that target kinases in disease.
plos-pone-0009555:
Susumu Tanaka and Makoto Honda measured antibody levels in sleep disorder patients in PLOS ONE in 2010. Narcolepsy makes people fall asleep without warning. It is closely tied to one immune gene variant, which hints the immune system plays a role. The team measured total IgG, a main class of antibody, in the blood of patients. They included people with narcolepsy and with related excess sleepiness.

Their readings found abnormalities in IgG levels in these patients. Odd antibody levels add weight to the idea of an immune fault behind the disorders. The work does not prove the immune system attacks the sleep switch. It does give clinics a measurable sign to study further.
plos-pone-0009655:
Renee Baran and co-authors studied nerve defects in a mutant worm in PLOS ONE in 2010. The worm C. elegans has a simple, well mapped nervous system. Motor neurons drive its movement through synapses onto muscles. Their long fibers, called axons, depend on tubulin, a building block of the cell's inner rails. The team examined a worm with a fault in alpha tubulin.

In the mutant, motor neuron axons and synapses formed with clear defects. That shows how much wiring leans on one building block protein. A simple worm thus exposes rules that also govern larger nervous systems. The work helps link single gene faults to failures of nerve connection.
plos-pone-0009755:
Federica Bertaso and co-authors published a brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study asks how two kinds of glutamate receptors in mouse neurons talk to each other. A scaffold built from the proteins Homer and Shank links the two receptors in the cell.

When a fast-made protein called Homer1a broke that link, a drug for one receptor family could block the other receptor's current, the team found.
