The block ran through G-protein parts, not through calcium stores inside the cell. It showed only at negative voltages. The authors call this a new way the first receptor family can tune the second.
plos-pone-0009855:
Body clocks tick in nearly every tissue, but not always in step. Hamid Dolatshad, Andrew Cary, and Fred Davis compared clock gene patterns in mother and embryo mice. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010.

The circadian clock is the roughly twenty-four-hour cycle that times sleep and hormones. Differential expression means the clock ran differently in maternal and embryonic tissues. The comparison covered several tissues in both generations. Early embryos may keep time differently from their mothers. Knowing when clocks start matters for development research. Mothers and embryos share blood flow but not always timing.
plos-pone-0009955:
Reading signals inside many cells at once, over time, takes both microscopes and math. Yu-ichi Ozaki and colleagues presented a quantitative technique for that work. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Quantitative means turning pictures into numbers.

Image cytometry measures glowing signals in single cells from microscope pictures. The technique suits time series and population analyses of signaling networks. Signaling networks are the chains of messages cells use to decide actions. Counting signals cell by cell reveals variation that averages hide. Single cells in one dish can act in unlike ways.
plos-pone-0010155:
The authors were Paula Sampaio, Marlene Santos, Alexandra Correia, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study followed a yeast that kept coming back. Candida albicans causes bloodstream infections that can relapse after antifungal treatment. Relapses usually involve the original strain, which may rearrange its genome while living in the patient.

The team studied genetic variants taken from one patient with a recurrent infection. They found the variants had become less virulent, meaning less able to cause harm. That softening may help the yeast persist quietly in the body, trading attack for survival.
plos-pone-0010255:
Sanggu Kim, Alice Rusmevichientong, and Beihua Dong examined a new human retrovirus in 2010. The virus, XMRV, is related to mouse leukemia viruses. Reports had linked it to two human illnesses, prostate cancer and chronic fatigue syndrome. Whether it actually causes human disease, and how it might do so, had not been established in that early work.

Retroviruses copy their genome into host DNA when they infect cells. The team studied the fidelity of that copying and where the virus prefers to integrate. Their PLOS ONE findings bear on how XMRV could disturb human genes after infection.
plos-pone-0010355:
Mark Herrera, David Roberts and Natali Gulbahce mapped how science itself changes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fields borrow ideas from each other all the time. Yet no clear account existed of how fields grow, split, or fade. The authors treated ideas as a network, with links showing how concepts connect. They then watched that network shift over time.

A network view can reveal when a field is about to branch or merge. It can also show which ideas act as bridges between distant topics. Funders and universities plan around such maps, often by gut feeling. A formal map offers something firmer to plan with. The paper turns the tools of science onto science itself. Its subject is how knowledge organizes its own growth.
plos-pone-0010455:
Simone Mader and colleagues compared antibody binding to two forms of a water channel in a nerve disease, for PLOS ONE in 2010. Neuromyelitis optica attacks the optic nerve and spinal cord, causing blindness and paralysis. Patients make antibodies against aquaporin-4, a water channel in nerve tissue. The channel comes in two forms that differ at one end. The team asked whether patient antibodies prefer one form.

Binding preference could affect test accuracy and disease mechanism. Diagnostic tests for this disease rely on catching those antibodies. Knowing which channel form they grip helps design better tests. It may also explain why certain tissues are attacked. The study refines a marker already used in clinics.
plos-pone-0010555:
Eric Rosenberg and colleagues tested a therapeutic DNA vaccine in people with early HIV infection in PLOS ONE in 2010. A treatment vaccine that strengthens immune control could delay the need for daily drugs. The trial, run by a national trials group, enrolled people treated during acute or early infection. It was randomized and placebo-controlled, with neither patients nor doctors knowing assignments. Safety came first, immune responses second.

Such careful design gives believable answers about a vaccine's promise. Treating early may preserve immune strength that later treatment cannot. Even a modest vaccine effect could matter over a lifetime of infection. The study reports both safety and immune outcomes for the approach. It marks a step in the long search for immune-based HIV control.
plos-pone-0010655:
Daniel Thorek and colleagues pictured B cells inside living mice during antibody treatment, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Antibodies that remove B cells treat lymphoma and some autoimmune diseases. Doctors could not easily watch where B cells go during that treatment.

The team tagged B cells and followed them with several imaging methods at once. Treatment cleared cells from some organs faster than others. Some pockets of B cells survived the first wave. Seeing those pockets matters, because leftover cells can restart disease. Imaging of this kind could help time repeat doses more wisely.
plos-pone-0010755:
Zhaoyang Li and colleagues studied a protein that moonlights as a cancer promoter, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein Eef1a2 normally helps build new proteins and appears mainly in muscle, brain, and heart. It also shows up in many solid tumors, where it does not belong.

In mouse plasmacytomas, a cancer of antibody-making cells, Eef1a2 sped cell growth. It blocked programmed cell death as well. Two growth pathways, JAK/STAT and AKT, switched on under its influence. A translation helper turned growth driver is a tempting drug target, since blocking it might hit tumor cells while sparing most healthy tissue.
plos-pone-0010855:
Kristen Stevens, Hakon Hakonarson, Cecilia Kim and co-authors published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Congenital heart disease is the most common birth defect, yet its causes stay unknown in most cases. The authors focused on ISL1, a gene that marks early heart-forming cells and helps generate several heart cell types.

In a two-stage study, they compared hundreds of children with complex heart defects against thousands of healthy controls, checking variants in and around the gene. Several variants were tied to disease risk in the first stage, and a second, larger sample confirmed the link. Stevens and colleagues argue that common spelling differences in one developmental gene can nudge a baby toward heart defects. That finding supports genetic screening research for a condition long treated as mostly chance.
plos-pone-0010955:
Dimitri Nowicki and Hava Siegelmann published this computing study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Associative memory networks store patterns and retrieve them from partial cues, but classic models struggle when inputs change size or when memories must be added without retraining. The authors introduce a flexible kernel memory that handles both yes-no and continuous inputs.

Built on kernel theory, the model behaves like a neural memory in a transformed feature space, and its stored attractors can be added, deleted, or updated online without harming older ones. Inputs may grow or shrink in dimension without relearning, and a consolidation process groups inputs into clusters, demonstrated on handwritten digits. Nowicki and Siegelmann even add a reconsolidation-like step echoing human memory. Their design points toward memory systems that keep learning without forgetting.
plos-pone-0011055:
Li Shao, Leihong Wu, Hong Fang and co-authors published this genomics methods study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Models that predict patient outcomes from tumor gene profiles often fail when tested on new samples. One suspected culprit is extrapolation. That means applying a model to patients unlike those it was trained on. In drug safety science that boundary is called the applicability domain, and the authors asked whether it exists for microarray models.

They built predictive models and graded test samples by how far they sat from the training population's genomic space. Performance degraded with extrapolation degree, supporting the idea that a model's trustworthiness has borders. Shao and colleagues argue that genomic predictions should ship with a domain statement, just as chemical models do. Ignoring those borders helps explain the field's trail of failed clinical validations.
plos-pone-0011155:
Calounova, Livera, Zhang and colleagues studied mouse eggs in PLOS ONE in 2010. Before an egg can be fertilized, it must mature through a careful series of steps. The team examined an adapter protein called SHB, which passes signals inside cells, for its role in that process.

They found SHB helps regulate how mouse eggs mature. A fault in such a step can lower fertility even when eggs look normal. Naming a new control factor expands the map of egg development. That map guides research on fertility problems and may one day aid treatments that support egg quality.
plos-pone-0011255:
Booij, Tremblay, Leyton and colleagues followed boys into adulthood in PLOS ONE in 2010. Men who had shown frequent physical aggression as children took part in brain imaging as adults. The team measured how their brains make serotonin, a chemical tied to mood and impulse control, more than twenty years later.

Adult brain serotonin synthesis differed in men with that childhood history. The finding suggests early aggression leaves a long term mark on brain chemistry. That does not doom any child, but it argues for early prevention and support. Helping aggressive children early may change brain paths that reach far into adult life.
plos-pone-0011355:
Xinhui Ge and colleagues built a chip-based test in 2010 to read many immune responses at once. Helper T cells each recognize a tiny piece of a germ, shown to them bound to a display protein. Testing one response at a time is slow when a pathogen carries many possible pieces, as complex germs do.

Their cellular microarray places many germ pieces in tiny spots and lets T cells settle on the ones they recognize. A new analysis system reads the pattern and names which responses are present in a single run. The tool could speed vaccine research by showing, in one experiment, which germ pieces draw strong responses. It may also help track immunity in patients whose infections or vaccines raise broad, mixed T-cell reactions.
plos-pone-0011455:
Phatthanaphong Wanchanthuek and co-authors read the complete genome in 2010 of a corkscrew-shaped germ that infects the gut. Brachyspira pilosicoli causes intestinal inflammation in pigs and can also infect people, especially where sanitation is poor. A full genetic blueprint had been missing, leaving its disease tricks hard to study.

With the whole code in hand, the team compared it against related Brachyspira species to spot what sets this one apart. Shared and unique genes together expose how it survives in the gut and harms its host. Veterinarians gain targets for tests that distinguish this germ from harmless relatives. For a neglected infection of farms and vulnerable communities, the genome turns guesswork into a defined list of genes to investigate.
plos-pone-0011555:
Greta Snellman and co-authors compared in 2010 the commercial tests that report a person's vitamin D status. Vitamin D guides decisions about supplements, bone health, and more, and clinics choose among several assays sold for the purpose. If the assays disagree on the same blood, the same patient can be called deficient by one and sufficient by another, and the team tested that risk head to head.

Run on identical samples, the leading commercial assays did not always agree. The comparison tells doctors and patients how much trust a single number deserves and which tests earn more of it. Assay choice is an invisible part of medical decisions everywhere; endocrinology is not the only field with this problem. By publishing a direct showdown, the study pushes makers to standardize and gives laboratories evidence for choosing.
plos-pone-0011655:
Cristina Paulo and colleagues offered a new explanation for the deadliness of the 1918 flu pandemic, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The later waves of that pandemic killed a far larger share of patients than the first wave. The standard view blamed a genetic change in the virus itself for the shift.

Drawing on animal studies linking the starting dose of flu virus to disease severity, the authors propose that dose did much of the work. Heavier exposures in crowded wartime settings may have driven the higher deaths. Their hypothesis reframes a historic mystery as partly a question of exposure, not only viral change.
plos-pone-0011755:
Sayaka Akieda-Asai and co-authors studied how a longevity-linked protein controls thyroid hormone release, in PLOS ONE in 2010. SIRT1 adjusts many endocrine and metabolic functions by removing acetyl tags from proteins. It is abundant in the pituitary, the gland that releases thyroid-stimulating hormone, but how it governs hormone release there was unresolved.

The team showed SIRT1 raises the activity of an enzyme called PIP5K gamma by stripping acetyl tags from specific sites. That boost supports release of thyroid-stimulating hormone. The chain connects the body's fuel sensing to thyroid control in mammals.
plos-pone-0011855:
Jongsun Jung and colleagues used genome-wide markers in 2010 to trace how genes have flowed between the Korean peninsula and nearby countries. They studied 320 people from 24 regional groups, including North Koreans, using more than fifty thousand single-letter DNA markers spread across the genome.

With that many markers, the team could test how ancestry patterns link Koreans to surrounding populations. The peninsula sits between mainland Asia and island groups, so its people's genes record centuries of movement in several directions. A careful map of those links gives historians and geneticists shared evidence about how populations of the region mixed, rather than treating any one group as sealed off.
plos-pone-0011955:
Max Chang and colleagues compared in 2010 two widely used programs that predict how drug-like molecules dock into proteins. Virtual screening uses such docking to rank compounds before any are tested in a lab. The team set both programs, AutoDock 4 and the newer Vina, the same task: selecting compounds active against HIV protease.

Ranking the same compound library with both tools showed how their choices agree and differ. Docking programs are cheap compared with lab screening, but only if their rankings can be trusted. A head-to-head test on a well-studied drug target gives screening teams an evidence-based reason to pick one tool, or to combine them.
plos-pone-0012055:
Hua Zhu and co-workers reported in 2010 that a membrane protein best known for cell structure also helps repair broken DNA. Caveolin-1 is the main component of caveolae, tiny flask-shaped pockets in the cell membrane, and it regulates many signaling molecules. Broken DNA, by contrast, belongs to the nucleus's repair crews.

The team found caveolin-1 involved in damage repair through both of the cell's main routes: homologous recombination, which copies a matching template, and non-homologous end joining, which glues ends directly. A scaffolding protein serving two repair systems suggests coordination between the membrane and the genome that textbooks do not yet draw. Damage repair is central to cancer and aging, so unexpected helpers deserve attention.
plos-pone-0012155:
Shilu Tong, Xiao Yu Wang, and Adrian Barnett compared ways of defining a heatwave in Brisbane, Australia, for PLOS ONE in 2010. There is no single world definition, since people adapt to their local climate and cities differ in what counts as dangerous heat. Even within one city, definitions vary by temperature level and by how many hot days in a row count.

The authors tested how each definition lines up with real health harm in Brisbane. A definition that matches actual illness and death lets warnings go out at the right moment, neither too late nor so often that people ignore them. As heat extremes grow, that calibration becomes a frontline public health tool.
plos-pone-0012255:
Wataru Teramoto, Souta Hidaka, and Yoichi Sugita showed that sound alone can make a still object seem to move, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sight dominates our sense of motion, yet hearing also carries cues that bend what we see. Their experiments used sounds with no motion or position information of their own, played alongside a static visual display.

Even those neutral sounds induced a clear illusion of visual motion. The result shows the brain does not merely combine senses; sound can rewrite the visual scene itself. Illusions like this are tools: each one reveals a rule the brain uses to build the world, rules that displays, simulators, and virtual reality must respect or exploit.
plos-pone-0012355:
Gregory Boggy and Peter Woolf tackled a math problem behind a daily lab method in their 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Quantitative PCR counts how much of a DNA target sits in a sample, and labs use it for tests from virus loads to gene studies. The standard way of reading the results leans on a reference curve and can drift from the truth.

The authors built a model that follows the chemistry of PCR step by step, as copies build up cycle by cycle. Their model reads the same raw data more accurately than the standard curve method. Better counting matters wherever a small error in DNA amount can change a diagnosis or a research claim.
plos-pone-0012455:
Pavel Pugach, Anders Krarup, Agegnehu Gettie and colleagues tested a designer binding protein in monkeys, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. DARPins are small lab-built proteins that can grip chosen targets tightly and are cheap to make. Their candidate grips CD4, the doorway HIV uses to enter cells, raising hopes of blocking infection at the door.

In macaques, the CD4-specific DARPin bound its target and stayed in the body long enough to matter. A blocker that lingers is what prevention needs, since daily dosing fails many users. The monkey results support taking this low-cost blocker design toward HIV prevention trials.
plos-pone-0012555:
Zhiqiang Zheng, Robb de Iongh, Peter Rathjen and colleagues tested a growth signal in early embryo-like cell culture, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Embryonic stem cells promise replacement tissues and drug screening platforms, but steering them through real developmental steps is the hard part. One early step forms the primitive streak, the embryo's organizing line, from primitive ectoderm.

The team showed FGF signaling is required to form primitive streak-like intermediates in culture. A required signal is a control knob for the whole differentiation recipe. Protocols that add FGF at the right window can push stem cells more faithfully toward the body's germ layers.
plos-pone-0012655:
Laiakis, Morris, Fornace and co-authors ran a pilot study of chemical fingerprints in children with severe pneumonia in The Gambia. Pneumonia still kills more young children than any other illness, and doctors often cannot tell its cause fast enough. Their 2010 study used metabolomics, the measurement of many small chemicals in body fluids.

Patterns in those chemicals may one day sort cases by cause or by risk of death. The pilot shows such sampling works in a West African hospital setting. Better sorting would guide antibiotics and save scarce hospital beds for the sickest children.
plos-pone-0012755:
Karlsson, Eroukhmanoff and Svensson asked how social crowding changes mating behaviour after populations split into new forms. Animals that can adjust their behaviour to match conditions may cope better as settings shift. Their 2010 study worked with a species in the middle of splitting into distinct ecotypes, forms fitted to different habitats.

They varied how many animals were kept together and the balance of males to females, then watched mating behaviour bend in response. Flexible mating behaviour could speed or slow the split into new species. The work shows social setting is an active force in evolution, not background noise.
plos-pone-0012855:
La Starza, Matteucci, Gorello and co-authors linked losses of the NPM1 gene to gross chromosome damage in leukaemia. NPM1 sits on chromosome 5 and is caught up in many leukaemia rearrangements. It is also mutated in about sixty percent of adult acute myeloid leukaemia with otherwise normal chromosomes.

Their 2010 study found that outright deletion of NPM1 goes together with large-scale rearrangements. That pairing suggests losing the gene entirely is a different event from the common small mutations. Sorting these cases refines diagnosis for a major leukaemia group.  Chromosome breaks were mapped case by case in patients.
plos-pone-0332355:
Sudip Silwal and co-authors reported in 2026 on a soil bacterium that helps wheat grow under harsh conditions. The strain, Burkholderia gladioli ST3M-39a, lives around plant roots and frees up phosphate from the soil, making this key nutrient available to the crop. The team tested it where farming is hardest: salty soil, drought, and extreme acidity or alkalinity.

In their trials the bacterium matched the effect of chemical fertilizer on the wheat. A living alternative that holds up under stress could cut fertilizer costs and the pollution that comes with heavy use. Such biofertilizers matter most for farmers on poor land, where yields are lowest and purchased inputs are hardest to afford.
plos-pone-0335155:
Vasile Chasciar and a team of colleagues surveyed three hundred eighty-four construction workers in Brașov County, Romania, about working through the pandemic. Building sites stayed fairly active there while much of Europe shut down, so these workers kept their jobs but under new rules. The survey, run in early twenty twenty-two, asked about changed workloads, hardships, money worries, and thoughts of working abroad.

Most workers said their workload and conditions had changed little. The sharpest difficulties were masks, hygiene rules, and projects running late. Few planned to leave for work abroad overall, but those who felt the financial squeeze were more willing to go. The study gives a ground-level record of an essential trade during closed borders, useful to anyone planning how labor moves in the next crisis.
plos-pone-0335655:
Liurui Deng, Xiaoying Hu, and Ying Xiao model how a multinational firm should enter online markets abroad when it also owns a store in the same market. Sellers on big platforms sometimes post poor product images, and blockchain checks can verify quality. Their 2026 study builds a supply chain model spanning a high-tax manufacturing base and low-tax retail markets with several seller types.

Bigger tax gaps shrank the firm's total profit whether or not the verification tech was used. Without the tech, one entry route alone paid best; with it, a mixed route won. Market size and service gaps also tipped the best choice. The model gives global firms a way to think through entry and trust tools together.
plos-pone-0337255:
Vinson Wai-Shun Chan leads a team of eight publishing the plan for a national exercise to set research priorities in interventional oncology, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The field delivers cancer treatment through needles and catheters, precisely and with small wounds, and it is expanding faster than its evidence base or its funding. DEFINE-IO will first run three rounds of an online Delphi process, where experts propose topics anonymously, then rate and refine one another's suggestions toward consensus.

The process is designed to end with twenty-five agreed priorities. A final in person session will then score those priorities against urgency, feasibility, and affordability, producing a ranked strategic roadmap. The protocol promises the results to conferences, journals, funders, and policymakers. In a specialty drowning in possible questions, the authors argue, a transparent shared agenda is itself a research tool, steering money toward the studies patients most need.
plos-pone-0338755:
Maria Hälleberg-Nyman leads a team of eight examining how hospital teams were helped to adopt guidelines against urinary retention, in PLOS ONE in 2026. National guidance exists, yet wards rarely change practice on paper alone. The OPTION program gave local teams of nurses, rehabilitation staff, and managers monthly expert support for a year. It ran across seven orthopaedic sites. This study evaluated that process through interviews, logs, and photographs.

Teams grew in knowledge of the guidelines and in skill at running small improvement cycles on their own wards. Having managers on each team mattered, because it authorized quick changes to local routines. One year proved enough for first implementation steps but not for full understanding, which arrived only as teams persisted. The authors conclude that guideline uptake is slow local work needing dedicated teams, real authority, and follow up beyond a single year.
plos-pone-0339255:
Dahesihdewi and colleagues tested a fast urine method for spotting infections in a 2026 study across hospitals in Indonesia. Urine infections are very common, yet the standard lab culture takes time and drives extra use of germ-killing drugs. A flow machine that counts bacteria and white cells in urine could give answers much sooner.

More than seven hundred patients with suspected infection took part in the checks. One machine flag caught most true infections but also flagged many people without infection. Stain checks agreed well with culture for one broad class of bacteria and poorly for another. The method looks best as a quick first screen, with culture still needed to confirm.
plos-pone-0339755:
Karsten Berg and five colleagues examine sleep-time blood pressure signals in a 2026 study. They compare healthy sleepers with patients who have obstructive sleep apnea. In apnea, breathing pauses trigger pressure surges all night. Clinicians often estimate pressure from pulse arrival time, a timing measure taken from simple sensors.

Directly measured pressure showed a clear pattern across time scales. Short-range behaviour looked organised, long-range behaviour looser, in every sleep stage. In apnea patients that contrast was blunted, hinting at stiffer cardiovascular control. Pulse arrival time told a different story. Its patterns were weak and barely resembled true pressure at all. The authors caution that this popular shortcut is a poor stand-in for real blood pressure during sleep.
plos-pone-0340955:
Agness Thawani and colleagues tested whether Malawi's lay HIV diagnostic assistants can run the rapid tests that identify advanced HIV disease as accurately as laboratory staff. Advanced disease care hinges on a CD4 count and two infection tests, yet labs are scarce. Three hundred eight patients gave paired samples: the lay workers and technicians ran a simple CD4 strip test, judged against a nurse-run machine count.

The lay workers' strip readings caught low CD4 counts with sensitivity and specificity both in the low-to-mid nineties, beating the laboratory technicians on the same test. Their follow-on infection tests agreed with nurses' results ninety-eight percent of the time, and each lay-run test cost less. Task-sharing here is not a compromise: on these assays the community-level workers were the stronger pair of hands, which argues for scaling the model.
plos-pone-0341955: Ryu and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on offshore wind farms in southwest Korea. Turbines steal wind from those behind them, an effect called wake loss. The team modeled how wakes from outside a cluster cut yearly power output at the Shinan cluster, and what that loss costs. Honest wake math matters when nations bet billions on offshore wind.
plos-pone-0343055:
Saito and Takahashi, in a 2026 theory paper, build a model of a market where several investors trade and consume, but cannot insure every risk. Each investor holds different views about the future and different patience for waiting. Shares pay dividends at set dates, like real coupons, rather than in a smooth stream.

Using a mathematical method that pairs each problem with its mirror image, the authors derive the market's pricing rule and from it the curve of long-term discount rates. They then run examples where the supply of government bonds changes over time. Those shifts move the discount curve, and with it the computed value of insurance products such as death benefits and pension annuities. The authors stress the examples show direction, not measured fact. Their point is that who holds bonds, and how patient holders are, quietly shapes the long-term rates insurers rely on.
plos-pone-0345155:
Soki Hattori and six colleagues describe two fossil braincases in this 2026 PLOS ONE paleontology paper. The skull bones come from Thailand's Khok Kruat Formation, a Lower Cretaceous rock unit in Nakhon Ratchasima province. They belong to the meat-eating dinosaur group called carcharodontosaurs, known for huge sizes and blade-like teeth.

Features such as a tall crest at the back of the skull tie the fossils to Siamraptor suwati, the only carcharodontosaur known from that site. The authors also name two traits not reported in related dinosaurs, including deep pits along the front bone's edge. Their family-tree analysis keeps Siamraptor as an early branch of the group, and comparisons with relatives trace how these skull features evolved.
plos-pone-0347055:
Ken-yu Hironao, Yoko Yamashita, and co-authors studied a plant compound that may calm inflammation in the brain linked to fatty diets. Fats common in animal foods can activate microglia, the brain's immune cells, and stir inflammation in the region that controls hunger and energy use. Their 2026 experiments used mouse microglia in dishes and mice fed a high-fat diet.

The compound, called protocatechuic acid and found in many plant foods, blocked a key inflammation switch inside the cells and lowered their output of irritant signals. In the diet-fed mice it also reduced the buildup of activated microglia and prevented obesity. The authors say the work is early, but it points to one way plant compounds in food might protect the brain and body from fatty diets.
plos-pone-0347555:
Meng Wan and Zhihui Liu built a computer model of how asphalt cracks. They treat the road material not as a uniform slab. It is the random jumble of stones and binder it really is. Their 2026 study converts real stone size distributions into simulated mixtures. It inserts breakable seams both around stones and through the binder. Cracks can then start and wander the way they do on real roads.

Unlike simpler models that predict implausibly straight cracks, this one produced jagged paths deflected by stones. The paths closely matched laboratory observations. Pavement engineers could use such realism to test mix designs virtually. They could learn which stone gradings resist cracking before committing to expensive road trials. The authors note a three-dimensional version is still to come.
plos-pone-0347755:
Felicia F. Wang and colleagues re-analysed gene activity data from the cricket Gryllus bimaculatus, an insect that can rebuild parts of its adult hearing system after injury, a feat mammals cannot match. Their earlier data had been read against a rough draft catalogue of cricket genes. Aligning the data to the cricket's published genome let them refine that catalogue substantially.

The update added nearly four thousand genes and more than nine thousand transcript variants, including likely regulatory RNAs. Injury responses peaked in the first three days, with signals involving molecular switches, hormones, and, surprisingly, muscle-related genes in nerve tissue. The resource should sharpen hypotheses about how adult brains reorganise after damage.
plos-pone-0348055:
Laura Langton and colleagues interviewed eleven officials from Irish racing bodies about the support available when professional jockeys retire, a moment that injury can impose without warning. The 2026 study catalogued services from the jockeys' trust, injured jockeys fund, academy, and associations, then probed what stops riders using them and what might encourage them.

Two barriers dominated: a racing culture that prizes toughness and silence about the future, and poor communication between the organisations offering help. Easier access to further education, treating career planning as normal from the start, and one model service tying everything together were the leading facilitators. The authors say wellbeing after racing depends on normalising the conversation.
plos-pone-0348355:
Kun Chang, Jun-Phil Uhm, and Hyun-Woo Lee surveyed two hundred thirty-nine esports players who had bought purely cosmetic in-game items, the skins and outfits that change looks but not power. Free-to-play games live on such sales, yet the psychology behind them is thinly studied. The 2026 survey chained together motivation, attitudes, and behaviour, and compared generations of players.

Wanting to present oneself well in-game fed favourable attitudes and social pressure to buy. Attitude, social norms, and feeling in control each strengthened buying intention, which strongly predicted actual purchases. The strength of these links differed between generations, suggesting marketers should not treat all players alike.
plos-pone-0348455:
Alexander D Duggan, Matthew P Newman, and David R McMillen built a tool for tuning protein production, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The rate at which a gene is translated into protein depends partly on a stretch of sequence before the gene, called the upstream untranslated region. Their language model generates such sequences on demand.

Duggan's team trained the model so users can request sequences that speed up or slow down translation. The tool targets non-model organisms, species that lack the rich toolkits of standard lab organisms. Giving researchers a dial for protein output in neglected species can open work on microbes and crops that current methods barely touch, from biofuels to local food strains.
plos-pone-0348955:
Chaohao Shi and colleagues weighed the price of mepolizumab, a premium injected drug for severe asthma, against its benefits for Chinese patients whose disease carries a particular immune signature. Their lifetime model cycled patients through health states in fortnightly steps. It imported attack rates from a major trial. Costs and quality-of-life weights came from the literature and national data. Everything took society's viewpoint.

The cost per year of good-quality life came out remarkably low, below even the bottom of the accepted willingness-to-pay range, and the verdict held across patient subgroups and stress tests. That is an unusual result for a biologic drug, which often fails such tests on price. The authors conclude the therapy represents good value in China and argue the analysis supports wider adoption.
plos-pone-0349155:
Bin Sun, Yiqiao Lu, Wei Liu, and Chengze Wang hunted for drug targets in antiphospholipid syndrome, an autoimmune clotting disorder with no targeted therapy, by layering several computational methods. Their 2026 systems pharmacology study combined gene network analysis of blood cells, single-cell sequencing of B cells, a drug signature database search, and molecular docking simulations.

Two gene programs stood out: one driven by type I interferon signaling, another by innate immune activation. Some B cells looked reprogrammed toward a myeloid-like state, an unexpected identity shift. Fourteen approved drugs touched the implicated genes, and a three-gene signature separated patients from controls decently. The authors offer the two programs as druggable axes awaiting laboratory and clinical testing, not as proven treatments.
plos-pone-0349555:
Ruping Zhang, Farhan Aadil, and co-authors built a computer model that judges how well a mobile app performs by reading what users write about it. Instead of sorting reviews into just positive or negative, their 2026 model rates apps as high or low on qualities like clarity, accuracy, and usefulness. It pairs two learning methods, one that sharpens how text features are picked out and one lightweight language model built for phones.

Reviews were labeled by hand, checked with an explanation tool, and expanded with synonym swaps to train the system. In repeated testing the model sorted reviews correctly close to nine times out of ten. Because it is small and fast, the approach could let app makers track user opinion in real time, even on limited hardware.
plos-pone-0349755:
Montserrath Abigail León Flores, Gerardo Ramírez Rico, and co-authors investigated two plant compounds from a wormwood relative traditionally used against parasites, testing whether they might also calm inflammation. Their 2026 study combined quantum chemistry calculations, computer docking against an inflammation enzyme, and lab tests on immune cells exposed to the compounds alone and mixed together.

Both compounds fit the enzyme's active site, though less snugly than a standard pain drug, and their predicted grip points to possible blocking action. In cells, they raised several protective immune signals, including one that surged dramatically when the mix met a bacterial trigger, while lowering a signal that recruits inflammation. The authors are careful: direct proof of enzyme blocking is still missing, and animal studies come next.
plos-pone-0349855:
R P Karthik and J Anitha led a drone project to spot mango leaf disease from the air. Sick leaves cost farmers yield each year. The team flew cameras over orchards and took more than six thousand shots. The set covered four common leaf diseases. They then trained a family of vision models the same way. Each model had to find and name the sick spots.

The newest model scored highest on raw accuracy. But an older model, tuned with the team's step-wise method, beat it on the harder test set. It also ran leaner on small field computers. On one cheap board it cut delay and power use by up to a quarter. The team pitches the setup for live farm use.
plos-pone-0349955:
Stefan Pettersson and co-authors tested a handheld saliva device for judging hydration in elite athletes in 2026. Field friendly hydration checks are prized, since blood and lab urine tests do not travel well to training grounds.

More than one hundred Olympic level athletes gave paired morning saliva and urine samples, with urine density as the reference. Repeated saliva readings from the same sample agreed very closely, so the device is steady. Yet saliva values barely matched urine at all and sorted hydrated from dry athletes no better than chance. Reliability without validity, the authors stress, is not enough for team decisions.
plos-pone-0350455:
Counting saxaul shrubs across deserts helps track land restoration, and drones offer a bird's eye view, but the crowns blend into sand. Dongze Li and colleagues built a sharper image model for outlining these crowns in drone photos, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Their design swaps the usual image backbone for a leaner one and adds an attention step that mixes pooled features. On held-out test images it marked crowns more precisely than the standard model, with far fewer false alarms and misses. Small crowns, the hardest cases, improved most. Heat maps showed the model focusing on crowns rather than background, a practical tool for desert monitoring.
plos-pone-0350555:
Tolera Gudissa Damme, Sileshi Garoma Abeya, and Dereje Bayissa Demissie explored emergency care for mothers and newborns at state hospitals in Ethiopia's West Shoa Zone in 2026. Poor quality care, more than distance, now drives many deaths in such settings, yet local views on what blocks quality were scarce.

Sixty-five women and health workers shared their experiences through group talks and interviews at four hospitals. Accounts pointed to staff shortages, missing supplies, and weak referral links as barriers, while training, teamwork, and supportive supervision helped. Hearing both sides of the ward gives planners a grounded list of fixes that cost less than new buildings.
plos-pone-0350655: AI-generated images — detected via adversarial perturbation-induced reconstruction discrepancy. ADRD is that detector. The method exposed diffusion models’ fingerprints. The findings armed the fight against synthetic media — truth’s technical defense.
plos-pone-0350855:
Christian Mesia-Montenegro and Angel Sanchez-Borjas recorded four groups of ground drawings, or geoglyphs, in two dry valleys of the middle Chillon Valley in Peru. Ground art is hard to date without direct evidence. Walkover survey and drone recording mapped the art, while pottery finds were logged nearby and random placement simulations tested whether art sits closer to old routes than chance would allow.

Formative period pottery appeared only near the Huarabi group, hinting at nearby activity rather than dating the art itself. Distance tests supported a route link for Huarabi under narrow assumptions, but not for Pichausa, and results shifted with wider maps. Authors stress how fragile such claims are: method choices shape the story.
plos-pone-0350955:
Stina Ingesson-Hammarberg and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE on thinking skills in people with moderate alcohol use disorder. Executive functions, the mental abilities behind planning, self-control, and flexible thinking, are known to suffer in severe alcohol problems, but most earlier samples mixed in heavy psychiatric illness. The Stockholm team tested patients from addiction clinics who had moderate disorder and little other psychiatric illness, before treatment began, and compared them with a non-clinical group.

Surprisingly, the patients performed no worse than the comparison group on any of the eight computerized tests, which covered flexibility, attention, memory, inhibition, and impatience for rewards. Test scores also failed to predict who cut down drinking over the following months of treatment. The authors suggest that in moderate disorder without heavy comorbidity, thinking skills may be largely intact, and treatment planning should not assume impairment testing does not show.
plos-pone-0351055:
Sen Yang, Yi Liu, and Liping Xu studied visitors who came to Zibo in Shandong, China, for its famous food scene. More than four hundred tourists answered an online survey about what they saw, smelled, tasted, and touched while eating. The team then tested how those sense experiences shaped whether visitors wanted to return, give feedback, or recommend the trip.

Tasty, vivid food experiences made visitors far more likely to stay involved with a place. Two mental steps helped carry that effect. People first stored strong food memories, and they also rebuilt the meal in their minds. Recalling a meal in detail pushed recommendations most, while stored memories mattered more for wanting to come back.
plos-pone-0351155:
Older people on long-term dialysis often grow frail, yet frailty comes in different shapes. Fangping Chen and colleagues sorted about two hundred twenty older dialysis patients in Guangdong, China, into hidden subgroups based on their frailty signs, in this 2026 PLOS One study.

Two groups appeared. One, a little over half the patients, moved little and scored highly frail; the other stayed more active and less frail. High blood pressure alongside dialysis raised the odds of landing in the weaker group. The authors argue care plans should match the subgroup: activity support for one, closer medical watching for the other.
plos-pone-0351555:
Sanjoy Mukharjee, Md Faruk Hasan, and Biswanath Sikdar sequenced the full genome of a salt-tolerant bacterium from rice roots. They hunted for a microbe that helps crops grow on salty, climate-stressed land. Nearly three hundred root isolates were screened first. One strain stood out for its stack of plant-helping traits. It frees phosphate and potassium, makes a growth hormone, and fixes nitrogen. It also forms protective films on roots.

The strain shrugged off heavy salt, drought-like stress, heat, and wide swings in acidity. It halved the growth of a fungus that attacks crops. Its genome explains the toolkit gene by gene. No single microbe will rescue saline farming alone. A mapped, stress-proof helper with this many trades is still a strong candidate for field trials.
plos-pone-0351655:
Juan Carlos Suarez and co authors followed eighteen cacao clones through a full day in the Colombian Amazon. Cacao trees supply the beans for chocolate and support many farm families. The team tracked light, heat, leaf traits, and signals that show how well leaves turn light into food without taking damage.

Clones differed a lot in how they handled midday heat and bright light. A few, including FGH-4, FSV-41, and IMC-67, kept their leaf machinery working well and moved energy fast. One clone leaned instead on safely dumping extra energy as heat. Another carried more protective pigments and coped well with harsh light. Such contrasts can guide which clones farmers plant as the climate warms.
plos-pone-0351855:
Tatsuya Yoshihara and co-authors used insurance claims from millions of Japanese women under forty to compare infection rates by menstrual health. Their 2026 PLOS One study covered women seen in 2023 and separated those with endometriosis or painful periods from those without such diagnoses.

Five sexually transmitted infections, including chlamydia and herpes, all appeared far more often in women with menstrual disorders. The team also split results by disorder type and by whether women took hormone treatments. Because claims data show visits rather than causes, the authors present the gap as a prompt for closer clinical attention, not proof one condition causes the other.
plos-pone-0351955:
Muhammad Khan, Yun-Ji Kim, and Jae-Hwan Ahn wash pesticide off vegetables with plasma-treated water in this 2026 study. Perilla leaves and broccoli were spiked with two common insecticides. Four washes were compared: plain soaking, bubbling water, chlorine water, and water treated by a microplasma device. The plasma water was applied both as a bath and as a fine spray. Four minutes of washing was timed for each method.

Plasma water matched chlorine, the industry standard. Both stripped roughly four-fifths or more of the residues from perilla leaves. Broccoli, with its knobbly surface, gave up less, around half to two-thirds. Temperature flipped expectations. Plasma water worked better cold, while chlorine worked worse. No wash changed the produce's colour, even after a week in the fridge. A chemical-free wash performing like chlorine could interest growers and processors seeking gentler food safety tools.
plos-pone-0352155:
Lv and colleagues built a decision method for judging whether regions have enough water in a 2026 study. Water carrying capacity weighs supply against the demands of people, farms, and industry. Their method handles fuzzy, mixed evidence and the way decision makers weigh gains and losses.

Applied to four cities on one Chinese river basin, the method split the cities clearly. Two cities looked comfortable, one sat near the limit, and one faced severe shortage. The sharper split between results helps officials target limits and investment. Fuzzy methods fit water questions, where data mix hard measures with expert judgment.
plos-pone-0352255:
Khushboo Goel and Sirjana Dahal follow young adults with aggressive gum disease in Kathmandu, Nepal. Their 2026 study covers sixty-three patients, average age under thirty. Grade C periodontitis destroys support tissue unusually fast. All patients received full-mouth disinfection therapy with antibiotics. Researchers then tracked their teeth through five years of maintenance care. Over seventeen hundred teeth were at stake. The question was which teeth, and which patients, would lose ground.

Only fifteen teeth were lost across the whole follow-up. That is under one percent, a strong result for such aggressive disease. Keeping maintenance appointments protected teeth. So did the molar-incisor pattern of disease and moderate starting bone loss. Once bone loss passed sixty percent, the hazard of losing a tooth jumped dramatically. The clinical message is hopeful but conditional: aggressive periodontitis in young adults can be held, provided patients actually return for maintenance care.
plos-pone-0352355:
Firoz Akhter and colleagues traced a source of toxic sugar-damaged proteins, called advanced glycation end products, that build up in Alzheimer's disease. Earlier work tied their buildup to failing mitochondria, the cell's power plants, but the direction of cause was unclear. Using Alzheimer's-model mice and cell experiments, the team tested whether stressed mitochondria themselves drive the accumulation.

The toxic products gathered inside cortical mitochondria as the disease model progressed, tracking with amyloid and oxidative damage. Deliberately stressing mitochondria with a toxin raised the products further, in whole cells and in mitochondria. A mitochondria-targeted antioxidant did the reverse, lowering the products and improving mitochondrial function. The loop matters because it names a druggable step: calm the power plant's stress, and one class of brain toxins may slow its rise.
plos-pone-0352455:
Erick Jacob Okek and seven co-authors review malaria control in two Ugandan districts with heavy spread of the disease. They used five years of national health records. They compared indoor spraying and treated bed nets, alone and combined. They also compared the chemicals used in each campaign. The outcome was the share of malaria tests that came back positive in Yumbe and in Gulu.

After adjusting for weather, Yumbe's positive rate fell several times faster than Gulu's. One net brand spread in 2020 made no clear change to Yumbe's trend. In contrast, one spray formula showed a strong impact. The authors argue that which products are deployed matters a great deal. The mix matters as much as the act of deploying itself.
plos-pone-0352555:
Zheng Liu examines whether vocational students can actually judge the curriculum designs that artificial intelligence produces for them, in this 2026 classroom study from a Chinese vocational college. Thirty-nine second-year students in a study-tour curriculum course completed AI-assisted planning tasks, then sat a closed-book, handwritten diagnostic test with no AI access. Their responses, amounting to nearly two hundred substantive claims, were analyzed for depth of judgment.

Students could recite sound criteria, accuracy, feasibility, fit to learners, safety, and the need for human revision. Applied diagnosis was thinner. Most spotted surface problems like mismatched learners, time pressure, overloaded sites, and safety gaps. Few caught weak curriculum logic, unworkable assessment plans, unchecked facts, or blurred responsibility for the work. Liu calls this a stated-applied judgment gap and argues no-AI diagnostics expose where AI help has not yet become professional skill.
plos-pone-0352755:
Pérez Molina and colleagues reviewed recent evidence on yellow fever prevention in a 2026 paper. Yellow fever still breaks out in Africa and the Americas despite a strong vaccine that has existed for decades. New outbreaks in Brazil and Colombia showed that coverage stays uneven and responses often start only after spread begins.

The review gathered studies and official reports from 2020 to 2025 in three languages, with focus on global, Latin American, and Colombian findings. It maps what is known about vaccine plans, safety, and immune responses, plus newer ideas for calming harmful immune reactions. Gaps in coverage and in early action stand out as the main lessons for health officials.
plos-pone-0352855:
Dongxiao Fu and five colleagues model how cars follow each other around mountain curves, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study aimed at safer roads. Mountain highways in China combine tight bends, harsh weather, and mixed driving styles, and accidents cluster there. Drones filmed traffic on a curved stretch in Yunnan, and the cleaned trajectories were sorted by algorithm into aggressive, conservative, and standard driving styles.

The three styles differed clearly in speed, acceleration, and following distance. Adding curve radius to a standard car-following model, then calibrating it separately for each style, sharply improved how well the model reproduced real trajectories. Traffic simulators that ignore both bend and temperament, the authors show, will misjudge mountain roads.
plos-pone-0353155:
Gandhi and colleagues tested a leading AI chatbot on judging bias in clinical trials in a 2026 study. Fifty trials drawn from fifty reviews were rated by the original reviewers, by a masked human panel, and by the chatbot using structured prompts from the standard bias tool.

The chatbot called far more trials high risk than either human group did. Agreement with humans was modest at best. Overcalling bias can distort evidence summaries just as undercalling can. The authors' verdict is caution: AI bias ratings are not yet a stand-in for trained reviewers, though they might serve as a first pass with human checks.
plos-pone-0353355:
Erdem Maraşlı, Erkan Ozduran, and Volkan Hancı published this 2026 study grading artificial intelligence chatbots on knee osteoarthritis, a worn-joint condition behind most arthritis disability. They posed common search terms as questions to three leading chatbots and scored the answers for readability, reliability against medical benchmarks, and overall quality.

The chatbots wrote at reading levels many patients would struggle with, and their reliability and quality scores raised real concerns about scientific soundness. The authors argue that medical chatbot answers need an effective oversight system before patients can safely trust them.
plos-pone-0353555:
Ochoa Capera and colleagues compared a key DNA control stretch across thousands of vertebrates in a 2026 study. The stretch governs copying and reading of the cell's small power-station genome, yet its evolution was poorly mapped. More than five thousand species across eleven classes were analyzed for length, repeats, and conserved blocks.

Land vertebrates carried longer, more repeat-rich control stretches than fishes. Copying events appeared only on land lineages, especially birds and reptiles, while birds and mammals later trended shorter. Core working motifs stayed conserved throughout. The survey gives the first full framework for how this control region balances sameness and change.
plos-pone-0353655:
Tianning Li interviews thirty young ethnic-minority migrants who moved from China's countryside to the city of Wuhan, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The participants, from Miao, Tujia, and Tibetan backgrounds, described in depth how their ethnic identity helped or hindered settling into urban life. Their accounts were analysed for recurring lived patterns rather than counted.

Five strands ran through the stories: how they labelled themselves, language skill in ethnic and local tongues, keeping cultural practices, facing discrimination, and stitching two identities together. Ethnic identity worked both ways at once — a shield against prejudice and a source of belonging, yet also a boundary with local residents. Policies, Li argues, must support identity while dismantling structural barriers.
plos-pone-0353755:
Javiera Cartagena-Farías and co-authors study in 2026 whether poor housing raises the risk of falls for older people living at home in England. Two decades of ageing survey data fed models designed to handle cause running both ways and uneven follow up. A cost model then priced the health and social care that followed such falls.

Homes with electrical or plumbing faults or too little space raised fall risk, and homes described as too dark raised both falls and later service use. The yearly care cost tied to poor housing was estimated in the billions of pounds range. Housing fixes could serve as fall prevention, the authors argue.
plos-pone-0353955:
Andrea Ciricugno and co-authors present in 2026 a trial plan joining brain stimulation with immersive virtual reality to train social prediction in people with cerebellar damage. The cerebellum helps predict others' intentions, and damage from birth defects or later disease can blunt social life. Two patient groups will train in interactive virtual scenes over eight daily sessions.

During training, each person receives either real or sham stimulation tuned to their own brain rhythm, measured beforehand. Main checks cover reading intentions, emotions, and traits in social scenes, with brain measures and daily functioning as extra checks. The plan is registered and reports no results.
plos-pone-0354255:
Chen, in a 2026 literary study, reads a novel by Tan Twan Eng through the lens of language patterns. The novel follows a judge who, after trauma and war, apprentices herself to a Japanese gardener in Malaya. Chen asks how the book's word choices carry the main character's personality and shifting feelings.

The analysis pairs a standard five-trait model of personality with a method that studies how language builds meaning. Three phases of the story are tracked: remembering trauma, learning in the garden, and reflective closing. Early passages lean on obligation words and tight sentences, a pattern Chen links to anxious, dutiful self-control. Later passages open into balance and warmth, matching growing openness and easing distress. Two softer traits, kindness and sociability, run quieter but follow the same arc. Chen argues that in this novel, feeling is not fixed weather but a slow adaptation that the language itself performs.
plos-pone-0354355:
Javad Yoosefi Lebni and four colleagues published this 2026 interview study on why young couples divorce in western Iran. They spoke with thirty-two people who had lived through divorce plus sixteen key informants, sorting hundreds of coded remarks into themes about the person, the marriage, and the wider family and culture.

Sexual problems, mental strain, and clashing personalities met weak communication skills and marriages entered for shallow reasons. Family interference and stigma around asking for help added pressure. Lebni recommends teaching couples before marriage, normalizing counseling, and helping families resolve conflict rather than inflame it.
plos-pone-0354455:
Wan Wang and co-authors build in 2026 a scenario based method to judge risks faced by power grid maintenance workers in China. Dangers span worker actions, equipment state, surroundings, and management, making full identification hard. Their method breaks a live line job into stages, weights the factors at each stage, and traces how risk passes from one stage to the next using network logic.

Human and environmental factors carried the highest overall weight, matching real accident patterns. Workers' physical and mental health stood out as an overlooked driver. Poor work early in a job directly endangered later steps. Stage specific control, the authors argue, beats a single blanket checklist.
plos-pone-0354755:
Andrea Bernal-Rivera and co-authors measured blood sugar control across many Neotropical bat species to learn what shapes it. Sugar handling underpins the bats' varied diets, from fruit and nectar to insects and blood. Their 2026 field study used portable glucose meters and weighed diet, family relatedness, season, and body traits.

Fasting glucose tracked diet group and evolutionary kinship, but not sex or body mass. Sugar uptake speed depended on sugar type, diet specialisation, and time of day and year. Fruit eaters flexed their sugar handling with the seasons. Closely related species living side by side showed hints of metabolic separation, as if dividing the menu. The authors link physiology to how bat communities share food.
plos-pone-0354855:
Ayben Leblebici and four colleagues test what Turkish medical students know about acute rheumatic fever, in a study published in 2026 using a survey from the 2019-2020 academic year. The disease follows untreated strep throat and can permanently damage children's hearts; Turkey sits in a moderate-to-high risk band. The authors surveyed first-year students, who had only basic science training, and sixth-year students fresh from clinical rotations, scoring both against American Heart Association guidance.

One hundred sixty-five students responded. Sixth-year students knew significantly more than first-years, as expected. But the study's point is the gap structure itself: awareness of a preventable disease that still harms young hearts depends heavily on clinical exposure. The authors argue that teaching about preventable diseases like rheumatic fever should be woven deliberately into medical curricula rather than left to chance encounters on the wards.
plos-pone-0355055:
Adam Harriman and co-authors look back in 2026 at intensive care patients in Britain who needed a breathing tube through the neck for long term support. Letting air out of the tube cuff is a key step toward speaking and coming off the machine. Records were split by how soon that step happened after the tube was placed.

Later cuff release linked to longer time on the machine, slower removal of the tube, and more chest infections. Those patients also stayed longer in intensive care, felt more anxious, and died more often. The authors stress the link may reflect illness rather than cause it, and call for direct trials.
plos-pone-0355155:
Fawzia Irhayyim Al-Assadi, Osamah Abdulmunem Al-Tameemi, and Aya F Alobaidi study what a breakthrough looks like in modern Iraqi architecture, using three major buildings erected since the early two thousands. Iraqi design has wrestled with honoring deep local identity while absorbing global technology. Through site observation, documents, and interviews analyzed with qualitative software, the team compares a government headquarters, a set of Chinese-built schools, and the new central bank building.

Breakthrough, they find, is never just bold shape. The strongest cases fuse new technology with local values so the building restates Iraqi identity rather than importing a foreign one. Al-Assadi and colleagues propose a framework linking breakthrough, innovation, and transformation, offered as a guide for architects rebuilding in culturally loaded settings.
plos-pone-0355655:
Retraction notice. The PLOS One editors formally withdrew a published study of KIOM-C, a herbal medicine tested on human fibrosarcoma cells. The original paper had claimed the mixture drove cancer cell death through stress pathways. This 2026 notice records why the journal lost confidence in that work.

Editors found panels in several figures that appear to overlap while claiming to show different conditions. The authors could not produce the original image files, so the overlaps could not be explained or ruled out as assembly errors. The notice also faults the statistics for ignoring multiple comparisons. It further records an undisclosed patent interest held by the corresponding author. Readers should not rely on the retracted findings.
plos-pone-0355855:
Takayuki Yamaguchi and colleagues measure a natural germ-fighting peptide in the blood of people with sleep apnea, the disorder where breathing repeatedly stalls at night. Apnea stirs body-wide inflammation and may weaken defenses against viruses. The team compared peptide levels in several dozen patients and healthy controls against detailed sleep study records, including how often breathing dipped and how much deep sleep each person got.

Peptide levels ran lower in patients with more severe apnea and tracked sleep quality closely: lower with more light, broken sleep and more breathing dips, higher with more deep and dreaming sleep. Light sleep share stood out as the independent link. Yamaguchi and colleagues propose the peptide as a blood marker worth testing for apnea's immune toll.
plos-pone-0355955:
Zeinab Ghesmati and co-authors compare tiny parcels released by two lab-grown fat cell types, heat-making brown-like cells and storage white-like cells, across four kinds of human cells. Such parcels carry signals between cells, and fat-derived ones might steer other tissues. Targets included ovary cells, a breast cancer line, and two stem cell sources, treated either with the cells' full broth or with the isolated parcels.

Brown-cell parcels raised a key hormone output from ovary cells. Broth, more than parcels, pushed cancer cells toward death. Both treatments nudged fat stem cells toward bone making while cooling their stem identity, and brown parcels reshaped their fat content most. Ghesmati and colleagues map a cell-by-cell pattern that could inform future fat-based therapies.
plos-pone-0356055:
Catrina MacPhee and three colleagues publish the protocol for a trial of a game-based treatment for spatial neglect after stroke, in this 2026 paper. Neglect leaves patients unaware of one side of space and predicts poor recovery; prism glasses can retrain attention, but the therapy is repetitive, equipment-bound, and little used. Their version, a whack-a-mole style computer game played through prism goggles, is designed to be engaging, portable, and usable at home or in rehabilitation units.

Forty-two patients with right-hemisphere stroke will be assigned, under double-blind conditions, to real prism strength or a much weaker active control, playing for fifteen minutes daily over two weeks. Outcomes span standard neglect tests, daily living skills, patients' and caregivers' reports of impact, plus mood and fatigue. The authors hope the gamified format will show whether prism therapy can finally travel beyond specialist labs.
plos-pone-0356255:
Stefanie M Jungmann and fellow psychologists survey women and mothers about mental load, the invisible work of planning, remembering, and organizing family life. Public debate on the topic has grown, but research has lagged behind. In two online studies, women rated how stressful visible chores felt against invisible ones. The first study had several hundred women. A much larger second study covered mothers only. Participants also named what drives the burden.

Mothers found invisible tasks more stressful and less fairly shared than visible chores. The load tied to worse mood and to higher anxiety and low mood, and endless thinking about unfinished tasks was the most named cause. Personality mattered too, especially worry-prone traits. Jungmann and colleagues draw lessons for partners, workplaces, and policy.
plos-pone-0356955:
The PLOS One Editors issued this Expression of Concern in 2026. It concerns a study of constipation in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. That study had linked gut problems to a disrupted chemical signaling pathway and cell stress responses. An Expression of Concern warns readers that a published article's reliability is under question. The warning stands while issues are examined.

Editors list many figure panels that look alike across figures. Some look alike across other papers. They list spliced gel images. They also list raw data originally missing from the article's files. The authors acknowledged several panels were incorrect. They supplied corrected figures and the missing data. Some similarities were explained as shared control samples and combined gels. The journal's notice leaves the article flagged. Its claims should be read with caution until the case closes.
plos-pone-0357355:
Correction notice: the entry here amends an earlier banana study by Swarup Roy Choudhury and colleagues on a gene-switch protein tied to flowering and fruit ripening. After publication, readers spotted that panels in one figure looked the same across two panels meant to show different fruit zones. The authors confirmed the first set of panels was wrong and supplied replacement images taken during the original experiment.

All underlying images for the affected figure panels are attached to the notice. The authors also note that one older dataset behind another figure is no longer available, while the rest can be requested from them. Roy Choudhury's team leaves the study's claims standing, with the figure record now repaired for anyone checking the ripening evidence.
plos-pone-0357755:
Seung-Hwan Kim published a 2026 modeling paper in PLOS ONE on how childhood leukemia changes over time inside individual patients. Tumor growth in these cancers is pushed around by chance, body development, and treatment, yet doctors rarely sample often enough to see the motion. Kim fitted a Bayesian version of a classic random-walk model, the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, to repeated measurements from children whose leukemia carried a specific gene rearrangement.

The fitted parameters hinted that random fluctuation ran higher in hard-to-treat and very early stages, but uncertainty ranges overlapped too much to claim sharply separate regimes. Simulations showed the Bayesian approach stayed stable and gave honest uncertainty estimates even with sparse sampling, though prediction remained limited. The framework is presented as a careful way to read stage patterns in thin clinical data, not as a tool for forecasting one child's course.
plos-pone-0358255:
Precious Makiyi and seven colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on youth mental health. It traces the referral paths followed by depressed young people in places where services are scarce. The study is qualitative and comes from Ghana and Zimbabwe, two countries where specialist mental care is scarce.

A referral trajectory is the real path a young person travels between teachers, clinics, families, and healers while seeking help. Mapping those paths exposes dead ends and delays that official charts hide. Mental health planners in low-income countries can use such maps to build referral routes that young people can actually complete.
plos-pone-0358455:
Ingrid A Wise led a team of eight authors studying a hormone and diabetic eye disease, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Erythropoietin, best known for boosting red blood cells, may also signal damage in diabetic retinopathy, a leading cause of blindness. The team worked within the LANDMark cohort, tracking the hormone over time.

Wise's longitudinal study links levels of the hormone in the body with the course of eye disease, testing its value as a biomarker. A blood test that warns of worsening eye disease could trigger earlier eye checks and treatment. Cohort data gathered over years are precious for this, since eye damage builds slowly. The study adds a candidate signal to a field that needs early warnings.
plos-pone-0358555:
Yankuba Singhateh led a team of six authors tracking measles and rubella control in Lesotho, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Lesotho, a small mountain kingdom in southern Africa, has worked toward eliminating both diseases for years. The team reviewed progress across the period from 2011 to 2025.

Singhateh's record shows how far the campaign has come and what still blocks zero cases. Elimination efforts often stall on the last hard-to-reach children, so knowing the remaining gaps is vital. The fourteen-year view also shows whether gains held through shocks such as the pandemic years. Other small countries can learn from Lesotho's path, both its wins and its stubborn obstacles.
plos-pone-0358755:
Tobias Gummer, Ko-Hsuan Lu, and Karolina von Glasenapp assessed in 2026 how well survey data gathered in Germany during the COVID-19 pandemic meet the FAIR principles. FAIR data are findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable: in short, data that other researchers can actually locate and work with years later. The pandemic produced a rush of surveys about health, work, and behavior, collected under time pressure.

The authors check that body of data against the FAIR standard and report where it falls short, in documentation, formats, or archiving. Their audit matters because crisis data are often reused for decades, and sloppy stewardship quietly wastes the effort of everyone who answered. The lessons apply to any future emergency data collection.
plos-pone-0360055:
Jennifer Grauer and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies bobcats across the northeast of the United States. The authors map where and when these wild cats were exposed to anticoagulant rodenticides, poisons used against rats and mice that also stop blood from clotting.

The pattern is spatiotemporal, charting exposure across both place and time. Bobcats likely pick up these chemicals by eating poisoned prey, so their exposure signals a wider problem in the food web. Wildlife managers and regulators weighing limits on such poisons are the readers who most need maps like these.
plos-pone-0360155:
Thu Hoang Thanh, Nhan Nguyen Thi, and Toan Nguyen Khac wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on teenage weight. It studies factors linked to overweight and obesity among adolescents, using the 2023 Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System survey in the United States. The authors stress broader factors, beyond diet alone.

The analysis is survey-aware, meaning it respects how the national survey sampled students, and it adds calibrated AI-assisted classification. Combining careful statistics with machine learning can sharpen which groups face the highest risk. School health planners reading this get a wider view of what surrounds teen weight, from habits to environment.
plos-pone-0360355:
Thitirut Jongutchariya and three colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It is a randomized trial comparing two treatment plans for a painful shoulder and neck condition. The condition is myofascial pain syndrome of the upper trapezius, the muscle running from neck to shoulder.

Both plans use magnetic pulses applied again and again to ease pain. Comparing two versions head to head shows which settings deserve wider use. Therapists treating stubborn neck and shoulder pain are the readers who need this kind of direct comparison before adopting a device-based therapy.
pmc-13241055:
Jerome and colleagues in Tamil Nadu pooled the evidence on treating children's broken wrists, the commonest pediatric fracture. Forty-five studies covering five thousand three hundred forty children entered the review. Twelve comparative studies fed the meta-analysis directly. The team split metaphyseal breaks from growth-plate injuries throughout.

Casts alone let twenty to thirty-five percent of metaphyseal breaks slip, versus almost none with added wires. Healing was near universal and long-term function equal either way. Children under eleven remodeled even fully shifted breaks without surgery. Jerome holds wire fixation for genuinely unstable patterns.
pmc-13242455:
Alice Guionnet and Jiaoyang Huang studied two famous families of symmetric polynomials in the limit as their variable count grows without bound. Their paper appeared in Communications in Mathematical Physics in 2026. Macdonald and Jack polynomials sit at the crossroads of algebra, probability, and physics, but their large-scale behavior had resisted a full description. The authors characterize the limits through variational problems, where an energy-like quantity is minimized.

A key step proves a large deviation principle for a deformed version of non-intersecting random walks. At the special value of one, those walks match random lozenge tilings of strip-shaped domains. That connection lets the paper recover a celebrated tiling result of Cohn and co-authors by a new route. It then extends the principle to every positive value. The work ties polynomial limits to the study of random surfaces.
pmc-13243155:
Elizabeth Valles-Capetillo and colleagues charted the brain networks behind social communication and what personal traits predict how well they run. Their study appeared in Cognitive Neurodynamics in 2026. Forty-five neurotypical adults completed tests of language, executive function, social cognition, and reasoning, plus an autism traits questionnaire. The team measured these networks for language, mentalizing, and both combined, then repeated the check in a second sample that included autistic adults.

Language skill was the strongest and steadiest predictor of how well the networks ran, above all in regions that blend meaning with context. Executive function predicted frontal control areas, and reasoning skill tied to a hub used in social inference. Autistic traits changed the strength of several brain-behavior links rather than simply weakening the networks. The authors argue social communication rests on an efficient, flexible system shaped by each person's cognitive profile.
pmc-13243755:
Liang Wang, Xia Lei, and Lingfei Li report a stubborn nail disease that finally yielded to a targeted immune drug. Their case report appeared in the Journal of International Medical Research in 2026. The patient, a woman in her late forties, had nail lichen planus, a chronic inflammation that ridges, roughens, and splits the nails. Standard creams and systemic treatments had repeatedly failed her, as they often do in this condition.

She was started on abrocitinib, a drug that selectively blocks the JAK1 signaling switch inside immune cells. Her nails improved markedly on measured scores, and normal nail function returned. The benefit held through a slow taper and even after the drug was stopped, and her safety record stayed clean. The authors argue the drug hits the core immune mechanism driving the disease. One case cannot set policy, but it strengthens a growing set of reports behind this approach.
pmc-13244955:
Eric Amelunxen and colleagues test whether community pharmacies can catch heart, kidney, and metabolic risk earlier than clinics do. Their trial protocol appeared in BMC Nephrology in 2026. The APOSCREEN-1 study runs in twenty pharmacies in Germany's Schleswig-Holstein state. One thousand adults aged forty and over who meet risk criteria get point-of-care testing on the spot: glycated hemoglobin, blood lipids, urine albumin, and blood pressure, plus a clinical history.

Results flow to a study center through an online platform. Anyone crossing thresholds is sent for confirmatory laboratory testing at the center or their general practitioner. The trial's main questions are practical: will people accept screening at the pharmacy counter, and how much undetected disease it finds? Primary-care screening uptake is low, and the syndrome often surfaces only after organ damage. If pharmacies prove feasible and high-yield, they offer an accessible front door to prevention.
pmc-13247555:
Jiang and co-authors tracked eight reintroduced giant pandas to watch their movement styles settle, in this 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. Pandas run on an unusually tight energy budget, eating bamboo they digest poorly, making them a model for how animals move under energetic constraint. GPS collars followed the released animals for well over a year, and the team distilled ten movement measures into two behavioral axes, exploration versus exploitation and path straightness versus consistency.

Early on, individuals differed repeatably: explorers roamed widely while exploiters stayed put.
