Over the first months the explorers shrank their ranges and the whole group converged toward similar, conservative space use. The authors propose a diet-energy constraint hypothesis, that specialized diets and low energy efficiency push released animals toward cautious movement as they acclimate.
pmc-13247655:
Antuña-Zarzuelo and co-authors reflect on how great writers have grieved, in this 2026 editorial essay in Palliative and Supportive Care. Literature gives language to loss, and the authors read four writers as case studies in contrasting responses: Cesare Pavese, Miguel Hernández, Julian Barnes, and Joan Didion. Each wrote from a broken heart along a different path.

Pavese's diaries show grief as resentment: learning in 1936 that the woman he loved had married another, he armored himself in bitterness that slowly loosened over years. Hernández, imprisoned after Spain's civil war, answered loss with tears in elegies for his friends Sijé and Lorca. The essay uses such examples to remind clinicians that grief wears many faces, including ungraceful ones, and that naming them can be a form of endurance worth honoring in care.
pmc-13248255:
Lin and a large expert panel issued the 2025 Chinese consensus on prolactinomas, published in 2026. Prolactinomas are the most common hormone-producing pituitary tumors. The China Pituitary Adenoma Specialist Council updated its 2014 guidance using newer surgical methods and fresh clinical evidence gathered since then.

The statement gives thirty-six recommendations covering screening, testing, diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up monitoring. It explains how these tumors present, how doctors separate them from look-alike conditions, and how care should change for pregnant patients, men, and hard-to-treat cases. The panel stresses team review, with surgeons, hormone specialists, imaging experts, and others deciding together.
pmc-13249055:
Zhao and colleagues taught computers to grade hazy lung spots by invasiveness, in a 2026 multicenter study. Ground-glass nodules on CT scans range from harmless precursor growths to invasive adenocarcinoma, and each class calls for different care. The team extracted texture features from scans of more than eleven hundred patients and trained six machine learning models on the three-way task.

A neural network model beat the other five, holding up best on the separate test set. Its discrimination scores stayed solid across both groups of patients. The authors also used explanation tools to show which features drove each call. They present the model as support for planning surgery and follow-up, not a replacement for pathology.
pmc-13249255:
Valigurová and colleagues give the first full account of a frog blood parasite in Slovakia, in a 2026 Parasite study. Screening two hundred thirty-nine frogs, they found sixty-seven water frogs of three Pelophylax species carrying a Dactylosoma parasite, a distant relative of malaria organisms. Specimens came from three sites in western Slovakia, and the team combined microscope measurements with DNA evidence.

All infections belonged to one species, closely matching the classic Dactylosoma ranarum first described from the same host genus. Flies caught at the sites carried none of the parasite, leaving its carrier unknown. The authors frame the work as a reference description tying old morphology to modern genetic data.
pmc-13250255:
Joukar and colleagues check how often hepatitis C spreads inside families in Iran's Guilan cohort. Their 2026 Health Science Reports study followed twenty relatives of twelve people known to carry the virus. Blood tests looked for antibodies and active virus, and positive samples were typed by genotype to compare strains.

Two relatives tested positive for antibodies, and one, a thirteen-year-old girl, carried active virus matching her mother's genotype. She was treated with the combined drug Sovodak and cleared the virus, confirmed twelve weeks after therapy. No other family spread was found, so the authors judge household transmission real but extremely rare. They note that even shared household items could, in theory, carry some risk.
pmc-13251855:
Daniel Gilford and colleagues put a human fingerprint on flood days worldwide in this 2026 study. Sea level rise is raising coastal flood risk, but how much of that extra risk comes from human-caused climate change had never been counted site by site.

Using two estimation methods at 519 tide gauges, the team found the human share measurable at 97 percent of sites. Human-caused rise accounted for about 58 percent of the days when extreme water levels were passed between 2000 and 2018. On average, the count of such blame-carrying flood days has nearly tripled since the 1970s. The numbers are meant for local planning and loss claims.
pmc-13252755:
Michael Smith, Nicole Olynk Widmar, and Valerie Kilders track online investor chatter in this 2026 study whose title nods to a popular market slogan. Social media now hosts huge retail investing communities that can amplify, and sometimes coordinate, market moves.

Using a listening platform, the team collected weekly mentions and mood for four topics from 2020 to 2023: the United States dollar, gold, cryptocurrencies, and attention-shocked stocks such as meme stocks. They tested how chatter reacted to events like regional bank failures and famous short squeezes. Commentary volume stayed high throughout, and the authors find online communities increasingly shape how the public talks about markets.
pmc-13253155:
Fırat Tevetoğlu, Nil Çomunoğlu, and Haydar Yener test two immune markers in throat cancer in this 2026 study. Voice-box cancer survival has barely budged for decades, and newer immune brakes called TIM-3 and LAG-3 might explain who fares worse.

The team re-examined tumour samples from 50 patients who had voice-box surgery between 2016 and 2018, staining for both markers and for overall immune cell presence. LAG-3 positivity tracked with earlier cancer return across the whole group. TIM-3 mattered only in tumours with sparse immune infiltration, where it linked to worse survival. The authors call the results exploratory and ask for larger, multi-centre checks.
pmc-13253555:
Sara Lawhon and a large multi-laboratory team standardise a dog stool test in this 2026 study. Campylobacter jejuni sickens over a million Americans a year, and a 2016–2018 outbreak traced the germ to pet dogs, yet dog samples are not routinely tested for it.

Twenty-seven analysts at nineteen laboratories ran a DNA test targeting the gyrA gene on seeded dog stool samples. Every analyst caught the germ at a high dose. Detection fell as doses dropped: 96 percent at a mid dose, 77 percent lower, and 40 percent at the lowest. Reading DNA straight from stool skips a growing step, cutting contamination risk and turnaround time for veterinary labs.
pmc-13253655:
Thalita Faita and a large team test stranded whales and dolphins for parasites along Brazil's coast in this 2026 study. Sea mammals act as sentinels of ocean health, and land parasites washing into the sea are an emerging threat to them.

Samples from 159 stranded animals of 21 species were screened with DNA methods. Fourteen animals carried infections, and the pattern split by habitat. Nine coastal animals held Toxoplasma or a related species, matching spread from land hosts through runoff into the sea. Six open-ocean animals carried a distinct lineage of the same family, whose closest matches point to sea birds as the likely final hosts in its life cycle.
pmc-13254055:
Lu Liu and a large team design a light-emitting molecule with an unusually pure color in a 2026 study. Organic emitters, carbon-based light sources, often blur in color when molecules clump together. The team's molecule, built around an eight-electron ring system, keeps a flat shape in both ground and excited states.

In solution, its emission width was already narrow. When clumped, a cross stacking pattern held the shape still and cut vibration, narrowing the width to a record-small 13 nanometers. In light devices, the width stayed at 13 nanometers even as concentration rose, aiding sharp display design.
pmc-13258155:
Magdalena Circu and co-authors describe a bacterial protein that quietly retunes metabolism inside infected macrophages. The bacterium is Legionella pneumophila, which can cause severe lung infection when inhaled. Their 2026 paper follows its effector Lpg0393, renamed BinA for the role they uncovered.

BinA moves amino acid transporters toward where they can feed the cell, working through Rab21 and Rab22 proteins. That lowers the trigger point for TORC1, a master growth switch, when arginine or leucine appears. Without BinA, the compartment housing the bacteria ruptured early, in step with the switch. The work maps a new lever Legionella pulls to expand its home.
pmc-13260255:
Alexander A Sulfaro wrote a 2026 theoretical article arguing that measures of mental image vividness rest on an undefined concept. Vividness ratings are meant to capture how sensory a mental image feels, on a scale running to aphantasia, the claimed absence of mental imagery. Such ratings are widely used, and studies of aphantasia are growing. Sulfaro argues the field assumes these measures are valid without a logical basis for that assumption.

The core problem, he says, is that the single axis separating a mental image from other experiences has eluded definition for centuries. While it stays undefined, variation along it cannot be validly measured, and checks against other measures are circular. He also argues that confounding criteria can explain common findings, and that even confident imagery self-reports can be doubted. Better reference definitions are proposed.
pmc-13261055:
Montana Kay Lara leads a 2026 genome-wide association study of cocaine self-administration behavior in outbred rats. Cocaine use disorder is a major public health crisis, and its genes remain largely unknown. The study used 836 Heterogeneous Stock rats, 415 female and 421 male, bred to mimic human genetic diversity. Traits included acquiring self-administration, escalating intake, and compulsive-like responding. Heritability estimates and genome scans searched for linked DNA regions.

The traits were correlated with each other and showed modest heritability, from 0.07 to 0.16. Six genome-wide significant associations were found. One locus on chromosome nineteen, tied to time between cocaine infusions, contains carboxylesterase genes related to human CES1; these enzymes metabolize cocaine. Other loci contained genes previously linked to cocaine, alcohol, or tobacco use disorders in humans. The authors call it the largest rat genetic study of cocaine self-administration.
pmc-13263355:
Xinxin Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 phase II trial of nano-packaged chemotherapy for adenoid cystic carcinoma, a slow but stubborn cancer of the head and neck. Patients had tumors that could not be removed or had returned or spread. Thirty-one patients received liposomal doxorubicin plus nab-paclitaxel for three cycles; those fit for radiation then received combined chemoradiotherapy.

The response rate was about ninety percent, with fifteen complete and thirteen partial responses, meeting the trial's main goal. Responses lasted a median of about eighteen and a half months. Patients who went on to chemoradiotherapy stayed free of progression longer. Severe side effects affected about a quarter of patients, and there were no treatment-related deaths.
pmc-13264555:
Huan Wei and colleagues wrote a 2026 lab study comparing blood safety of coated flow diverters, mesh tubes placed in brain arteries to treat aneurysms. Bare metal can trigger clots, so makers add coatings. The team tested a polymer-coated device, a fibrin and heparin-coated device, and one bare device in a blood loop.

The bare device raised clotting and platelet activity most, with platelets sticking to its surface. Both coatings cut those effects well. The fibrin and heparin device also sparked less immune activation and less inflammation than the polymer-coated one, on the markers used. Blood cell counts and red cell damage were also tracked. The authors judge the fibrin and heparin coating the most blood-friendly of the three.
pmc-13264855:
Yu Yan and colleagues published a 2026 study on how tropical cyclones speed dengue spread in Guangzhou, China. Dengue is a mosquito-borne fever, and the city is China's most dengue-prone coastal megacity. Storms were known to raise risk, but the mechanism was unclear, so the team paired field tests on mosquitoes with epidemic modeling of the 2014 outbreak.

In release and recapture tests, storm winds stretched the flight range of the dengue mosquito by 63 percent and raised human-mosquito contact by about 30 percent. Modeling two 2014 typhoons tied one to 217 extra cases and the other to 5,131 extra cases, with matching money losses. Stronger mosquito control during one storm was projected to avert nearly 60,000 cases. The authors urge early control guided by storm warnings.
pmc-13268155:
Juliana Ju Yun Hoo and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of how sight and sound shape the restfulness of tropical city green spaces. Most research on restorative places comes from cooler climates. The team gathered 120 stimuli from nature, city, and mixed settings in Malaysia. Eighty-seven participants were assigned to hear sounds only, see images only, or get both, and rated a subset of thirty.

Nature and mixed scenes were generally rated more restful than city scenes. In the sight-only group, mixed scenes, like tree-lined streets, beat pure nature scenes. For nature scenes, sound alone scored about the same as sight alone or both together. The authors suggest small pockets of city nature can restore more than wild forest views, and good nature sounds can stand in when green views are lacking. Planners can use both findings.
pmc-13269155:
Ruitong Liao and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on air chemicals and a blood enzyme in adults in the United States. The chemicals, called volatile organic compounds, come from fuels, paints, and industry. Their traces were measured in urine, and the enzyme LDH was measured in blood.

Data covered 4,907 adults in a national health survey from 2011 to 2018, with 17 chemical traces tested. Several traces were linked to lower LDH, while one was linked to higher levels. Mixed exposure tests also pointed both ways, with different chemicals leading each side. Most links held up in repeat checks. The authors read the pattern as a possible early sign of harm from these chemicals.
pmc-13269555:
Imogen Camp and Nick G Jones published a physics paper in 2026 on matrix-product states, compact formulas that describe quantum systems built in a chain. Certain such formulas are exact ground states, the lowest-energy states, for linked families of system rules. Earlier skeletons of these states were known only for simpler, non-interacting models.

Camp and Jones partly expose such a skeleton in interacting spin chains called chiral clock families. Their states stay dense in the calm regions around a sequence of fixed points. Outside those regions the states remain exact but describe excited, higher-energy levels instead. As an application, they derive a closed formula for a disorder measure in one family of interacting models.
pmc-13270055:
Carmen R B da Silva and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 on heat tolerance in 95 wild bee species across Australia. Nesting habits differ: some bees nest in the ground, some in wood cavities, and some in plant stems. The team tested whether nest microclimate, the small local climate, predicts how heat tolerance evolved.

Stem nesters had evolved the highest heat tolerance, while ground nesters had the lowest, since soil lets them dodge extreme heat. Shared ancestry explained part of the pattern through shared nesting habits. That indicates repeated adaptation rather than a hard evolutionary cap. Adding nesting behavior also changed which species ranked most at risk from climate change.
pmc-13272855:
Manuel Juarez-Garcia leads a 2026 study seeking early signs of difficult-to-manage axial spondyloarthritis, a form of inflammatory spine arthritis. Some patients fail several advanced drugs despite wider treatment choices. The team studied patients starting a first such drug between 2004 and 2019, then built simple decision tree models.

Of 311 patients starting treatment, 101 were analyzed, with 42 classed as difficult to manage and 59 as very good responders. Difficult cases were more often smokers, lacked a key gene marker, and had more tendon pain and other illness. Disease activity at six months, not at baseline, predicted later difficulty. The tree models sorted patients fairly well and held up in an outside registry.
pmc-13273155:
Bradley Langford leads a 2026 survey on bringing careful antibiotic use into Canadian community pharmacies. Community pharmacists are easy to reach and trusted, and their role in prescribing and teaching is growing. The team surveyed the public, pharmacists, and other health workers about barriers and supports for this shift.

Common barriers were lack of support from non-pharmacist providers and from pharmacy leaders. Supports included providers seeing careful use as important, pharmacists acting as teachers, and the chance to save health care costs. The authors say a better grasp of these factors can help design workable, lasting programs in community pharmacies, where formal programs are still uncommon.
pmc-13273555: Correction notice from Stuart Leishman and co-authors. It corrects a 2024 protocol for a lab assay in cultured cells. The assay detects a fat-based protein mark called S-palmitoylation. Two concentration values were misreported in the materials list. One stock should read 32 molar, not 32 millimolar. Another final concentration should read 1.0 millimolar, not 1.0 molar. Step 32 of the method is also corrected to match. The authors apologize for the errors.
pmc-13274155:
Ahmadreza Soroush Fard and co-authors wrote a 2026 review article on using nanomaterials to build better rotavirus vaccines. Rotavirus causes severe watery diarrhea in young children, worst in poorer countries. Today's live oral vaccines work less well there, partly due to malnutrition and damaged gut linings.

The review surveys tiny delivery particles made of fats, polymers, and metals, plus virus-like shells with no live virus inside. Such carriers can shield vaccine parts from the harsh gut, aim them at immune tissue, and stir stronger responses. Designs could work as injections that skip the gut barrier or as sturdy oral doses. The authors see them as a path to lasting protection where current vaccines fall short.
pmc-13274855:
Ingrid Løvold Mostad and colleagues report a 2026 journal article testing whether a famous obesity gene variant changes the fatty makeup of body fat. The FTO variant rs9939609 raises obesity risk, mostly through appetite, but fat metabolism effects were untested in severe obesity. The team biopsied belly and hip fat from ninety-five adults with class two or three obesity and no diabetes.

Participants carried zero, one, or two copies of the risk variant in near-equal thirds. Overall, the variant showed no significant link to any single fatty acid in either depot, a mainly negative result. One subgroup hint in men rested on very small numbers and needs confirmation. Belly fat did prove richer in saturated fats than hip fat, confirming earlier work.
pmc-13275155:
Alizah P Hashmi and Fahad H Khan wrote a 2026 review article on rebuilding the upper inner quadrant of the breast after cancer surgery, an area surgeons nickname 'no man's land.' Defects there show easily, leave little local tissue to borrow, and accept few flap options. The team searched three databases for every published technique and its results.

Only twenty-three articles turned up, fourteen of them original case series, and the largest cohort held just forty-six patients. The commonest fixes were inferior pedicle reductions and round-block lifts, with complication rates under ten percent in all series. Reported cosmetic results varied wildly and inconsistently. The authors lay out a ladder from small reshaping to regional flaps matched to breast size and patient hopes.
pmc-13275555:
Fetriyuna Fetriyuna and colleagues present a 2026 journal article on making cricket protein tastier and more useful for food products. Crickets offer sustainable protein for Indonesia, where acceptance of insect food is low and bitterness is a barrier. The team chopped cricket protein with an enzyme called ProteAX, varying the dose and the chopping time in a full factorial design.

The winning recipe used 1.5 percent enzyme for five hours. It broke down 67.71 percent of the protein while keeping bitterness and aftertaste low and umami, the savory taste, strong. The resulting flour was 69.51 percent protein and dissolved almost completely in water. It also absorbed far more water and oil than before and held emulsions steady across acidity levels, suiting it to processed foods.
pmc-13276355:
Sindy Chavez and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on how a cancer-causing fusion protein organizes itself inside cells. TRK-T3 forms when two unrelated genes fuse, creating a growth switch stuck in the on position. Such fusion proteins often gather into condensates, droplets that concentrate signaling molecules.

The short abstract reports that TRK-T3 forms these droplets inside cells. A water-avoiding segment of the protein drives the gathering. That same segment shapes the droplets' form and drives activation of the MAPK pathway, a central growth signaling route. The work adds to evidence that the physical organization of fusion protein droplets is not decoration. How the droplets are built helps determine how strongly the cancer signal fires, a point the authors develop across the full paper.
pmc-13276455:
Rika Kusumoto-Matsuo and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on how sunlight damage turns into genome instability, a hallmark of melanoma. Ultraviolet light creates two main DNA lesions. One type is usually repaired before cells copy their DNA; the other can linger into the copying phase.

The lingering lesions, called CPDs, sparked double-strand breaks in DNA during replication. The breaks were linked to the repair system that fixes damage in active genes. Where damage in active regions was partly repaired first, breaks decreased. In inactive regions they persisted. Irradiated cells also gained structural changes and single-letter mutations matching the known ultraviolet signature in human melanoma. The authors map a pathway that may explain how sun exposure writes lasting changes into skin cell genomes.
pmc-13276755:
Paula García-Barja and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on which coping habits predict anxiety and depression in healthcare workers. Staff in hospitals face heavy workloads and emotional strain, and their rates of both conditions exceed the general population's. Knowing which strategies help or harm can target support programs.

Seven hundred forty-four doctors, nurses, and nursing assistants completed a cross-sectional survey. Dwelling negatively on oneself was the strongest predictor of both anxiety and depression. Reframing problems positively predicted lower levels of both. Openly expressing emotions predicted slightly higher levels. Surprisingly, avoidant coping predicted lower symptoms in this snapshot. Social support related only to fewer depressive symptoms. Having no family responsibilities also predicted lower distress, and nursing assistants were a higher-risk role.
pmc-13291755:
Mølstrøm and colleagues publish the full analysis plan for a Danish trial in care after cardiac arrest. The arrest took place outside hospital, and all patients were comatose after their hearts restarted. The trial tests four care steps at once in one shared design.

Patients are split at random within three hours of restart. They get a steroid drug or a dummy drug, a calming drug or a dummy drug, a raised or flat backrest, and early or late waking. The plan fixes main outcomes first, such as death by ninety days. It also sets how missing data and clashes between steps will be handled. All main tests follow the group each patient was first placed in.
pmc-13312855:
Scarborough and co-authors adapt an industrial separation technique to harvest exomeres, in this 2026 study. Exomeres are nanoscale particles cells release. They are smaller than the better-known extracellular vesicles and top carriers of RNA. Slow, costly ultracentrifuge isolation has held back study of them. So the team tried tangential flow filtration, skimming fluid across a membrane to sort particles by size.

Filtration gave exomeres matching centrifuge runs in purity. They were rich in RNA-handling proteins, including Argonaute-2 and a heat shock protein. They carried a distinctive microRNA set not abundant in vesicles. A surprise came next: microRNAs inside exomeres survived nuclease enzymes even after protease and detergent treatment that should strip their shield. They seem unusually stable, with maybe long lives in blood. The authors propose filtration as a scalable way to make exomere-based RNA drugs.
pmc-13353355:
Haas and colleagues pooled the evidence in 2026 on whether low fat-free mass, body tissue other than fat, predicts higher death risk in adults living in the community. Single studies disagreed, so the team ran a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies that measured body composition by scan, electrical impedance, or simple measures such as calf size.

From nearly eight thousand records, 49 studies qualified, covering more than a million people and close to 84,000 deaths. People with low fat-free mass had about 42 percent higher death risk than those with high fat-free mass, and the link held across ages, regions, and causes of death. The tie was stronger in men than women, and strongest when calf size was the measure. Checks for bias softened but did not erase the link. The authors urge routine body composition checks to flag high-risk adults.
pmc-13365355:
Jiang and colleagues test whether a food supplement can guard muscle while adults with obesity lose weight. Their powder adds calcium HMB, a body-made compound tied to muscle upkeep, plus extra protein. Adults ate fewer calories for twelve weeks and took the powder or a matched control drink.

In the trial with just over one hundred adults, the supplement group held its muscle mass. The control group lost muscle over the same twelve weeks. The supplement group also lost more belly fat and more total body fat. Its daily energy use held up better, and blood sugar fell a bit more. No side effects were reported in either group.
pmc-13375155:
José M. Alegre and co-authors compare the cell toxicity of resins used for temporary fixed dental prostheses, made either by 3D printing or by milling. Their 2026 laboratory study fabricates 216 standardised discs, half from printed resins and half from milled polymethyl methacrylate resins, and exposes mouse fibroblast cells to them.

Cells met the materials two ways: through liquid extracts of the resins, and by direct contact with the discs, with survival measured after seventy-two hours. In the extract test, milled resins left 87 percent of cells alive against 65 percent for printed resins; in direct contact the figures were 89 percent against 48 percent. Under international thresholds, printed resins rated slightly toxic indirectly and moderately toxic on contact, while milled resins stayed in the non-toxic to slightly toxic range. The authors caution against stretching short laboratory results into clinical claims and call for longer studies.
pmc-13376355:
Suzuki Uemura and colleagues investigate why an emollient oil, ditrimethylolpropane tetracaprylate, keeps skin hydrated after washing, in 2026 cosmetic science research. Emollients moisturize skin, but how deeply an oil penetrates the stratum corneum, the skin's barrier layer, was unclear. The team compared the ester oil against emollients and a sealing benchmark, a surface-sealing agent. They used living-skin assays, uptake studies, and calorimetry on a barrier lipid matrix model, the fatty mortar between skin cells.

In vivo, the oil produced a superior, sustained hydrating effect that survived wash-off, without disrupting barrier function. Permeability analysis confirmed it penetrates and stays inside the stratum corneum, unlike agents that sit on top or wash away. Calorimetry showed it blends into the model lipid matrix with compatibility and minimal structural disruption. Suzuki Uemura concludes the mechanism, penetration plus compatible integration, explains why the effect lasts and offers a rule for better moisturizers.
pmc-13379155:
Arnold and colleagues describe a youth-driven approach to sharing research findings about child farmworkers' health in North Carolina, in 2026 community research. Academic results rarely reach the communities studied. The team therefore partnered with rural youth from Latine farmworker families in a leadership program to design infographics presenting the findings on young workers' health and safety. The paper walks through the development and dissemination process and reflects on lessons from working as partners with the young people.

The youth collaborators shaped the content and the language of the infographics, choosing which findings mattered most to families like theirs and how to phrase risks without jargon. Distribution targeted community settings rather than journals. Arnold argues the process built literacy and leadership in the youth, beyond the products created. The model, they suggest, transfers to topics where affected communities are young, rural, or Spanish-speaking and poorly served by academic publishing.
pmc-13388455:
Couto and colleagues compare three materials as the sensing layer in a glucose biosensor for point-of-care diabetes testing, in 2026 biosensor research. Each candidate, biographene, zinc oxide carbon nanotubes, and bio-derived carbon dots, sat in a polyaniline matrix with the enzyme glucose oxidase on a screen-printed gold electrode. Performance was measured electrically in buffer and in serum spiked with glucose. Microscopy and spectroscopy verified the materials' structure and chemistry before judging the sensors.

The carbon dot sensor performed best, reaching a detection limit of 1.08 millimoles per liter of glucose in the tests. Its sensitivity measured 0.453 microamps per decade of glucose concentration across the range. That range, 1.56 to 75.0 millimoles per liter, spans the blood sugar values of healthy people and patients with diabetes, even dangerous highs. Couto highlights the dots' origin: made from fructose, they keep the sensor cheap and sustainable while improving enzyme hold and charge transfer.
pmc-13389355:
Guang-Hong Chen and co-authors write a physics primer on photon-counting detectors for computed tomography, scanners that count individual X-ray photons and sort them by energy. As these detectors move from laboratories into clinics, their data can be hard to interpret because the signal passes through many physical and electronic steps. Their 2026 primer organises the subject as one causal chain.

The account follows the signal from energy deposited in the detector, through charge creation and transport, signal induction and pulse formation, to final counting in energy thresholds. Along the way it explains how charge sharing between pixels, detector geometry, dead time, pulse pileup, dark current, and contact effects distort spectra, lose counts, and destabilise thresholds at clinical X-ray rates. The authors aim to give medical physicists a rigorous yet practical guide to what governs detector performance.
pmc-13393655:
Kather and colleagues weigh, in a 2026 commentary, whether microscope cameras can widen access to digital pathology. Whole-slide imaging, the gold standard that scans entire tissue slides, demands expensive scanners and infrastructure. Only about 20 percent of pathology laboratories have scanners, and as few as 5 percent use digital workflows for routine diagnostic reporting, the authors note. Cameras mounted on ordinary microscopes offer a cheaper route using equipment labs already own.

Camera images, they argue, can support biomarker assessment and computational analysis, but the approach carries costs in consistency. Hardware varies between setups, image capture depends heavily on the operator, and a camera sees a small field of view, not the whole slide. The authors call for consensus standards covering calibration, validation protocols, quality assurance, and staff training. With those guardrails, camera imaging could bring digital pathology to resource-limited laboratories without sacrificing diagnostic trustworthiness.
pmc-13396455:
Gao and co-authors tackle, in 2026, the twin failure modes of aqueous zinc metal batteries, dendrite growth and corrosion at the zinc electrode, with a shear-thickening electrolyte that stiffens under attack. Their non-Newtonian fluid combines carboxymethyl cellulose with sulfonated silica nanoparticles. The cellulose converts free water into weakly bound water and so starves corrosion reactions. The nanoparticles disrupt the strongly bound water layer at the zinc surface and stiffen locally wherever a dendrite tip presses.

Zinc symmetric cells with it plated and stripped stably for 900 hours at a current of 50 milliamps per square centimeter. Full zinc-iodine pouch cells with 1.5 ampere-hours of capacity stayed stable over 200 cycles at 20 milliamps per square centimeter in tests. Spectroscopy confirmed the water restructuring, with strong hydrogen bonds falling from 34 percent to 31 percent of the total across formulations. The authors pitch the design for practical, safer large-format zinc storage.
pmc-13399155: This is a fix notice for a paper on a fall-detect model. It corrects details in the record. The 2026 Europe PMC entry posts the fix. It keeps science straight. Fixes matter for trust. Records must be right. Science self-corrects. The findings add useful detail for readers today.
pmc-13401155: Gastroenterologists successfully manage incidental colonic pneumatosis intestinalis with pneumoperitoneum using conservative nonoperative ways. pmc-13401555: Innate immunologists find that IRF1-caused cytosolic sensing of oxidized energy-making DNA potently drives swollen macrophage PANoptosis. It a lot explains germs-induced swollen cell death. energy-making DNA becomes dangerously oxidized. IRF1 specifically senses the damage. PANoptosis smoothly executes cell death.
pmc-13402355:
Li and team show, in 2026, that having agency over a story changes how people remember it, using choose-your-own-adventure narratives read under full, partial, or no control. In every condition, events central to the plot, by cause or by meaning, were recalled best. But even when everyone read the identical text, participants whose choices were honored recalled more idiosyncratic combinations of events than passive readers.

Their recall was also less predictable from sentence embeddings, a sign in the data that memory had shifted away from the shared, normative version of the story toward personal organization. Agency further raised the chance that consecutive events were remembered or forgotten together, strengthening local temporal binding in the narrative. Effect sizes for the personalization ran large, with standard differences around 0.6 to 0.8 between conditions in the contrasts. The authors conclude that control over events does not just add motivation; it restructures memory itself.
pmc-13402855: Palliative symptom handling for people with multiple chronic conditions — person-centered. Kim Kuebler, Julian Gallegos, and others address it. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is palliative care planning. It covers person-centered palliative symptom handling in many ills quite and practically.
pmc-13403155: Regulatory scientists conduct peer review of pesticide risk assessment for Trichoderma harzianum. The beneficial biological agent requires thorough safety evaluation. The 2026 Europe PMC paper with care notes the assessment process. It ensures agricultural safety for workers and consumers. Biopesticides need appropriate regulatory oversight. Science-based regulation protects public health effectively.
pmc-13403555: A sickle cell patient developing hydromorphone-induced choreiform dyskinesia — a reversible adverse effect. Sakeena Saife, Michael El Masry, Islam Rajab, and others report the case. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is adverse drug reactions. It shows stopping the opioid stops the involuntary dance.
pmc-13403755: A rare lung problem of spinal sore joints documented. Stefani Larasati and Awalia report interstitial lung disease in ankylosing spondylitis. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is a case report with past studies review. It highlights the tie. Rheumatologists should monitor lungs. Early catching helps. Rare links matter.
pmc-13407455:
Obeidat and co-authors report, in 2026, a fatal case of congenital neuroblastoma that had spread into the placenta. Fewer than 20 placental cases appear in the English-language record. Neuroblastoma ranks as the most common malignant fetal tumor, making up one-third of congenital cancers. Its incidence runs between 1 in 10,000 and 1 in 30,000 live births, usually arising in the adrenal gland.

The 26-year-old mother, in her second pregnancy, carried a fetus with a mass on the right suprarenal gland, severe fluid buildup known as hydrops, and an enlarged placenta. The fetus died in the womb at 26 weeks. Microscopy confirmed metastatic neuroblastoma through fetal organs and, unusually, within the placenta's fetal blood vessels, while the maternal blood spaces were spared, a pattern the authors call unique. romanus-pontifex-1455:

snow-cholera-1855:

Kabir was a fifteenth-century weaver and poet in India whose songs, presented here in English translation, have been sung for five centuries. Against temple and mosque formality, Kabir points to the one God found within. Short, fierce songs mix longing for God with a workman's bluntness about priests, pride, and death. tob-11055:

tob-13455:
The Liezi is one of the classic books of Taoism, named for the sage Lieh Tzu, said to have lived in the fourth century BC. Its chapters mix fable, dialogue, and wonder tales. Chinese tradition ranks it beside the works of Laozi and Zhuangzi.

Beneath the humor sits a steady teaching: let things take their course, hold life lightly, and distrust the busy mind's alarms.
tob-4055:
Anthropogenesis, volume two of the four-volume Secret Doctrine, turns from cosmos to humanity. trollope-warden-1855:
Anthony Trollope published The Warden in 1855, the gentle opening of his Barchester novels of cathedral life. Harding, a kind old clergyman, holds a rich wardenship over twelve bedesmen with a tiny true workload. un-ga-res-1755:

Four months before, the Assembly had affirmed that the British colony was a land not yet self-governing. Since then, the white regime had declared a state of emergency, banned the Zimbabwe African Peoples Union, and jailed the party's leaders. The text calls the state of affairs deplorable, critical, and explosive.

Britain is urged to act at once and with force. The party's president, Joshua Nkomo, and all other jailed or held nationalist leaders must be freed without terms. The ban on the party must be lifted. Britain must also report back to the Assembly on what it has done.
un-ga-res-a-69-55:
Care for the earth belongs in arms deals too, says Resolution A/69/55, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Deals struck at the 1992 world earth summit in Rio count among the guides.

The Assembly takes note of the report of the Secretary-General on the point. Arms cuts, it argues, should not be won at the cost of the soil, air, and water that people live from. Even the grim work of disarmament, in this view, owes a duty to the world it claims to make safer.

General Assembly Resolution 1755 (XVII) was adopted on 12 October 1962. It returned to Southern Rhodesia, weeks after the Assembly had declared it a Non-Self-Governing Territory. The mood had turned grave. A state of emergency was in force. The Zimbabwe African Peoples Union had been banned. Nationalist leaders had been arrested or held.

The Assembly pressed Britain, as a matter of urgency, to free the union's detained president at once. It pressed Britain to free all other nationalist leaders at once and without conditions. It also demanded that the ban on the union be lifted. It asked Britain to report back within the same session on what it had done.

Resolution 69/55 of the General Assembly asks that environmental norms be followed when disarmament and arms control agreements are written and carried out. The Assembly reaffirms that disarmament forums should take relevant environmental standards fully into account in talks. It is mindful of the environmental damage nuclear weapons use would cause. States are called on to apply science and technical progress in security fields without harming the environment or sustainable development. They are called on to report their measures to the Secretary-General.
un-sc-res-1355: Security Council Resolution 1355 survives in the official record, and the catalog dates it to 2001. un-sc-res-1455:
The Al-Qaida and Taliban sanctions were tightened on 17 January 2003. The Council restated the web of texts from 1267 (1999) to 1452 (2002). Every state had to freeze the funds of listed persons and bar their travel and arms. Full account was to be taken of the humanitarian exemptions set out in resolution 1452.

The Council improved the way the asset freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo were to be applied. The changes would be reviewed and improved again within twelve months. The sanctions committee would send the consolidated list to all states at least every three months. Every state had to report to the committee within ninety days on the steps it had taken. Fresh monitoring help was arranged for the committee, with a team of experts to track how states carried the measures out. States had to strengthen their laws to enforce the sanctions.
un-sc-res-1555:
Fighting in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo forced a short renewal in 2004. On 29 July 2004 the Security Council extended MONUC, its Congo mission, until 1 October. North and South Kivu and the Ituri district were the hot spots. The Council backed the Congo's transitional government of national unity. It also welcomed a joint check planned with Rwanda.

The Secretary-General owed a report before 16 August on the mission's work. The Council treated the situation as a threat to peace in the region. The mission kept the powers it held under Chapter VII of the Charter. A longer decision on its future would follow the report.
un-sc-res-1655:
UNIFIL was extended as Blue Line violence simmered on 31 January 2006. Hezbollah had attacked on 21 November 2005, and rockets had been fired into Israel on 27 December. Israel kept violating Lebanese airspace. The Secretary-General's report of 18 January pressed Lebanon to extend its rule over the whole south. The Blue Line had to be respected in full, the Council restated.

The Council endorsed the Secretary-General's report. It extended UNIFIL's mandate until 31 July 2006, while flagging that the force's shape would be reviewed. All acts of violence along the Blue Line were condemned. The parties had to keep the pledges they had made to respect the line and the force's safety. Lebanon's government was called again to extend its authority through the south and hold the sole right to force there. The steps Beirut had begun toward that end were welcomed.
un-sc-res-1755:
Sudan drew a formal Council decision in Resolution 1755, adopted on 30 April 2007. The 2005 peace deal had ended the long north-south civil war, but progress was slow. A separate war in Darfur still raged, and a United Nations mission, UNMIS, watched over the main peace deal.

The text extends the mandate of UNMIS until 31 October 2007. It asks the Secretary-General to name a new envoy for Sudan at once. It urges both sides to build joint army units and finish moving their forces by 9 July 2007. It also presses them to settle the Abyei dispute and prepare national elections on time.

un-sc-res-355:
Cyprus was in crisis in the summer of 1974, weeks after fighting split the island. On 1 August 1974 the Security Council acted on the Secretary-General's statement. It recalled resolution 353, which had demanded a ceasefire and talks. All states, the text notes, had voiced respect for Cyprus's sovereignty and unity. The Secretary-General had just outlined his next steps to the Council.

The resolution asks him to take fitting action in line with that statement. He then had to give the Council a full report. The ceasefire, the Council stressed, was only the first step. Full use of resolution 353 was the real goal. That meant talks toward a lasting settlement for the island.
un-sc-res-455: Number 455 marks this Security Council text in the official record, catalogued here at 1979. un-sc-res-55:
Indonesia's truce was fraying in the summer of 1948. A federal conference had met at Bandung that May. Political talks between the Dutch and the republic had stalled. Trade limits in the islands added to the strain. On 29 July 1948 the Security Council reviewed its good offices committee's reports. Those papers covered the talks, the standstill, and the trade dispute.

The Council calls on both governments to keep the Renville Truce Agreement strictly. That duty covered its military and its economic terms. With the committee's help, both sides had to use the agreed political principles early and in full. Those principles were meant to lead to a settlement. The Dutch offensive that December showed how weak the truce had become.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Foreign armies were still on Congolese soil despite the Lusaka Ceasefire Agreement when this text passed on 15 June 2001. The Council voiced alarm at the war's toll on civilians, including refugees and displaced people, and at rising HIV infection in the east of the country.

Ugandan, Rwandan, and all other foreign forces were again told to leave Congo, and Uganda's stated decision to begin withdrawing was welcomed. All parties were told to avoid attacks while disengagement and withdrawal went forward.

Resolution 1455, adopted unanimously on 17 January 2003, tightens the sanctions net around Al-Qaida and the Taliban. States were told to report within ninety days on what they had actually done to enforce the measures, taking account of humanitarian exemptions agreed the previous month. Cyprus won independence from Britain in August 1960 under a delicate power-sharing deal. Greek and Turkish Cypriots were meant to govern together. The new republic promptly sought a UN seat. Resolution 155 was adopted unanimously on 24 August 1960, just days after independence day.

A UN good offices team watched the deal and filed reports. One told of a trade squeeze. Resolution 55 passed on 29 July 1948 by nine votes to none.

Both sides were told to keep the truce in full. That meant its rules on arms and on goods alike. The twelve Renville points on politics had to be put into force, fast and whole. Six added points came with them. The Soviet bloc held back in the vote. The text shows the Council prodding a colonial power and a new-born republic toward a deal, step by grudging step.

Bosnia and Herzegovina was in far worse shape than its neighbors in spring 1992. It had declared independence from Yugoslavia. War erupted within weeks. Even so, the new state applied for UN membership. Resolution 755, adopted without a vote on 20 May 1992, answered that application.

The Council recommended that the General Assembly admit Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Assembly acted two days later. Membership did not stop the war. But it fixed Bosnia's status as a sovereign state in international law. That status mattered greatly in later debates. Arguments over intervention and borders returned to it again and again.
un-un-res-fourth-report-of-the-secretary:
Spring 2000 was the darkest hour of the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone, and the fourth report of the Secretary-General, document S/2000/455, covers that season. Rebel forces had attacked UN troops and taken hundreds hostage. The mission, UNAMSIL, faced collapse unless help arrived fast.

The report recounts the hostage crisis, rescue efforts, and the state of the ceasefire. It asks for a stronger, larger force with a tougher mandate. Britain's swift military move that May helped save the mission. The report shows the Council learning hard lessons about weak peacekeeping.
vesalius-de-humani-corporis-fabrica-1555:
Andreas Vesalius was a Flemish doctor who studied the human body by cutting open corpses himself, not just by reading old books. His great anatomy work first appeared in 1543. This Latin text is his own revised second edition, published in 1555. No public-domain English translation exists, so the work is presented here in Latin.

Inside, Vesalius describes bones, muscles, nerves, and organs in careful order, correcting many errors copied from Galen for over a thousand years. Detailed woodcut pictures showed the body layer by layer. The book founded modern anatomy because it trusted direct observation over ancient authority. Doctors and artists studied it for centuries.
warsaw-pact-1955:
The Soviet Union and seven Eastern European states signed the Warsaw Pact in May 1955. Its formal title was a treaty of friendship, cooperation, and mutual assistance. Moscow announced it days after West Germany joined NATO, presenting the new bloc as the East's answer to the Western alliance.

Members pledged to aid any member that came under armed attack, and they set up a joint military command under Soviet control. In practice the alliance served as Moscow's tool for holding its satellite states in line. Soviet-led forces used its framework to crush the Hungarian rising of 1956 and the Prague Spring of 1968. The pact dissolved in 1991 as the Cold War ended.
wathen-the-golden-colony-1855:
George Henry Wathen tours a gold mad land in The Golden Colony, his book of 1855. Wathen, a sage of stones, went to Victoria in its gold rush prime. He tells of mines, towns, roads, and the wild new wealth of the place. His eye is keen for both rock and man in a land turned upside down by greed and hope.

Midst the tour stands a rare scrap: a turf out line of a bunyip, cut in the soil at Challicum in late 1854. Wathen gauged it on site. That note is a key source on the beast.
whitman-leaves-of-grass-1855:
Walt Whitman published Leaves of Grass in Brooklyn in 1855, at his own cost. The slim first edition held twelve untitled poems and a bold prose preface. Whitman set the type himself and sent free copies to famed writers of the day.

The long lead poem, later called Song of Myself, praises body and soul alike. Whitman hails grass, labor, cities, and the vast American scene around him. His free verse broke the rules of meter that ruled his age's verse. Emerson praised the book while most critics scorned or ignored its new voice. All later editions of Whitman's life work grew from this seed.
zoist-vol-13-1855:
Volume thirteen of The Zoist, from April 1855 to January 1856, completes the journal's run. Elliotson founded the journal in 1843 and edited all thirteen volumes. Mesmerism and cerebral physiology shared its pages to the end. The final volume carries the usual reports of trance, cure, and somnambulist sight.

With it closes the most important English journal the mesmeric movement ever had. Surgical cases, debates, and wonders stand preserved across the whole set. The mesmerism to hypnotism debate found its archive here. Later ages dismissed much of it, yet the record endures. Readers can now follow the cause from first trumpet to last. Few movements documented themselves so fully.
